course.title: Control Valve Engineering 1
course.summary: An introductory engineering course covering the full control-valve engineering fundamentals scope: loop-behavior framing, body/closure-member selection, flow characteristic and rangeability, shutoff/pressure-temperature standards, actuator force/torque sizing, packing and fugitive-emissions selection, liquid/compressible Cv sizing, installation practice, and the decarbonization context that frames why fugitive-emissions performance matters. Drawn from the Control Valve Handbook and the four industry sourcebooks (Oil & Gas, Power & Severe Service, Refining, Pulp & Paper). See Competency Hierarchy — CVE1, CVE2, CVE3 v3.md.

chapters.title: Control Loop Fundamentals & the Valve's Role as Final Control Element
chapters._source: Enabling Competency `eng.foundations.control-loop-and-final-control-element` — see Curriculum — CVE1.md and Competency Hierarchy — CVE1, CVE2, CVE3 v3.md, Chapter 1. Modules below are STUBS ONLY (status: outline, empty keyConcepts) pending a real Stage 1 arc-cut per module.

modules.title: Feedback Loop & Valve Body Families
modules.stakes: An engineer who can't place the valve inside the loop, or confuses body families, has no foundation for any of this course's later selection decisions.
modules.objective: Frame the control valve as the final control element in a feedback loop — the one component that actually changes the process — and build the sliding-stem vs. rotary body-family vocabulary every later selection decision assumes.

primitives.t: A control loop runs on one skeleton — sensor and transmitter measure the process variable, a controller compares it to setpoint and computes a correction, and a final control element carries that correction into the process — and in the large majority of process plants, that final control element is the control valve: body, trim, actuator, and accessories together, not the body alone. Every calculation this course teaches — Cv, actuator force, packing, standards — only matters because it is sizing and specifying that one block correctly; misidentify what the valve actually is here and no downstream spec catches it.
primitives.templateRationale: One sequential mechanism — a single signal loop with each block needing a name — fits role-mechanism's fig+list shape directly; the source figure already draws its own Manipulated/Controlled Variable arrows around the loop, so no added .tpl-flow-arrow is needed.

primitives.t: Sliding-stem valves throttle by moving a stem in a straight line — actuator on top, then bonnet, then body, with trim inside the body under the bonnet — and the family covers more than one body geometry without changing that core action: the globe body is the baseline, the angle body swaps in perpendicular ports, and the three-way body adds a third connection for combining or diverting flow instead of simple two-port throttling. All three are still 'a sliding-stem valve' for every selection decision later in this course — what varies is port geometry, not the family.

items.t: The globe body — the baseline sliding-stem product, a globe body under a spring-and-diaphragm actuator.
Assembly stack-up, top to bottom: actuator, packing flange and locknut, bonnet, then the body — trim (plug, cage, seat ring) sits inside the body, under the bonnet.
The angle body — inlet and outlet perpendicular instead of straight-through; same sliding-stem action, different port geometry.
The three-way body — a single body with three flow connections, combining or diverting flow rather than simple two-port throttling.

primitives.templateRationale: Four distinct product photos, not parts of one image — composed as a multi-image figure per Style Guide §5.14, each photo carrying its own numbered dot (none are printed-labelled) matched to a 4-entry list; well inside the tp-003 comfortable-capacity ceiling (7). has-wide-fig applies — four photos in a row read as a landscape figure.

primitives.t: Rotary valves throttle by turning a shaft instead of sliding a stem — the same actuator-drives-closure-member relationship, just rotational motion. The family's three closure-member types are the segmented ball, the V-notch ball — contoured with a V-shaped notch specifically for finer throttling and better rangeability than a plain segmented ball — and the eccentric-disk, butterfly-style design.

items.t: The rotary product overview — a butterfly-style body with actuator and positioner mounted, the rotary counterpart to the sliding-stem overview photo.
Segmented ball — a flanged, shaft-mounted ball segment; one of three rotary closure-member types.
V-notch ball — a contoured V-shaped notch cut into the ball, shaped for improved rangeability and throttling control over a plain segmented ball.
Eccentric-disk, butterfly-style — the disk-type closure member rounding out the three rotary types.

primitives.templateRationale: Four distinct product photos, not parts of one image — composed as a multi-image figure per Style Guide §5.14, each photo carrying its own numbered dot (none are printed-labelled) matched to a 4-entry list; well inside the tp-003 comfortable-capacity ceiling (7). has-wide-fig applies — four photos in a row read as a landscape figure.

primitives.t: Side by side: the sliding-stem valve moves a stem in a straight line through the body's ports; the rotary valve turns a shaft to swing its closure member across the flow path. Same job in the loop — final control element — different motion, and that difference is exactly what later drives which family a given service calls for (rangeability, shutoff class, actuator torque versus thrust).

items.t: Sliding-stem — linear stem motion through the body's ports (globe body shown).
Rotary — a turning shaft swings the closure member across the flow path (butterfly-style body shown).

primitives.templateRationale: Exactly two body families to compare — the canonical two-panel contrast shape; reusing the two family-overview photos already shown on slides 6 and 7 anchors the comparison to imagery the learner has already seen rather than introducing new figures at the summary step.

reground.hook: Think of a shower: your hand feels the water get too hot, so it turns the knob to fix it. A process plant does the same thing, just automated and instrumented — and the control valve is the 'hand turning the knob,' the one part that actually reaches out and changes what's happening in the pipe.
reground.bridge: That 'hand' role has a name — final control element — and it comes in exactly two physical flavors: sliding-stem valves that push a stem straight through the flow path, and rotary valves that twist a shaft across it. Every valve specified in this course is one of those two families.
reground.depth:
A feedback control loop keeps a process variable (pressure, flow, level, temperature) inside a required range despite disturbances: a sensor and transmitter measure the variable, a controller compares it to setpoint and computes a correction, and a final control element implements that correction in the process — in the large majority of process plants, that final control element is the control valve, and 'control valve' here means the whole assembly (body, trim, an actuator supplying motive power, and accessories), not the body alone.

Physically, that assembly comes in two families distinguished by how the closure member moves. Sliding-stem valves move a stem in a straight line — actuator on top, then bonnet, then the body, with trim (plug, cage, seat ring) inside the body under the bonnet — and the family covers several body geometries without changing that basic action: the globe body (straight-through ports, the baseline), the angle body (perpendicular ports), and the three-way body (a single body with three connections, for combining or diverting flow rather than simple two-port throttling).

Rotary valves instead turn a shaft to swing a closure member across the flow path, and the family's three closure-member types are the segmented ball, the V-notch ball (a contoured V-shaped notch, shaped specifically for finer throttling and better rangeability than a plain segmented ball), and the eccentric-disk (butterfly-style) design. Both families do the same job in the loop; which one, and which style within it, a given service calls for is exactly the selection question the rest of this course exists to answer.

activities.title: Body Family Sort & Loop Placement
activities.description: Hand each small group a loose set of unlabeled valve photos pulled from the figures just shown — a globe body, an angle body, a segmented-ball rotary, a V-notch-ball rotary, an eccentric-disk rotary. Groups sort each photo into 'sliding-stem' or 'rotary' and name its specific body/closure-member style. Then, using the feedback-loop block diagram from earlier in the module as a job aid, each group picks one sorted valve, places it as the final control element in a simple stated loop (e.g., a tank-level loop), and states in one sentence what physically changes in the process when that valve's stem or shaft moves.
materials: Loose photo set: globe body, angle body, segmented-ball rotary, V-notch-ball rotary, eccentric-disk rotary (Figures 1.2, 1.4, 1.14-1.16)
Feedback-loop block diagram (Figure 1.1) as a job aid

modules.title: Gain, Rangeability, Deadband & Dynamic Response
modules.stakes: Undersizing rangeability, ignoring deadband, or overlooking dynamic response produces a valve that passes a static spec check but cycles or lags in real service — exactly the loop misbehavior Chapter 2 learns to diagnose.
modules.objective: Introduce the four behavior properties — flow characteristic/installed gain, rangeability, deadband/friction, and dynamic response — that determine whether a nominally correct valve actually controls the loop well.

primitives.t: Flow characteristic always has to be qualified as inherent or installed: inherent is the flow-versus-travel relationship measured on a test bench at a fixed, held pressure drop, and valve gain — the local slope of that curve, how much flow changes per increment of travel — is likewise an inherent property of the trim design at that condition. Installed characteristic and installed gain are the same relationships once the valve is in a real loop, where the process itself lets pressure drop across the valve drift as flow, upstream pressure, and downstream demand change. A loop's stability depends on the controller seeing roughly the same installed gain everywhere it operates the valve — a spec built only from the catalog's inherent curve, with no check on how the installed system will actually load it, is the seed of exactly the low-flow and oscillation problems the rest of this module names individually.
primitives.sourceNote: figures: [] in the CVE1 asset-variant registry for this competency (CVH §1.4/§1.5, pp. 26-27, 29-30, is prose, 'not figure-anchored'). cvh-cmp-inherent-characteristics-graph exists in the Source Library and visually anchors this same inherent-vs-installed distinction, but it is registered against ch4's eng.selection.flow-characteristic-and-rangeability.distinguish-inherent-characteristics competency, not this one — noted under Asset-variant gaps rather than borrowed without confirmation.
primitives.templateRationale: Introduces the two-condition contrast (bench/fixed-ΔP vs. installed/varying-ΔP) as a single mechanism, at introductory depth — the full inherent-vs-installed divergence math belongs to ch4's distinguish/predict competencies, not here. No figure is currently registered for this competency; Stage 3 will need an originated two-condition schematic, not a Source Library redraw, pending confirmation (see Asset-variant gaps).

primitives.t: Rangeability is the ratio of a valve's largest usable flow coefficient to its smallest, within the range where the installed characteristic still tracks its stated deviation limit — expressed either as Cv-max ÷ Cv-min or as maximum-to-minimum controllable flow. The Handbook's own reference point: a valve that still controls well out to 100 times its minimum controllable flow carries a rangeability of 100 to 1. Rangeability is a rated property of the trim you can look up on a data sheet — the sizing task is comparing that rating against what the specific loop actually needs, which is the calculation the next slide walks through.
primitives.sourceNote: figures: [] in the CVE1 asset-variant registry for eng.foundations.control-loop-and-final-control-element.calculate-rangeability — the Source Library's own cvh-topic-rangeability entry notes 'No figure anchors this concept at all in this chapter,' prose-only (CVH 6th ed. §1.4, p.27).
primitives.templateRationale: Defines the ratio and the source's own worked reference point before slide 12 turns it into a comparison procedure — a definitional mechanism, not yet the calculation. No figure exists in the registry for this competency; Stage 3 will need an originated ratio/scale graphic illustrating Cv-max:Cv-min rather than a Handbook redraw — flagged under Asset-variant gaps.

primitives.t: Work rangeability as a direct comparison, not an abstract ratio: (1) state the loop's required turndown — the ratio of the largest flow the process will demand to the smallest flow it must still be controlled at; (2) pull the candidate valve's rated rangeability off its data sheet (Cv-max ÷ Cv-min at the stated deviation limit); (3) compare the two directly — the valve's rated rangeability must meet or exceed the loop's required turndown. Using the Handbook's own reference case: a valve rated at 100:1 clears a loop that only ever needs 50:1 turndown, with margin to spare; the same valve fails a loop that needs 150:1 turndown, because 100:1 caps how far down it can still resolve flow accurately, regardless of what the process asks for.
primitives.sourceNote: figures: [] in the CVE1 asset-variant registry for eng.foundations.control-loop-and-final-control-element.calculate-rangeability — the Source Library's own cvh-topic-rangeability entry notes 'No figure anchors this concept at all in this chapter,' prose-only (CVH 6th ed. §1.4, p.27).
primitives.templateRationale: Three-step comparison procedure, not a photographed physical sequence — list+single-diagram (procedure-image) fits better than procedure-callout, since there is no physical figure to mark up with leader lines. No figure exists in the registry for this competency; the supporting diagram will need to be an originated worked-comparison graphic (Cv-max:Cv-min against required turndown), not a Handbook redraw — flagged under Asset-variant gaps. This is also the worked model the module's own activity (cve1-ch1-m2-act1) has the class repeat with new numbers immediately after the caution slide.

primitives.t: If a valve's rated rangeability doesn't clear the loop's required turndown, it cannot resolve flow changes once demand drops below the bottom of its usable range — **the loop hunts, cycles, or loses control at low flow, and no amount of controller retuning fixes a valve that is mechanically incapable of resolving that flow.** This is a specification failure, not an operating one: it passes every static check — correct Cv at design flow, correct pressure class — and still fails the loop the moment demand turns down.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure in the registry for this competency (see the rangeability sourceNote on slides 11/12); not a gap here specifically, since the caution card's photo is optional (Template Gallery caution-09.html) and the card carries the consequence sentence alone.
primitives.templateRationale: Single caution consequence sentence with the failure clause bolded, per Style Guide §8.3/§4.4 — no figure needed, matching the caution role's own Axis-3 treatment directly. Recorded as `slide--tmpl-caution`, not `slide--role-caution`: gallery.css §7 documents Template 6 (`.slide--tmpl-caution`, already in emerson-workbench.css) as the caution role's real master template — it was not redesigned into the gallery's `.slide--role-*` naming, and no `.slide--role-caution` class exists anywhere in the CSS. This matches the class Control Valve Basics' own caution slide already uses in production.

primitives.t: Deadband is the range an input signal can be reversed through before any observable change shows up in the output — for a valve assembly, controller output is the input and process variable is the output, and Figure 1.18's open loop is exactly that gap made visible: reverse direction anywhere on the plot and the process variable doesn't move again until the loop has crossed the whole deadband width. Two real mechanisms produce it: backlash — slack or looseness in a mechanical connection — and, more often, static friction (stiction): the force that has to be overcome before there is any relative motion at all between two surfaces in the assembly. A spec that never asks how much stiction a packing/trim combination carries is specifying a number that ignores the mechanism most likely to produce it.
primitives.templateRationale: Direct use of cvh-cmp-deadband-graph (CVH Fig. 1.18) per Style Guide §5.4 — a genuine single-series case (one hysteresis loop, no line labels/key in the source), the same figure and direct-use call CVB's cvb-017 already made; keyed here to the causal mechanism (backlash/stiction) rather than CVB's flatter loop-reading list, since this course's audience and level go one step past 'what the loop shows' into 'what produces it.'

primitives.t: Deadband has two distinct mechanical causes, not one: backlash is slack or looseness in a mechanical connection — a linkage, a coupling, a loose stem connector — that lets the input reverse through some travel before it engages the next part in the chain. Static friction (stiction) is different: it is the force that must be overcome before there is any relative motion at all between two surfaces in the assembly, most often at the packing or seating surfaces, and it is the more common of the two causes in a valve assembly. Once stiction is overcome, dynamic (running) friction — a smaller force — is what sustains the motion; a packing selected against a running-friction spec alone can still deadband badly on stiction it was never checked against.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure backs either cause in the registry (figures: [cvh-cmp-deadband-graph] anchors the deadband plot itself, already used directly on slide 14 — it does not distinguish backlash from stiction). Both panels are text/diagram content for Stage 3 to compose, not photographed parts.
primitives.templateRationale: The source names exactly two mechanical causes of deadband — backlash and static friction — a genuine two-way pairing, not a spectrum, so contrast is the correct role. Neither cause has a registered figure; flagged under Asset-variant gaps as needing either an originated two-panel diagram or a plain comparison-table treatment (Axis 3 names both as valid contrast shapes).

primitives.t: A valve assembly's speed of response is measured as a timeline, not a single number: dead time (Td) is the interval after a step change in signal before any response is detectable at all; the time constant is measured from that first detectable response until the output reaches 63% of its final steady-state value; T63 is the two added together, and 'response time' as usually quoted for a valve assembly includes both — the entire assembly's dead time plus its time constant, not the trim alone. A loop tuned against a response-time number that only reflects the actuator, with the positioner's own dead time left out, is tuned against the wrong number.
primitives.sourceNote: figures: [] in the registry for this competency — the Source Library's own cvh-topic-dynamic-response-characteristics entry notes 'No figure anchors any of this content' (CVH 6th ed. §1.5, pp. 28-29, 31, prose-only).
primitives.templateRationale: A sequential timeline (step input → dead time → first detectable response → time constant → 63% point) is the mechanism role's core shape; a step-response curve with Td and the 63% point marked is the standard control-engineering visualization of exactly this timeline. No figure exists in the registry (topics-only, prose-only per the Source Library's own note); Stage 3 will need to originate a standard step-response diagram, not a Handbook redraw — flagged under Asset-variant gaps, human confirmation needed before authoring.

primitives.t: First-order and second-order response are not a matter of degree — they are different physical behavior. A first-order system has only one energy-storage element and responds with a single smooth exponential curve toward its new value, never overshooting. A second-order system has two energy-storage elements that exchange energy back and forth — kinetic and potential — which is exactly what makes overshoot and oscillation possible before the output settles; a valve assembly with enough moving mass and enough spring/diaphragm compliance can behave as second-order even though nothing about it looks obviously different from a slower first-order actuator. Specifying against a first-order assumption on an assembly that actually behaves second-order is how a loop that looked stable on paper turns out to ring in the field.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure exists for either state in the registry (see slide 16's sourceNote). Recommend the safer default: a plain comparison table (energy-storage-element count / response shape / overshoot risk) rather than an originated response-curve sketch for each panel, per Axis 3's own 'figure row or comparison table' allowance for contrast.
primitives.templateRationale: A genuine two-category physical contrast (one energy-storage element vs. two), not a spectrum — contrast is correct. No figures exist for either state; comparison-table format (property rows) is the safer default over an originated curve sketch — flagged under Asset-variant gaps.

activities.title: Rangeability Turndown Check
activities.description: In pairs, work two real-numbers scenario cards: each states a service's required turndown (max-flow-to-min-controllable-flow) and a candidate valve's published rangeability rating — one card where the rated rangeability clears the requirement, one where it falls short. Using the ratio just taught, each pair calculates the required rangeability from the stated turndown, compares it against the candidate valve's rated rangeability, and states in one sentence what happens at low flow on the card where the requirement is not met. Debrief contrasts the passing and failing cards side by side so the class sees both outcomes, not just a single worked answer.
materials: Two scenario cards, each with a stated turndown requirement and a candidate valve's published rangeability rating (one passing, one failing)
activities.sourceNote: Rangeability ratio, turndown framing, and the source's own '100 to 1' worked example are drawn directly from cvh-topic-rangeability (Control Valve Handbook, 6th ed., §1.4, p.27); the low-flow consequence applied on the failing card is the same one just taught on the preceding caution slide — a live calculation using what was just defined, no invented mechanism or unsourced performance claim.

reground.hook: A shower valve that's perfectly smooth from half-open to fully-open, but where the first quarter-turn off 'closed' does almost nothing and then a hair's-width twist suddenly scalds you — that valve is 'correct' in the sense that it passes the right amount of water and fits the pipe, and it is still miserable to actually use. Everything in this module is the difference between a valve that merely CAN pass the right flow and one that can be CONTROLLED smoothly across its whole working range.
reground.bridge: The quarter-turn that does nothing, then does too much, is flow characteristic and gain drifting between the bench-tested (inherent) curve and how the valve actually behaves once it's installed. How far down you can throttle before you run out of usable turns — before the shower stops responding to anything finer — is rangeability, and undersizing it is a spec failure the loop only discovers at low flow. The play in the handle before it does anything at all — backlash in the linkage, or stiction that has to be broken loose — is deadband. And how quickly the shower actually reacts once you do turn it — a beat before anything happens, then a smooth glide or an overshoot-and-settle — is dynamic response: dead time, time constant, and whether the assembly behaves as one energy-storage element or two.
reground.depth:
Inherent flow characteristic and inherent valve gain are measured on a test bench at fixed ΔP; installed characteristic and installed gain are the same relationships once the loop's own varying ΔP is allowed to act on the valve, and loop stability depends on installed gain staying roughly constant across the operating range — a spec built only from the inherent curve ignores exactly the condition the valve will actually operate under.

Rangeability is Cv-max ÷ Cv-min (or max-to-min controllable flow) within a stated deviation limit — the Handbook's own reference case is 100:1 — and the sizing task is comparing a candidate's rated rangeability against the loop's required turndown; undersized rangeability produces hunting or lost control at low flow that no controller retuning can fix, because the valve is mechanically incapable of resolving that flow.

Deadband is the range an input can reverse through before the output visibly moves, caused by backlash (mechanical slack) or, more often, static friction/stiction (the force overcome before any relative motion begins) — distinct from dynamic/running friction, which only sustains motion already started, and distinct from hysteresis, a separately measured quantity.

Dynamic response decomposes into dead time (Td, before any response is detectable), time constant (to 63% of final value), and T63 (their sum, what 'response time' usually means for the whole assembly, not the trim alone); a first-order assembly (one energy-storage element) responds as a smooth exponential with no overshoot, while a second-order assembly (two energy-storage elements exchanging kinetic and potential energy) can oscillate and overshoot — specifying against a first-order assumption on an assembly that actually behaves second-order is how a loop that looked stable on paper rings in the field.

chapters.title: Process Variability, Loop Performance & Valve Diagnostics
chapters._source: Enabling Competency `eng.foundations.process-variability-and-loop-performance` — see Curriculum — CVE1.md and Competency Hierarchy — CVE1, CVE2, CVE3 v3.md, Chapter 2. Modules below are STUBS ONLY (status: outline, empty keyConcepts) pending a real Stage 1 arc-cut per module.

modules.title: Reading Variability & Its Cost
modules.stakes: Plants pay for excess variability directly (off-spec product, energy loss, safety-margin erosion) — an engineer who can't read a variability trend as a cost has no case for fixing it.
modules.objective: Interpret process-variability distributions and connect variability directly to loop economics, and explain how oversizing distorts a valve's installed characteristic and gain.

primitives.t: Process variability is the ±2σ spread of a process variable around its set point under normal-cause variation — a tighter (smaller) spread lets the set point sit closer to a hard product-quality limit without producing off-spec material, while a wider spread forces the set point back from that limit as a safety margin, wasting product/energy on unnecessarily conservative operation. Extensive control-loop studies find up to 80% of real loops fail to adequately reduce this variability, and the control valve assembly — valve, actuator, and positioner considered together, not specified as separate parts — is a frequent, often-overlooked contributor to that failure rate.
primitives.templateRationale: Direct use of CVH's own distribution figure (two stacked bell-curve plots, same setpoint, different spread) — the visual definition of variability itself, so mechanism is the correct role for an introductory understand-level concept with a ready-made schematic. The figure's two distributions are keyed as a two-entry swatch key (wide/high-variability vs. narrow/tight-controlled) per Style Guide §5.3, not numbered features — there is nothing to mark as a point event.

primitives.t: A closed-loop test plots measured process variability against closed-loop time constant against two reference lines — 'Manual' (variability with no control attempted at all) and 'Minimum Variability' (the calculated ideal for a perfectly linear valve assembly) — and every real valve design falls somewhere between them, meaning valves that meet the same static purchase spec do not perform the same dynamically. The Handbook's own worked case makes this a real economic argument rather than an abstract quality claim: swapping a lower-performing valve for a higher-performing one at the same 2.0-second tuning yields a measured 1.4% variability improvement — a number that converts directly into reduced scrap, rework, and off-spec product cost.
primitives.templateRationale: Analytical graph (process variability vs. closed-loop time constant, three valve curves against a minimum-variability reference) plus a stated quantified takeaway is the canonical application-role shape — chart, key, and takeaway (Style Guide §5.10). Key carries swatches for Valve A/B/C plus the minimum-variability reference line (§5.3); the 2.0s / 1.4% comparison is the takeaway line rather than a numbered plot feature, since it names a relationship between two labeled series, not one plotted point. This is also the source data the module's own activity (cve1-ch2-m1-act1) has the class read and then extend.

primitives.t: Oversizing degrades installed gain two distinct ways, not one: it concentrates too much of the loop's total gain in the valve itself, crowding out the controller's own share — best dynamic performance comes from most of the loop's gain living in the controller, not the valve — and because an oversized valve produces a disproportionately large flow change per unit of travel, it spends more of its operating life at low openings, where seal friction (especially on rotary trim) is already worse, so the resulting friction/deadband penalty on process variability gets exaggerated rather than merely present. The net effect, regardless of the valve's nominal inherent characteristic: a badly oversized valve behaves like a quick-opening valve at low lift (high, hard-to-control gain) and goes nearly flat at high travel (too little gain to control anything) — its genuinely usable control range narrows to a fraction of its total travel.
primitives.templateRationale: Develops, not re-derives, the characteristic/gain relationship cve1-ch1-m2 already introduced generally (that module's own registry has no figure; this one does) — this concept is the oversizing-specific distortion of that same installed-gain-vs-travel curve, so CVH's own paired installed-characteristic/installed-gain graph (Fig. 2.5) is the direct figure fit. Key carries the two stacked series (characteristic, gain) per §5.3, terser than a from-scratch mechanism explanation since ch1-m2 already established what installed characteristic and gain mean.

primitives.t: Body style changes how badly oversizing narrows the usable control range: a globe valve holds a controllable installed gain across a wider share of its travel than a butterfly valve does for the same duty — which is exactly why high-capacity rotary designs, the styles most often selected at line size rather than sized to the process, are also the styles most exposed to the low-lift, high-friction distortion the oversizing mechanism produces. Specifying a rotary valve at line size without checking its actual control-range fraction against the loop's real turndown carries this narrowed-range risk silently, since the valve still meets every static spec check.
primitives.templateRationale: CVH's own Figure 2.6 is already a genuine two-panel this-vs-that pairing (butterfly vs. globe installed-gain/control-range) — the exact two-tpl-panel shape the contrast role expects, one source figure serving both panels (no `items` needed, single source). Ties the develops-stage oversizing content to a concrete body-style consequence rather than restating ch1-m2's general characteristic/gain mechanism or slide 21's general oversizing mechanism.

activities.title: Read the Economics, Then Predict the Oversized Valve's Curve
activities.description: Working in pairs from the real closed-loop random-load-disturbance chart just shown (Valve A/B/C on 4" valves tested at 600 gpm, process variability %2sigma/mu vs. closed-loop time constant, with the 'Manual' and 'Minimum Variability' reference lines): first, each pair reads off and states the real quantified economic result the chapter draws from it — replacing Valve B with Valve A at a 2.0s time constant yields a 1.4% variability improvement — and states in one sentence what that percentage would mean in scrap/rework/off-spec cost terms for a stated hypothetical product spec. Second, each pair is given a short scenario describing a badly oversized line-size rotary valve on a service needing only a fraction of its rated Cv, and must predict, using the two named oversizing mechanisms just taught (too much gain concentrated in the valve versus the controller; friction/deadband exaggerated at the low openings an oversized valve is forced to operate at), whether that valve's curve on this same chart would track closer to Valve A or Valve C, and justify the prediction in terms of both mechanisms, not just one. Debrief contrasts pairs' predictions and reasoning before revealing the source's own verdict.
materials: Closed-loop random-load-disturbance chart (Figure 2.7) from the slide just shown
Short written oversized-valve scenario card (one per pair)
activities.sourceNote: The economic read-off and its real numbers are drawn directly from cvh-topic-closed-loop-economics / cvh-cmp-closed-loop-disturbance-summary (Control Valve Handbook 6th ed. §2.1.6, Figure 2.7, p.49) — no invented data. The oversized-valve prediction applies the two real mechanisms from cvh-topic-valve-oversizing-effects (Control Valve Handbook 6th ed., pp. 46-49) to a stated scenario, a live application of what was just taught, not a new unsourced claim.

reground.hook: Cruise control that hunts up and down 5 mph around your target burns more gas and wears the system out faster than one that holds steady within half a mile per hour — even though both are technically 'controlling' the same speed. Now imagine that same cruise control's pedal is a truck's throttle bolted into a compact car: the smallest press near idle lurches the car forward, and the last half of the pedal's travel does almost nothing at all.
reground.bridge: The wide-swing-near-idle, dead-near-the-floor throttle problem is exactly what an oversized control valve does to its own installed-gain curve — too much of the loop's total gain concentrated in the valve rather than the controller, and worse seal friction at the low openings an oversized valve is forced to live at. That's why the ±2σ process-variability band this module opens with gets wider, not narrower, even though the oversized valve technically 'passes the right flow' at its rated capacity and clears every static spec check.
reground.depth:
Process variability is the ±2σ spread of a process variable around its set point under normal-cause variation; tighter control lets the set point sit closer to a hard quality limit without producing off-spec product, and up to 80% of real loops fail to reduce it adequately, with the control valve assembly (valve + actuator + positioner as a unit) a frequent, overlooked cause. The economic argument is not abstract — CVH's own closed-loop test data quantifies it: swapping a lower-performing valve for a better one at the same 2.0-second tuning yields a measured 1.4% variability improvement, which converts directly into reduced scrap/rework/off-spec cost.

Oversizing damages that same variability two ways: it puts too much of the loop's total gain into the valve rather than the controller, and it forces the valve to spend more of its life at low openings where seal friction (especially on rotary trim) is worse, exaggerating the resulting friction/deadband penalty. Independent of its nominal inherent characteristic, a badly oversized valve ends up behaving like a quick-opening valve at low lift (too much, hard-to-control gain) and goes nearly flat at high travel (too little gain to control anything) — narrowing its genuinely usable control range to a fraction of total travel.

Body style compounds this: globe valves hold controllable installed gain over a wider share of travel than butterfly valves for the same duty, which is exactly why high-capacity rotary designs — the styles most often picked at line size rather than sized to the process — are the ones most exposed to this narrowed-range failure.

modules.title: Diagnosing Valve-Level Causes
modules.stakes: An engineer who can't connect a variability trend to a specific valve-level cause chases tuning indefinitely instead of fixing the real problem.
modules.objective: Distinguish deadband from response time, describe performance-test-loop setup and signature-series testing, and interpret a signature-data overlay or ValveLink screen to identify a degraded valve.

primitives.t: The trend chart from the last module put a real cost on process variability — but a variability trend alone doesn't say why the valve is misbehaving. Is it dragging its heels before it moves at all, or moving too slowly once it starts? Deadband and response time look identical on a strip chart and call for two completely different fixes.
primitives.sourceNote: Prime opens on the stakes question rather than a figure — cvh-cmp-valve-response-time-summary-table is reserved for slide 188's contrast, where the real distinguishing data lives. The module's own stakes line ("An engineer who can't connect a variability trend to a specific valve-level cause chases tuning indefinitely instead of fixing the real problem") is the source for this framing, continuing directly from cve1-ch2-m1's own variability/economics content.
primitives.templateRationale: A stakes-framing question before any mechanism is shown, per Axis 3's prime role and the gallery's own PRIME comment — opens the module on the diagnostic tension (deadband vs. response time) rather than restating either mechanism, which cve1-ch1-m2 (pages 14-17, buildsOn) already covered at the general level.

primitives.t: Dead time (Td) and total response time (T63) are two different numbers for the same valve, and the real Valve Response Time Summary data shows them moving independently across tested assemblies — Valve A holds both small and close together across every step size and direction (2%, 5%, 10%, opening and closing); Valve B and C's dead time balloons on the smallest 2% step, and Valve C doesn't respond at all on a -2% closing step (recorded NR). A valve can fail on dead time — the deadband-driven delay before it moves at all — independently of how it behaves once it is moving, which is what T63 actually measures; reading which one is large is what tells you whether the fix belongs at the packing/linkage (deadband) or the positioner/actuator sizing (dynamic time).
primitives.sourceNote: Figure 2.4 verified directly against the real PDF (p. 41): three valve/actuator/positioner assemblies (A/B/C) tested at 2%, 5%, and 10% step sizes in both directions, reporting Td and T63 in seconds, with Valve C's -2% closing step recorded as 'NR' (no response) — confirms the table shows dead time and total response time as genuinely independent numbers, which is the distinguishing claim this slide rests on. Deliberately terser than cve1-ch1-m2 pages 14-17 (buildsOn) on what backlash/stiction and dead time/dynamic time individually are — this slide reads a real dataset rather than re-deriving those mechanisms.
primitives.templateRationale: The source's own Figure 2.4 is a multi-row data grid (three valves x three step sizes x two directions x two time metrics) that does not reduce to a two-panel comparison — a table treatment is the correct contrast shape (Axis 3 names 'a comparison table' as a valid option), reusing the real source figure directly per Style Guide §5.8 rather than compressing it into an artificial two-panel split.

primitives.t: This is Fisher's own performance test loop — a real closed-loop flow-test rig, not a simulation: a piping loop circulating process fluid through a motor-driven pump, the control valve assembly under test mounted in the line, and instrumentation reading flow and valve position throughout the loop. Every dynamic-performance number this chapter has cited so far — deadband, response time, installed gain, the closed-loop economics data — comes out of a rig built exactly like this one, not a calculation.
primitives.sourceNote: Figure 2.2 (p. 36) verified against the rendered page: two large process vessels, a grey piping loop, and motor-driven pump packages, with instrumentation mounted along the line. No native printed labels appear on the photo itself (confirmed both by the Source Library catalog note and by direct inspection), so this slot names the equipment categories the photo and the surrounding §2.2 text actually support (piping loop, pump drive, valve under test, instrumentation) — no specific instrument model or reading is claimed that isn't visible; Stage 3 places its own numbered markers per Style Guide §6.0/§6.1.
primitives.templateRationale: A labelled-parts figure of physical equipment is the nomenclature role's default treatment (Axis 3). The source photo carries no native labels, so this is the numbered-marker case (Style Guide §6.1), not the has-its-own-field-labels exception (§6.3) — Stage 3 places markers against real photo coordinates per §6.0's manifest discipline; this slot supplies the plain-language gloss for each equipment category, not exact marker placement.

primitives.t: Signature Series testing runs in three increasing tiers: Series 1 records the baseline — instrument configuration, a 50%-travel status check, the valve spec sheet, and the valve's own signature, dynamic error-band curve, and drive signal, all swept from -5% to 105% input. Series 2 adds a performance step test and expands the status check to 0/25/50/75/100% travel. Series 3 lets the user specify custom Series 1/2 tests with adjustable end points and scan times for a specific application. Once a FIELDVUE-equipped valve is in service, the same tests are re-run through ValveLink and compared against this factory baseline — Data Comparison — to catch developing problems before they show up as a loop complaint.
primitives.sourceNote: Verified against the rendered page (p. 50): a technician running a live Signature Series test on a green-bodied Fisher valve/actuator with a FIELDVUE digital valve controller, laptop running ValveLink — matches the Source Library's own catalog note on the caption/content mismatch (this figure's printed caption duplicates Figure 2.6's, but the photo itself is unambiguously the Signature Series test). Series 1/2/3 contents and the Data Comparison mechanism are transcribed from cvh-topic-signature-series-testing (CVH §2.3-2.3.3, pp. 50-51) verbatim against the real page text.
primitives.templateRationale: An ordered tiered sequence (Series 1 -> 2 -> 3, then Data Comparison) paired with the one real photo of the test physically being run — procedure-image's shape (list + supporting image) fits, not procedure-list (that variant is for a sequence with nothing to photograph, which doesn't apply here) or procedure-worked (no calculation).

primitives.t: The Data Comparison overlay plots two signature traces on the same axes for the same valve: the original factory-baseline trace and a new trace recorded once the valve is in service. Where the current trace's span — the width of the error band between its up-stroke and down-stroke lines — has visibly widened relative to the original baseline, that widening is the diagnostic signal: increased span indicates increased friction. The overlay itself, not a single number, is the diagnostic — degradation shows up as a shape change against the valve's own factory-recorded history.
primitives.sourceNote: Verified against the rendered page (p. 51, Figure 2.9): two overlaid signature traces with 'FAIL' marked at the top and callout boxes reading 'ORIGINAL TEST,' 'NEW TEST,' and 'INCREASED SPAN INDICATES INCREASED FRICTION.' This competency carries topics: [] in the registry (figures-only, confirmed) — the claim above states only what the figure's own callouts support, with no additional cvh-topic-signature-series-testing claims pulled in beyond what slide 190 (a different competency, topics-backed) already established.
primitives.templateRationale: How a signature overlay reveals degradation is a mechanism explanation (Axis 3: 'how it works'), directly keyed to the figure's own two-trace overlay and its own callouts — no interpretation beyond what those callouts state, per the figures-only sourcing for this competency.

primitives.t: A real ValveLink screen splits this diagnostic work into two windows: Total Scan, which holds the signature graph itself — the same kind of original-vs-new overlay just described, now inside the live software rather than a printed figure — and Valve Step Response, which runs and plots a step test instead of a full signature sweep. Reading a real screen means identifying which window you're in before reading anything off the plot: a widened span on the Total Scan graph is the friction signal just described; a trace on the Valve Step Response window is a different test entirely, checking how the valve moves rather than comparing it against a baseline signature.
primitives.sourceNote: Verified against the rendered page (p. 51, Figure 2.10): two side-by-side screenshots, a 'Total Scan' window showing a signature graph and a 'Valve Step Response' window showing a step-test graph. This competency carries topics: [] in the registry (figures-only) — the claim above names only these two windows and what each contains; it does not assert Total Scan is literally running slide 191's exact comparison, only that both show the same category of signature data inside the real software interface.
primitives.templateRationale: The mechanism (signature-overlay diagnosis) applied to a real piece of software the class will actually use — Axis 3's application default (a concrete case), not application-pick (nothing here is a menu of named items to choose among) or a decision table (no comparison being tabulated).

primitives.t: Once a signature overlay has traced a symptom to the valve assembly itself, retuning the controller does not fix it — **the fault is mechanical, and no amount of controller tuning changes a widened signature span.**
primitives.sourceNote: No new figure for the caution card, matching the caution role's own optional-photo treatment (Style Guide §4.4). This is the direct pedagogical consequence of what slides 191-192 just established (a signature overlay identifies a valve-level cause), and the module's own activity (cve1-ch2-m2-act1) already sets up exactly this retune-vs-repair contrast — not a new claim from cvh-topic-signature-series-testing, whose Data Comparison mechanism (cited on slide 190, a different, topics-backed competency) says nothing itself about controller tuning. Flagged under Wording I'm unsure of.

Recorded as slide--tmpl-caution, not slide--role-caution: no such class exists in the CSS (gallery.css documents Template 6 as the caution role's real master template).

activities.title: Deadband, Response Time, or Both — Read the Signature, Name the Fix
activities.description: In pairs, work a short scenario card describing a loop that is hunting at low flow: a stated controller-output trace plus a plain description of the valve's signature-test overlay (the as-found sweep sitting outside the healthy baseline band on one specific portion of the trace). First, using the module's own summary table, each pair states whether the described symptom pattern points to deadband, slow dynamic response, or genuinely both, and justifies the call from the trace description alone. Second, each pair states what a real ValveLink signature-comparison screen showing that same deviation would look like next to the healthy baseline, and names the one wrong 'fix' the scenario is designed to tempt (retuning the controller) versus the right one (address the valve-level cause the signature just identified). Debrief contrasts pairs' calls and reasoning before revealing the source's own verdict on the scenario.
materials: Scenario card: controller-output trace description + signature-test overlay description (one per pair)
activities.sourceNote: The deadband-vs-response-time distinction is the module's own summary-table concept (cvh-topic-deadband, cvh-topic-valve-response-time, cvh-cmp-valve-response-time-summary-table); the signature-overlay reading and the retune-vs-repair contrast apply cvh-topic-signature-series-testing and cvh-cmp-signature-data-comparison-overlay / cvh-cmp-valvelink-software-screens to a stated scenario — a live application of what was just taught, not a new unsourced claim.

reground.hook: Your car's brake pedal has a little play before it bites, and once it bites, the car still takes a beat to actually slow down. Those are two completely different problems — a pedal with too much free play before anything engages, and brakes that grab fine but respond sluggishly once they do — and a mechanic who can't tell them apart just keeps bleeding the brake lines when the real problem is worn pads, or the other way around.
reground.bridge: The play before the pedal bites is deadband — the input has to travel through a dead zone before anything downstream moves at all. How long the car actually takes to respond once the brakes do grab is response time — a beat of nothing (dead time), then however long the rest of the system takes to finish reacting. Telling those two apart matters because they point at different fixes, and the way you actually find out which one you have on a real valve is the same way a mechanic uses a shop's test bench: run it, compare it to how it worked when new, and read exactly where the difference shows up.
reground.depth:
Deadband and response time are separate diagnostic categories, not two names for the same 'sluggish valve' symptom, and the real Valve Response Time Summary data (Figure 2.4) proves it: dead time (Td, the deadband-driven delay before the assembly moves at all) and T63 (total response time to 63% of the commanded change — dead time plus dynamic time) vary independently across real tested valve/actuator/positioner combinations. One assembly holds both small and consistent across every step size and direction; another balloons on the smallest step, and one recorded case fails to respond at all on a small closing step. Diagnosing which one is present — rather than treating both as 'the valve is bad' — determines whether the fix belongs at the packing/linkage (deadband) or the positioner/actuator sizing (dynamic time).

The tool that generates the real data behind this distinction is Fisher's own performance test loop, a physical closed-loop flow-test rig, not a simulation; and once a valve ships, ValveLink Software's Signature Series testing extends the same discipline into the field: three increasing test tiers (Series 1's baseline signature/error-band/drive-signal sweep, Series 2's added step test, Series 3's user-customized version) create a factory benchmark that can be re-run in service and compared against the original via Data Comparison.

A signature-data overlay makes degradation visible as a shape change against the valve's own history — a widened span between the original and new traces indicates increased friction — and the same comparison appears inside the real ValveLink software as the Total Scan (signature) and Valve Step Response (step-test) windows.

The diagnostic payoff is the caution this module closes on: once an overlay has traced a symptom to the valve assembly itself, retuning the controller does not fix it, because the fault is mechanical.

chapters.title: Valve Body & Closure-Member Type Selection
chapters._source: Enabling Competency `eng.selection.valve-body-and-type-taxonomy` — see Curriculum — CVE1.md and Competency Hierarchy — CVE1, CVE2, CVE3 v3.md, Chapter 3. Modules below are STUBS ONLY (status: outline, empty keyConcepts) pending a real Stage 1 arc-cut per module.

modules.title: Body Family Taxonomy
modules.stakes: Picking the wrong body family locks in downstream limitations no trim or actuator engineering can fix later.
modules.objective: Classify a control valve's body family — globe, angle, three-way, rotary, gate, diaphragm, pinch, plug — from its own construction, building the vocabulary every later chapter assumes.

primitives.t: The double-ported shutoff ceiling is a practical selection consequence, not a footnote: because it can't reach the tightest metal-to-metal shutoff classes, double-ported bodies get reserved for less demanding shutoff duty, and a single-ported or soft-seated design gets specified instead whenever Class IV-VI shutoff is actually required.

items.t: Single-ported, post-guided construction — the default globe body for NPS 1-4 (DN 20-100) process service. Presents the full unbalanced port area to the actuator unless cage/retainer trim balances it, a direct actuator-sizing spec input.

Double-ported (reverse-acting) construction opens one port while closing the other, balancing dynamic plug force enough to permit a smaller actuator for the same capacity. Metal-to-metal seating tops out at Class II shutoff (Class III possible), and the industry has largely moved away from this design — specify it only where viscous or contaminant-laden service still justifies the tradeoff.

primitives.templateRationale: Two related globe constructions taught by how port count changes actuator-thrust demand — the default 'how it works' treatment for an understand/mechanism concept, laid out as a wide two-image comparison rather than a keyed list.

primitives.t: Angle and three-way bodies are both globe-family variants distinguished by piping geometry rather than plug/port count: angle replaces an elbow, three-way adds a third connection for converging or diverging flow.

items.t: Angle body — a single-port, cage-style construction that doubles as a pipe elbow. Specify it where piping space is tight, or for boiler-feedwater/heater-drain service; expanded outlets, restricted trim, or outlet liners are available where cavitation or flashing damage is a risk.

Three-way body — converges or diverges flow through three pipeline connections, throttling mid-travel in either mode. Cage-, port-, or stem-guided variants exist, so actuator and trim selection has to account for two flow paths moving together, not one.

primitives.templateRationale: Both are named, visually distinct body constructions the learner must recognize on sight — angle by its elbow-replacing geometry, three-way by its third connection — the labeling job nomenclature is built for, not a mechanism walkthrough of moving parts.

primitives.t: Every rotary body shares one mechanism — a shaft rotates a flow-blocking element across the bore instead of sliding a stem — but the element's shape (offset disc, notched-ball segment, or open ball) sets rangeability, erosion resistance, and control lag differently. Construction only at this stage; full selection tradeoffs are ch3-m3's job.

items.t: Butterfly — a disc rotates on a shaft across the bore; shaft-to-disc-center offset (single- vs. double-offset) is the geometry that later sets seal wear and rangeability.
Segmented/V-notch ball — a contoured ball segment stays in contact with the seal through rotation, shearing rather than clogging on slurries and erosive or fibrous fluids.

Full-port ball — presents almost no restriction to flow and allows pigging, but as a throttling device it must rotate 15-20° before it starts absorbing significant energy from the system, a control-lag consequence worth flagging even at the construction stage.

primitives.templateRationale: Rotary is one family taught through a shared mechanism (a shaft rotating a blocking element across the bore) with three named variants, so mechanism fits better than nomenclature — the teaching point is how each variant's geometry changes flow behavior, not just naming parts. Three images sits near the per-template capacity ceiling (Style Guide §6.4); flagged under Concept-map gaps rather than dropped, since the objective already scopes this slide to construction-level only.

primitives.t: Solid-wedge construction — handwheel, stem, wedge, seat — is the widely-used gate-valve body for air, gas, oil, steam, and water isolation service. Gate bodies are on/off only, never a throttling spec — the defining exclusion against every other family in this taxonomy.
primitives.templateRationale: One labelled cutaway naming the wedge/stem/seat construction — the direct labelled-parts case nomenclature exists for.

primitives.t: Weir-type construction — handwheel, stem, bonnet, compressor, diaphragm and backing, weir, liner, body — is the most common diaphragm-valve style: a raised weir gives the flexible diaphragm a shorter closing stroke than a straightway body, extending diaphragm service life, a maintenance-interval spec consideration.
primitives.templateRationale: One labelled cutaway naming the weir/diaphragm/liner construction — a straightforward nomenclature treatment.

primitives.t: An air-operated pinch valve closes by collapsing a flexible sleeve rather than moving a rigid closure member against a seat — no metal trim in the flow path, so it is the specification of choice for slurry and solid-powder flow that would erode or clog a conventional body; the sleeve itself becomes the wear item to spec a replacement interval against.
primitives.templateRationale: One figure naming the sleeve/air-tap construction and its two operating states (open / pinched closed) — nomenclature's labelled-parts treatment.

primitives.t: The plug-valve family splits sharply by function, not just construction: an eccentric plug is a genuine throttling control body, while a lubricated (tapered) plug is an on/off isolation cock — same family name, two different specs.

items.t: Eccentric plug — the disk's path minimizes seat contact on opening, cutting wear and holding tight shutoff to 1500 psi (103 bar) and 427°C (800°F) in either flow direction. Rate this as a real throttling body for erosive, coking, or hard-to-handle service, not an on/off cock.

Lubricated (tapered) plug — lubricant injected at the plug-body interface prevents seizing while holding a positive seal. This is an on/off isolation cock, not a control body — the wrong pick against a continuous-throttling spec, and ruled out entirely wherever lubricant contamination of the process is a liability concern.

primitives.templateRationale: Exactly two named plug constructions with a genuine functional split (throttling control body vs. on/off isolation cock) sharing one family name — the two-panel contrast template's core case, per teaching-philosophy.md's 'this vs. that' role.

primitives.t: All eight body families reduce to how each one blocks or throttles the bore — a sliding plug, a rotating element, or a collapsing/deflecting member — and which one a spec calls out determines the trim, actuator, and shutoff-class decisions every later chapter assumes were already made correctly.

items.t: Globe — flow turns through a seat-and-plug port; the default sliding-stem throttling body.
Angle — a single-port globe variant that also serves as a pipe elbow.
Three-way — converges or diverges flow through a third connection, throttled mid-travel.
Rotary (butterfly/ball) — a shaft rotates a disc, segment, or ball across the bore instead of sliding a stem.
Gate — a wedge slides across a straight-through body; on/off only, never a throttling spec.
Diaphragm — a flexible diaphragm closes against a weir; no metal trim in the flow path.
Pinch — a flexible sleeve collapses shut; the choice for slurry and solids service.
Plug — a tapered or eccentric plug rotates in the body; eccentric variants throttle, lubricated variants are on/off only.

primitives.templateRationale: An 8-way capstone doesn't fit slide--role-contrast, which is structurally exactly two .tpl-panel siblings — eight families would need four contrast slides stitched together, not one synthesis. slide--role-nomenclature-reveal's figure-less click-to-reveal grid fits instead: it names all eight families as a fixed set and recaps each one's distinguishing construction feature in one line, without re-displaying images already shown on slides 24-30 (each pane's source citation points back to that earlier figure).

reground.hook: Every valve body is just a different way of blocking or steering something moving through a pipe — a flat plate slid across it, a ball or disc spun through it, a rubber sheet pinched or pressed over it. Eight household ways of stopping or bending a flow, dressed up in engineering names.
reground.bridge: Those eight 'ways of blocking a pipe' are exactly the industry's eight recognized control-valve body families — globe, angle, three-way, rotary, gate, diaphragm, pinch, and plug — and naming which one a spec calls out, correctly, from its construction alone, is the vocabulary every later chapter in this course assumes is already in place.
reground.depth:
The eight families split first by motion type. Sliding-stem (globe-derived) bodies move a plug linearly into a port: single-ported globe is the default post-guided construction for NPS 1-4 process service, presenting the full unbalanced port area to the actuator unless cage/retainer trim balances it; double-ported (reverse-acting) globe balances dynamic plug force across two ports for a smaller actuator, at the cost of a shutoff ceiling around Class II/III, which is why the industry has largely moved away from it; angle is a single-port cage-style variant that doubles as a pipe elbow; three-way converges or diverges flow through a third connection, throttling mid-travel in either direction.

Rotary bodies replace the sliding stem with a shaft rotating a blocking element across the bore: butterfly (disc, shaft-offset from disc center, setting seal wear and rangeability), segmented/V-notch ball (a contoured segment that shears rather than clogs on slurries), and full-port ball (minimal restriction and pigging capability, but 15-20° of rotation before it starts controlling) are all one mechanism family, differing only in element geometry.

The remaining four are single-purpose specialty bodies, none of them sliding-stem or rotary: gate is a wedge sliding across a straight-through body, on/off only, never a throttling spec; diaphragm closes a flexible sheet against a raised weir, putting no metal trim in the flow path; pinch collapses a flexible sleeve shut, the choice for slurry and solid-powder service that would erode or clog anything else; plug splits sharply by function within its own family — an eccentric plug is a genuine throttling control body holding tight shutoff to 1500 psi (103 bar) and 427°C (800°F) in either flow direction, while a lubricated (tapered) plug is only an on/off isolation cock, ruled out wherever continuous throttling or lubricant-contamination liability is a concern.

The spec consequence threading all eight: body-family choice is made once, from construction, and it locks in the actuator sizing, shutoff class, and trim options every downstream chapter in this course takes as already decided.

activities.title: Eight-Family Construction Sort
activities.description: Hand each small group an unlabeled set of construction images — one per body family just taught: globe (single-ported), globe (double-ported/reverse-acting), angle, three-way, one representative rotary construction, gate, diaphragm, pinch, and plug (eccentric or lubricated). Groups sort each image into its correct family name and, for each one, state the single construction feature from this module's own slides that identifies it as that family (e.g., a wedge closing across a straight-through body means gate; a flexible sleeve pinched shut by an external mechanism means pinch; a shaft-mounted disc, ball, or notched ball rotating across the bore means rotary). Debrief resolves any family the group placed by shape alone rather than by the construction feature actually taught.

modules.title: Guiding & Restricted-Capacity Trim
modules.stakes: A poorly guided plug or a trim sized without regard to minimum controllable flow produces a valve that hunts or can't hold a low setpoint.
modules.objective: Compare valve-plug guiding methods against a stability requirement, and select restricted-capacity trim for a low-Cv service.

primitives.t: Why would a valve sized to the exact right Cv still hunt or drift off a setpoint in service? Unstable plug-to-seat alignment — not the capacity calculation — is frequently the cause, and which guiding method a spec calls out is a decision made against a stability requirement, before the body and trim are finalized.
primitives.sourceNote: Prime opens on the stakes question rather than a figure — no single figure represents 'why guiding matters' as a concept in its own right; the module's own stakes line ("A poorly guided plug ... produces a valve that hunts or can't hold a low setpoint") is the source for this framing.

No image is registered for this framing question and none of the three guiding-method figures reads as a generic hook without pre-empting slides 34-35's own reveal, so this uses the plain-tagline shape the CSS itself calls out as reading better with no image — not the .is-dark variant, which Style Guide/gallery notes reserve for the one prime slide per module that earns a harder pause, not a routine default.

primitives.t: Guiding, retention, and characterization living in one replaceable part is a maintenance advantage, not just an efficient design: swapping the cage alone re-characterizes the valve (a different flow shape) without touching the body or requiring a different plug — the basis for interchangeable cage trim sets built around one body.
primitives.templateRationale: A labelled cutaway naming cage, plug, and seat ring is the canonical nomenclature shape (Axis 3: 'name the parts... labelled-parts figure, sequenced before the mechanism concepts'), and cage-guiding is the construction this module's stability comparison is measured against on slide 35.

primitives.t: The Handbook names exactly two fundamental guiding approaches, and they trade stability for weight and fouling risk in opposite directions: body guiding gives a large, stable bearing surface at the cost of needing hard-facing and a larger valvehead in high-wear or scale-prone service; stem-bonnet guiding keeps the guiding surface out of the process media entirely, needing no hard-facing, at the cost of a larger stem diameter on big valves.

items.t: Body guiding — the closure element is guided directly against the valve body; large contact area gives stability, typical on larger globe and non-return valves, but generally needs hard-facing and is subject to binding/fouling if scale isn't controlled.

Stem-bonnet guiding — an external anti-rotation device guides the stem within the bonnet, off the process media; needs no hard-facing and keeps valvehead size/weight down, at the cost of a larger stem diameter on big valves.

primitives.templateRationale: cvh-topic-valve-guiding presents body guiding and stem-bonnet guiding explicitly as 'the two fundamental approaches' — a genuine this-vs-that pairing, not a spectrum, and exactly two figures — the structural precondition for slide--role-contrast's two-panel layout. This is the slide where the module's stability-requirement comparison (bloom: analyze) is actually made.

primitives.t: Restricted-capacity trim lets a body sized for anticipated future flow growth (or oversized in error) still control stably at today's lower flow: cage-guided construction achieves this with plug, cage, and seat-ring parts scaled from a smaller valve size, mated to the larger body with adapter pieces fitted above the cage and below the seat ring — avoiding a costly pipeline reducer or a custom-sized body.

primitives.t: Applied to a low-Cv service: when a body is specified oversized against today's actual flow — deliberately, for future capacity, or by a sizing error — restricted-capacity trim (commonly standardized around 40% of full-size trim capacity) is the standard spec call. It holds stable control today without a smaller body or a pipeline reducer, and full-size parts can be swapped back in later, with no new body required, once flow actually grows.

reground.hook: A wobbly drawer only really glides well when its rails hold it snug against the cabinet — held loose, it rattles and jams; held tight on just one side, it can still bind if that side gets dirty or worn. And if you plumb a big kitchen faucet onto a line that only ever needs to fill a bathroom sink, you don't buy a whole new smaller faucet — you drop in a restrictor insert that shrinks the opening down to the flow you actually need.
reground.bridge: A control valve plug is the drawer: how it's guided — cage-guided, snug against a cylindrical wall through its whole travel, versus guided at just the body or just the stem — determines whether it stays exactly on-axis to the seat ring or hunts under process forces, and that choice is made against a stated stability requirement, not picked by habit. And a body sized bigger than today's flow actually needs — for planned future growth, or by a sizing mistake — gets the faucet-restrictor treatment: restricted-capacity trim, smaller-valve internals adapted into the larger body, instead of a new smaller body or a pipeline reducer.
reground.depth:
Guiding method is chosen against a stability requirement, not by default. Cage guiding runs the plug OD close along the cage's cylindrical inside wall through full travel, so cage/bonnet/seat-ring self-align as the assembly is built — this is the everyday control-valve construction and the one the module's nomenclature slide labels.

At the whole-valve level, the Handbook names two fundamental guiding philosophies with opposite tradeoffs: body guiding (the closure element bears directly on the body) gives a large, stable contact area — good for larger globe and non-return valves — but usually needs hard-facing against wear and can bind or foul if scale isn't controlled, and on a non-return valve, seizure there kills the globe-valve function too; stem-bonnet guiding (an external anti-rotation device keeps the stem aligned in the bonnet) removes the guiding surface from the process media entirely, needs no hard-facing, keeps valvehead size and weight down, and on a non-return design still works as a plain globe valve even if seizure occurs — at the cost of needing a larger stem diameter on big valves.

Port-guided single-port construction is the extreme low end of this tradeoff: usually capped at 10 bar (150 psig) pressure drop, susceptible to velocity-induced vibration, and fitted with screwed-in seat rings that are hard to remove — fine for on/off or low-pressure throttling, never for severe service, where top-and-bottom-guided or cage-style construction is required instead.

Restricted-capacity trim solves an entirely different problem — a body correctly sized for structural strength, future capacity, or reduced inlet/outlet velocity, but carrying more Cv than today's service should ever see, which otherwise leaves the plug hunting near the closed end of its travel. Cage-guided bodies solve it by fitting plug, cage, and seat-ring parts scaled from a smaller valve size, mated into the larger body with adapter pieces above the cage and below the seat ring — no pipeline reducer, no custom-sized body, and full-size parts can be swapped back in later when flow actually grows. Most manufacturers standardize these reduced-capacity combinations, commonly around 40% of the full-size trim's capacity, because the need is common enough to stock rather than engineer one-off.

activities.title: Guiding Method Call-Out
activities.description: Hand out four short service descriptions (pressure drop and fluid/vibration conditions varying across them, at least one exceeding a 10 bar/150 psig drop with erosive or severe-service conditions, at least one a small-diameter low-flow throttling application). In pairs, pick a defensible guiding method for each and state the specific limitation or stability property that ruled the others out — e.g. a port-guided plug's ~10 bar (150 psig) pressure-drop ceiling, its susceptibility to velocity-induced vibration, and its hard-to-remove screwed-in seat ring versus a cage- or top-and-bottom-guided plug's stability under severe service. Debrief resolves any pair that picked on 'which sounds more robust' rather than the actual stated limitation.

activities.title: Oversized-Body Trim Call
activities.description: Walk a single case: a body was specified a size larger than today's flow needs to leave headroom for planned future capacity growth, and at today's flow the plug now spends most of its travel near the closed end of the port, controlling poorly. Students work through the alternatives — buy a pipeline reducer and a smaller body, run the existing body at low, unstable travel, or spec restricted-capacity trim (cage/plug/seat-ring parts scaled from a smaller valve size via adapter pieces, commonly standardized around 40% of the full-size trim's capacity) — and justify why restricted-capacity trim is the standard answer both today (stable control at present flow) and for the future (full-size parts can replace it without a new body when flow actually grows).
