modules.title: Rotary Subtypes & Selection Process
modules.stakes: Treating all rotary valves as interchangeable ignores real differences in rangeability, shutoff, and cavitation resistance between subtypes.
modules.objective: Distinguish rotary valve subtypes and match each to the application it actually fits, following a standard selection-process flowchart.

primitives.t: Every rotary vendor calls their own line 'universal' — segmented ball, full-port ball, eccentric plug, and butterfly are all marketed as if any one of them fits any rotary duty. None of them do: each subtype's own construction sets a hard ceiling on rangeability, shutoff class, or erosion resistance that no actuator or trim engineering downstream can fix later. Specifying by which name sounds toughest, instead of by which construction the service conditions actually require, is a real spec-liability risk this module exists to close.
primitives.sourceNote: Prime opens on the rotary-universality myth rather than a figure — ogas-topic-control-valve-selection-process's own framing (today's assortment of sliding-stem and rotary styles, 'some marketed as universal,' makes even experienced users uncertain whether they're getting the best value) is the source for this stakes question; no single figure represents the myth itself.
primitives.templateRationale: A stakes-framing question before any subtype is shown, per Axis 3's prime role — orienting the learner against the module's own stakes line before the four real subtype tradeoffs arrive on slides 40-43. No image is registered for the framing question itself, so this uses the plain-tagline shape rather than pre-empting any one subtype's own figure.

primitives.t: Same body family, same actuation mechanism, opposite selection driver: full-port ball buys capacity and pigging at the cost of throttling response; segmented ball spends some of that capacity to buy real control performance.

items.t: Full-port/through-bore ball — presents almost no restriction to flow and permits pigging; high capacity and low erosive wear suit high-ΔP throttling and on/off service to NPS 24. But as a throttling device it must rotate 15-20° open before it starts absorbing meaningful energy from the system — a real control-lag penalty across the first fifth of the stroke, and a liability if specified against a precision-throttling duty.

Segmented ball — a reduced bore with a contoured notch edge trades some of that capacity for markedly better throttling control and higher rangeability. Splined-shaft connections are engineered specifically to eliminate lost motion, and heavy-duty metal or fluoroplastic seals extend the usable temperature/fluid range. Specify it over a full-port ball wherever modulating control performance, not raw capacity, is the deciding requirement.

primitives.templateRationale: Exactly two named ball-valve constructions with a genuine, opposite performance tradeoff (capacity/pigging vs. control performance) — the two-panel contrast template's core case. Both figures were introduced construction-only in ch3-m1's rotary mechanism slide (page 26); reused here reframed around the actual selection decision per ogas-topic-rotary-valve-family and pss-topic-ball-valve-subcategories, not repeated as new nomenclature, consistent with buildsOn.

primitives.t: The same ball-valve family splits again by service driver, not construction: a segmented ball with added trim is the pick for erosive/particulate process duty; a full-port trunnion ball is the pick for fire-safe isolation duty — the two are not substitutes for each other.

items.t: Segmented ball with noise/cavitation trim — the contoured segment stays in continuous seal contact through rotation, shearing rather than clogging on erosive, viscous, or slurry service carrying entrained solids or fibers. Emerson's added trim options extend that base construction with moderate noise attenuation and cavitation protection for the same duty.

Full-port, three-piece trunnion-mounted ball — presents little or no flow restriction and is fire-tested and certified to API 6 and 6FA. Spec'd for automated bypass, batch, monitor, and emergency shutoff (ESD) duty on a clean-service line, not for erosive or slurry throttling — a safety-driven pick, not a process-driven one.

primitives.templateRationale: Two ball-valve subtype/trim variants matched to opposite service drivers (particulate/erosive throttling vs. fire-safe ESD isolation) — the two-panel contrast's core case. Distinct from slide 40's general full-port-vs-segmented capacity/control tradeoff: this pairs each subtype with the specific severe-service or safety duty that actually calls for it.

primitives.t: The eccentric plug valve is a genuine construction hybrid, not a rotary valve with a different name: rotary actuation like the rest of this family, paired with a massive, rigid seat design more typical of a sliding-stem globe body. The plug cams into the seat ring on closure for globe-style tight shutoff, plus excellent resistance to abrasive wear and flashing-induced erosion — within a practical selection envelope of sizes generally to 8 in and ratings to ANSI Class 600, flanged or flangeless. Labelled construction: retainer, valve plug, seat ring, face seals, bearing, taper and expansion pins, thrust washer, valve body, packing, valve shaft, bearing stop.
primitives.templateRationale: A single labelled-parts cutaway naming a real construction (retainer, plug, seat ring, face seals, bearing, shaft) is nomenclature's direct case. Checked against the registry and the Subject-Matter Index per this slot's instruction: pss-cmp-v500-eccentric-plug-cutaway is a genuinely more specific, parts-labelled figure than the general body-construction photo (cvh-cmp-eccentric-plug-valve-body) already used in ch3-m1 slide 30, so this avoids repeating that slide's own image under buildsOn while still grounding the transitional-hybrid claim in pss-topic-eccentric-plug-transitional-category.

primitives.t: Butterfly valves split by seal technology, not just size: a lined butterfly buys tight shutoff cheaply but caps its own pressure/temperature range; a high-performance butterfly buys a much higher ceiling on both, at the cost of overall control precision.

items.t: Lined butterfly — an elastomer or TFE liner against the disk gives tight shutoff and low cost, and protects the body's inner bore from the process fluid. But that same liner caps both pressure drop and temperature range, since sealing depends on disk-to-liner interference wearing predictably over time.

High-performance butterfly — double-offset shaft mounting pulls the disk clear of its seal once it starts to open, minimizing seal wear and letting a metal seal hold tight shutoff at temperatures an elastomer liner can't survive. That higher pressure/temperature ceiling costs control range: roughly a third of what a ball or globe valve delivers, so it's a general-service body, not a precision-throttling one.

primitives.templateRationale: Same body family, a real construction-driven capability split (elastomer-sealed, low-cost, limited-range vs. metal-sealed, high-temperature, still-limited-range) that only becomes a selection decision once the two are set side by side. Checked against the registry and Subject-Matter Index per this slot's instruction: pss-cmp-lined-butterfly-valve is a genuinely more specific figure for the lined side than ch3-m1's general offset-disc construction photo (cvh-cmp-butterfly-shaft-offset-disc-center), avoiding a repeat under buildsOn.

primitives.t: The same 6-step sequence governs every valve selection, rotary included, and it is what forces the process data to actually pick the subtype instead of the subtype being picked first: (1) fix service conditions — P1, ΔP, Q, T1, fluid properties, allowable noise, ANSI pressure class; (2) calculate a preliminary Cv and check the noise/cavitation levels it implies; (3) let that check choose the trim type — standard, noise-reduction, or cavitation-reduction — before the body is even selected; (4) select the valve body and trim size for the required Cv — this is where a rotary subtype (segmented ball, full-port trunnion ball, eccentric plug, or butterfly) actually gets chosen, noting travel, trim group, and shutoff option; (5) select trim materials compatible with the application and available in that trim group; (6) settle remaining options — packing, additional shutoff hardware. Skipping straight to step 4 without steps 1-3 already answered is how a spec locks in a rotary subtype the process conditions never actually supported.
primitives.templateRationale: The flowchart figure already carries the authoritative six-step structure — pairing it with a steps list that walks the sequence against the rotary body-and-trim decision at step 4 specifically, rather than redrawing it or treating it as a generic checklist. procedure-image (list + single image) fits because there is exactly one figure and no verified marker coordinates on it to place numbered callouts against (Style Guide §6.0) — procedure-callout was considered and rejected for that reason.

reground.hook: Think of the different kinds of taps and valves already around a house: a quarter-turn ball valve under the sink that's either fully open or fully shut, a butterfly-style air-vent damper you spin to any angle for fine adjustment, and a heavy, rugged shutoff valve on a gas line built to survive a fire. They all work by turning something, but nobody would swap one for another and expect it to do the same job.
reground.bridge: Control valve engineers face the same four-way choice inside just the 'rotary' family alone — segmented ball, full-port ball, eccentric plug, and butterfly all turn a shaft to block or open a bore, and treating them as interchangeable because they're all 'rotary' is exactly the selection mistake this module exists to prevent.
reground.depth:
The rotary family is not one interchangeable class — each subtype's construction sets a hard, non-negotiable limit on rangeability, shutoff, or erosion resistance that no amount of trim or actuator engineering downstream can fix. Full-port/through-bore ball valves present almost no restriction to flow and permit pigging, and their high capacity and low erosive wear suit high-ΔP throttling and on/off service to NPS 24 — but as a throttling device they must rotate 15-20° open before they start absorbing meaningful energy from the system, a real control-lag penalty across the first fifth of the stroke.

Segmented ball valves trade some of that capacity for markedly better throttling control: a reduced bore with a contoured notch edge, splined-shaft connections engineered specifically to eliminate lost motion, and heavy-duty metal or fluoroplastic seals that extend the usable temperature/fluid range — and for erosive, viscous, or slurry service carrying entrained solids or fibers, the segment's continuous seal contact shears rather than clogs, with Emerson's added trim options extending that base construction with moderate noise attenuation and cavitation protection.

Where the safety case dominates instead of the process case, a full-port, three-piece trunnion-mounted ball valve is fire-tested and certified to API 6 and 6FA specifically for bypass, batch, monitor, and emergency shutoff/ESD duty on a clean-service line — a genuinely different selection driver from either ball variant above, not a substitute for either.

The eccentric plug valve is a real hybrid, not a rotary valve with a different name: rotary actuation paired with a massive, rigid seat design more typical of a sliding-stem globe body, the plug camming into the seat ring on closure for globe-style tight shutoff plus excellent resistance to abrasive wear and flashing-induced erosion, within a practical envelope of sizes to 8 in and ratings to ANSI Class 600.

Butterfly valves split by seal technology, not just size: a lined (elastomer/TFE) butterfly buys tight shutoff and low cost at the price of a hard pressure/temperature ceiling set by the liner's own wear tolerance, while a high-performance (double-offset) butterfly pulls the disk clear of its seal on opening to hold tight metal-to-metal shutoff at temperatures too hot for any liner — at the cost of a control range only about a third that of a ball or globe valve, keeping it a general-service body rather than a precision-throttling one. None of these five tradeoffs resolve themselves by inspection; the standard 6-step selection-process flowchart — fix service conditions, calculate a preliminary Cv and check noise/cavitation, let that check choose the trim type, then select body/trim/materials/options in that order — is what forces the process data to actually drive the rotary-subtype decision at step 4, instead of the decision being made first and the conditions retrofitted to justify it afterward.

activities.title: Rotary Subtype Call-Out
activities.description: Hand out four short service-condition cards: (1) an erosive, viscous slurry service needing high rangeability throttling; (2) a fire-safe emergency-shutoff/bypass duty on a large, clean-service gas line; (3) a large-diameter, moderate-pressure-drop line needing tight shutoff but only general control precision; (4) an abrasive, flashing-prone service needing a rigid, massive seat design. In pairs, pick the rotary subtype that actually fits each (segmented ball with noise/cavitation trim, full-port trunnion-mounted ball, high-performance butterfly, eccentric plug) and justify the pick from the specific construction feature this module taught — not from which valve 'sounds tougher.' Debrief walks each pick back through the module's own selection-process flowchart (service conditions, trim/cavitation check, body-and-trim selection) to confirm it holds up as a real selection decision, not a guess.
materials: Four short service-condition cards (fluid/erosion, fire-safety, size/precision, and seat-material conditions varying across them)
activities.sourceNote: Service conditions and construction features drawn directly from this module's own sources — ogas-topic-rotary-valve-family and pss-topic-ball-valve-subcategories (through-bore vs. segmented-ball tradeoff, segmented-ball noise/cavitation trim), pss-topic-eccentric-plug-transitional-category (rigid-seat rotary hybrid), pss-topic-butterfly-valve-family-evolution (lined vs. high-performance butterfly), and cvh-cmp-valve-selection-process-flowchart (the 6-step selection sequence) — a live application of what was just taught, no invented service condition.

modules.title: Check Valves, End Connections & Pressure Class
modules.stakes: A valve specified against the wrong pressure class or end connection is a paperwork and fit-up failure discovered at installation, not a design failure caught on paper.
modules.objective: Select a check-valve style for backflow prevention, and apply end-connection and pressure-class criteria to verify a rated class from a body-bonnet or pressure-seal detail.

primitives.t: A check valve's whole job is one of the three functions this chapter's own taxonomy already named for every isolation valve — preventing flow reversal, not throttling or shutoff. Get the style wrong and the failure is not a control-quality defect, it is a real backflow event: a contaminated upstream system, a pump driven backward hard enough to damage its bearings or seals, or reheat steam returning into a turbine. Style selection is therefore a spec decision made against real installation geometry and reversal risk, not an interchangeable commodity call.
primitives.sourceNote: Prime opens on the stakes question rather than a figure — no single figure represents 'why check-valve style matters' as a concept in its own right. Grounded in cvh-topic-check-valve-selection's own selection framing and its related cvh-topic-valve-function-taxonomy (preventing flow reversal as one of three basic valve regulation functions, CVH 6th ed. §10.1, p.211).
primitives.templateRationale: A stakes-framing question before any check-valve construction is shown, per Axis 3's prime role and matching the module's own stakes line. No figure in the registry represents this framing without pre-empting slides 47-49's own reveals, so this uses the plain-tagline shape (no image) — the same call cve1-ch3-m2's own prime slide (33) made.

primitives.t: Stop function: valvehead and stem are mechanically connected, so the valve closes only when the handwheel or actuator is actually operated — an isolation valve with no backflow protection of its own. Stop-check function: valvehead and stem are NOT connected, so the same body closes either by actuator operation or by flow reversal, a check-valve function layered onto a globe body. Specifying a plain stop valve where reversal protection is actually required leaves the line with no automatic backflow defense at all.

items.t: Stop function — valvehead and stem connected by a captive split ring; the valve opens and closes only on handwheel/actuator operation, in either flow direction. No automatic protection against reverse flow.

Stop-check function — valvehead and stem free of each other, so the disk still seats and stops reverse flow even if the actuator or handwheel is left open or fails. The correct call whenever isolation AND backflow protection are both required from the same body.

primitives.templateRationale: Exactly two named functional configurations of the same globe-body construction, distinguished by one mechanical fact (stem-to-valvehead connection) with a direct spec consequence — the two-panel contrast template's core case.

primitives.t: Swing check is the baseline hinged-disk design — closes on reversal or gravity, but can slam and chatter on shock closure. Two anti-chatter variants correct that failure mode without changing the basic hinge: a lever-and-weight arrangement forces immediate closure on reversal, and a tilting-disk design routes flow both above and below the disk for greater stability, most advantageous above 6 inches and on higher-pressure, low-flow-rate service where a plain swing disk is otherwise unstable.

items.t: Swing check — cap, disk hinge, disk, body seat ring, body; the hinged disk swings open with flow and must be installed so it closes positively by gravity or reversal. Less flow resistance fully open than a lift check, but prone to shock closure and disk chatter with no further modification.

Lever-and-weight swing check — an external lever-and-weight arrangement added to the same hinge, forcing immediate closure on flow reversal specifically to minimize shock and disk chatter — a direct fix to the baseline swing check's own failure mode.

Tilting-disk swing check — flow passes both below and over the disk, giving greater disk stability than a plain swing check. Most advantageous above 6 inches and on higher-pressure, low-flow-rate applications, where disk stability is otherwise the limiting factor.

primitives.templateRationale: Three named, visually distinct check-valve constructions the learner must recognize on sight, two of them built as direct variants of the first to correct a named failure mode — the labelled-parts job nomenclature exists for. Three images sits comfortably within the per-template capacity Style Guide §6.4 documents (tp-003's 7-callout cutaway as the practical ceiling); laid out with the has-wide-fig arrangement rather than the two-panel default given the third item.

primitives.t: Horizontal lift check completes the family: cap, union cap ring, disk, body seat ring, body — its flow pattern corresponds to a globe valve's, so it is specified where pressure drop is not the binding constraint, and it is also available in a vertical-body version. Selecting among all four designs is a real spec decision made against flow resistance, disk stability, installation orientation, and shock-closure risk — not a matter of which name is most familiar.

items.t: Pick swing check for a straightforward, moderate-flow line with ample clearance and orientation for the disk to close positively by gravity, where shock or chatter is not a real risk.

Pick lever-and-weight swing check where the line is prone to shock closure or disk chatter — a plain swing check's own failure mode — and immediate, forced closure on reversal is worth the added external hardware.

Pick tilting-disk above roughly 6 inches or on higher-pressure, low-flow-rate service, where a plain swing disk's stability is marginal and the two-sided flow path is needed to keep the disk seated correctly.

Pick horizontal (or vertical) lift check where pressure drop is not the governing constraint and the globe-like flow pattern is acceptable — never where minimizing pressure drop is the priority, since it offers more flow resistance fully open than a swing design.

primitives.templateRationale: An evaluate-level 'select one of a small named set, see its worked selection criteria' task — application-pick's own shape (pick ONE, see its analysis) fits directly, rather than a graph/table application or a stepped case walkthrough. This is also the slide that completes the four-design set the module's own act1 application exercise immediately following actually needs.

primitives.t: Screwed (NPT) ends are the most economical end connection but are limited to about NPS 2 and smaller, are not recommended at elevated temperature, and complicate maintenance since a flanged or union joint elsewhere in the line has to be broken just to unscrew the body. Bolted-flange and welded ends are the two constructions actually specified once a line moves past that ceiling, and each carries its own opposite tradeoff.
primitives.sourceNote: Figures drawn from cvh-topic-end-connection-selection (CVH 6th ed. ch3, §3.2, pp.63-65) — verified directly in the Subject-Matter Index as depicting exactly the screwed/flanged/welded end-connection methods this concept teaches. Not in the CVE1 registry's own citation for this competency, which lists only pss-topic-end-connection-selection-criteria and no figures at all for end-connection types — a real registry gap closed by checking the Subject-Matter Index directly, per this pass's own instruction. Flagged under Concept-map gaps for the registry to be updated.

items.t: Bolted-flange ends (flat-face, raised-face, ring-type-joint) are easily removed for maintenance and cover the full working range most control valves are built for — from near absolute zero to about 815°C (1500°F) — the only end-connection style available across all valve sizes. Ring-type-joint reaches the highest pressure of the three, to 15,000 psig, but is not suited to high temperature.

Welded ends (socket-weld to about NPS 2, butt-weld for NPS 2-1/2 and larger) are leak-tight at all pressures and temperatures and economical to install, but are far harder to remove from the line once in service and limited to weldable materials. A piping spec calling for welded ends narrows the valve choice to sliding-stem construction only.

primitives.templateRationale: Two constructions with real, opposite installation/maintenance tradeoffs (easy removal vs. leak-tightness at the cost of removability) — the two-panel contrast case. Screwed ends are named and scoped in the concept's own overview text rather than given a third panel: no figure exists for a screwed connection in the Source Library (prose-only in the source), and contrast is structurally two .tpl-panel siblings, not three (Style Guide §6.4 / gallery.css).

primitives.t: Every isolation valve's body-to-bonnet joint is made one of two ways. A bolted bonnet — bolts and nuts compressing a gasket — spans ANSI classes 150 through 1500 and is the construction assumed unless the class specifically calls for more. A pressure-seal bonnet is reserved for classes 900 through 4500: naming a pressure-seal bonnet on a spec is itself a signal the rated class is at least Class 900, before any dimension is even checked.

items.t: Bolted bonnet — gland flange, packing gland, packing, bonnet bushing, gland eye bolts, yoke, bonnet nuts, bonnet gasket, bonnet studs, flanged-end connection. The baseline gate-valve construction, used across ANSI classes 150 through 1500.

Pressure-seal bonnet — used only on high-pressure classes 900 through 4500. Rising internal pressure itself increasingly loads the seal, rather than the joint relying solely on preset bolt torque the way a bolted bonnet does.

primitives.templateRationale: Two named body-bonnet junction constructions distinguished by exactly the fact that sets the rated-class floor before any dimension check — the direct two-panel contrast case, and the load-bearing setup for slide 52's own verification procedure.

primitives.t: Getting this wrong is a real safety hazard, not just a paperwork error: installing a lower-rated body into a service that exceeds its actual pressure class risks a body or bonnet failure under system pressure, which is exactly why this is a measured cross-reference against the ANSI table rather than trusting a worn or missing nameplate.

items.t: Pressure-seal construction detail — expanded graphite seal ring, segment ring, and stop ring, with pressure arrows showing how rising internal pressure itself increases the seal's own sealing force. Confirms why identifying a pressure-seal bonnet already floors the class at 900, before any dimension is checked.

ANSI dimension table, cast-iron gate valves — nominal pipe size vs. face-to-face dimension, Classes 125/250/800, solid-wedge and double-disk, flat- and raised-face. The reference table once step 2 confirms a cast-iron body.

ANSI dimension table, steel gate valves, Class 150 — nominal pipe size vs. face-to-face dimension, raised-face and beveled-end, solid-wedge and double-disk. The first of the steel series; a steel body whose measured face-to-face doesn't match this table is a higher class, not a rejected reading.

primitives.templateRationale: A real four-step verification sequence, not a physical assembly procedure, so procedure-image (steps + figure) fits over procedure-callout (no coordinate-verified marker positions exist for these figures) or procedure-worked (that variant is fixed to ONE figure; this sequence genuinely needs the mechanism detail plus two dimension tables together). The three source images compose as one figure per Style Guide §5.14 (separate <image> elements inside one <svg>, each with its own data-lightbox-caption) rather than one flattened raster, laid out with the has-wide-fig arrangement to give the composed figure the width three side-by-side images needs.

primitives.t: Two closing selection rules govern the body-family call this whole chapter has been building toward. Pressure drop and flow capacity: sliding-stem is generally superior at high or shutoff pressure drop because of its rugged moving parts, while rotary designs deliver much higher maximum capacity for a given body size where available pressure drop is small — but that capacity advantage means little in a high-pressure-drop application like letdown or pressure regulation, where sliding-stem's structural robustness matters more. Size-banded rule of thumb: below 3 inches, general-purpose sliding-stem wins on performance and service life for a minimal price premium; 4 to 6 inches favors transitional styles (eccentric plug or ball) on body-material cost and capacity; at 8 inches and larger, high-performance butterfly becomes viable on economy, shutoff, and capacity well beyond a globe design. Past that, remaining choices become a matter of price versus other operational advantages, not a hard technical criterion.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure backs this synthesis in the registry — grounded entirely in pss-topic-pressure-drop-capacity-selection-criteria and pss-topic-valve-type-selection-guidelines (both Power & Severe Service Sourcebook ch1) and pp-topic-flow-capacity-selection-tradeoff (Pulp & Paper Sourcebook ch1).
primitives.templateRationale: A decision/selection table is the content itself — the size-banded rule of thumb is naturally a Size band -> Recommended body style -> Rationale table, the tp-009 decision-table application variant (Style Guide §5.10/§9.2, `.slide--role-application:has(.tmpl-table)`). Unlike tp-009 itself, no corroborating figure exists in the Source Library for this synthesis (all three backing citations are topics, not figures) — flagged under Concept-map gaps; Stage 3 will need to either run the table full-width with no paired figure or originate one, not force-fit an unrelated image into the figure slot.

reground.hook: A check valve is a one-way gate for anything flowing through a pipe — the kind of flap you'd nail over a basement drainpipe so water can leave but can't come back in the moment the pump stops. And a valve's end connection and pressure class are just its wardrobe and its size tag: how it attaches to the pipe, and how much pressure that particular size and dress code was actually built to survive.
reground.bridge: Both halves of this module are 'don't take the wrong thing on faith' checks applied to a body-bonnet assembly: which one-way-gate mechanism actually belongs on this line given how it fails (chatter, slam, orientation), and which size tag the physical part in front of you is actually entitled to wear, verified against a table rather than assumed from a worn or missing nameplate.
reground.depth:
Check-valve selection is governed by disk-stability and flow-resistance tradeoffs among four real designs: swing (baseline, low resistance, prone to shock chatter), lever-and-weight swing (a forced-closure fix for that chatter), tilting-disk (two-sided flow for stability above 6 inches or on higher-pressure/low-flow service), and horizontal or vertical lift (globe-like flow pattern, specified where pressure drop isn't the binding constraint). A stop-check function — valvehead and stem NOT connected — layers this backflow protection onto an ordinary globe body; a plain stop function has none.

End-connection and pressure-class verification is a construction-driven cross-reference, not a nameplate read: screwed ends cap out around NPS 2 and complicate removal; bolted-flange spans the full working range on all sizes; welded is leak-tight everywhere but hard to remove and narrows the body choice to sliding-stem.

A pressure-seal bonnet by itself already floors the rated class at 900 (bolted bonnet spans 150-1500), and the class is then confirmed by matching the body's material family (cast iron to Class 800, steel through 2500) and measured face-to-face dimension against the correct ANSI table — the same discipline the chapter's closing pressure-drop/capacity and size-banded rule of thumb apply one level up, to the body-family choice itself.

activities.title: Check Valve Style Call
activities.description: In pairs, work four short service-condition cards: (1) a >6-inch line at high pressure/low flow where disk stability is at risk; (2) a horizontal line where pressure drop isn't critical; (3) a line prone to shock closure and disk chatter that a plain swing check can't tolerate; (4) a straightforward gravity-return line with ample room for a hinge to swing and close positively. For each, pick the correct check-valve style (swing, lever-and-weight swing, tilting-disk, or horizontal lift) and justify the pick from the specific criterion this module taught (flow resistance, disk stability, anti-chatter mechanism, or orientation/installation requirement) — not from which name sounds right. Debrief walks each pick back through the stop-vs-stop-check framing from the top of the module to confirm the class also knows when a dedicated check valve is even the right call versus an integrated stop-check trim.
materials: Four short service-condition cards (size/pressure/flow, orientation, and chatter-risk conditions varying across them)
activities.sourceNote: Service conditions and selection criteria drawn directly from cvh-topic-check-valve-selection (flow resistance, disk-stability, and pressure/size tradeoffs among swing, tilting-disk, and lift designs) and the stop-function/stop-check-function framing (cvh-cmp-stop-function, cvh-cmp-stop-check-function) — a live application of what was just taught, no invented service condition.

activities.title: Verify the Class, Justify the Connection
activities.description: In pairs, work a short stated piping spec (an end-connection requirement plus a service pressure/temperature and line size) against a body-bonnet construction detail and an ANSI dimension-table excerpt. Each pair must: (1) pick the correct end connection for the stated spec and state its real tradeoff or limitation — including recognizing when a welded-ends requirement narrows the choice to sliding-stem only; (2) identify whether a bolted or pressure-seal bonnet applies at the stated pressure class; (3) verify the rated class against the dimension-table data by matching nominal size to face-to-face dimension; and (4) justify the overall body-family pick using the module's own closing pressure-drop/capacity and size-banded selection rule. Debrief compares pairs' verified classes and connection choices before revealing the source's own answer.

Body-bonnet construction detail and ANSI dimension-table excerpt (cast-iron and steel Class 150 tables) from the slides just shown

chapters.title: Flow Characteristic & Rangeability
chapters._source: Enabling Competency `eng.selection.flow-characteristic-and-rangeability` — see Curriculum — CVE1.md and Competency Hierarchy — CVE1, CVE2, CVE3 v3.md, Chapter 4. Modules below are STUBS ONLY (status: outline, empty keyConcepts) pending a real Stage 1 arc-cut per module.

modules.title: Inherent Characteristics & How They're Made
modules.stakes: An engineer who treats flow characteristic as a catalog label rather than a physically manufactured property can't reason about how to change it when a selection doesn't fit.
modules.objective: Distinguish linear, equal-percentage, and quick-opening inherent flow characteristics from their curves, and explain how plug contour and cage-port design physically produce each one.

primitives.t: Inherent characteristic = Cv vs. travel at constant ΔP — a bench-test curve, not as-installed behavior. Three standard shapes: quick-opening (steep early rise, flattens fast), linear (Cv rises in direct proportion to travel), equal-percentage (each travel increment raises Cv by a fixed percent of the flow already passing — the exponential curve). Every characteristic selection starts from this inherent baseline; how it behaves once installed is a separate calculation (ch4-m2).
primitives.sourceNote: cvh-cmp-inherent-flow-characteristic-curves (ch3 Fig. 3.38) and cvh-cmp-flow-characteristic-curves-repeat (ch5 Fig. 5.1) in the registry are the same three-curve chart re-plotted in two other chapters. Only the ch1 instance (Fig. 1.19) is cited here; the ch5 instance is reserved for slide 56 — per the registry's own instruction not to cite all three redundantly. See Concept-map gaps.
primitives.templateRationale: A single analytical graph is the standard understand-level treatment for a defining concept; the source figure prints its own three curve labels directly on the plot, so no separate numbered key is needed and capacity is well within the mechanism template's single-figure shape.

primitives.t: Linear vs. equal-percentage is the real selection choice for continuous control. Linear: Cv directly proportional to travel, constant gain at constant ΔP — fits a loop where the valve itself carries nearly all the system's pressure drop (liquid-level control, constant-gain flow loops). Equal-percentage: gain rises with flow, so a given percent change in travel produces a small Cv change at low flow and a large one at high flow — fits the more common case where the piping and process equipment absorb most of the drop and only a small, variable fraction reaches the valve. Quick-opening (previous slide) isn't a contender here — its steep-then-flat curve is built for on/off service, not throttling.
primitives.sourceNote: One figure cited (ch5 Fig. 5.1) — the instance whose own backing topic (cvh-topic-flow-characteristics) states the distinguishing-behavior/service-use reasoning this slide teaches, rather than one of the other two registry instances of the same chart. Concept-map gap: this course's contrast template is fixed at exactly two panels, so Linear and Equal-Percentage take the panels and Quick-Opening (already shown in full on slide 55) is carried forward in text instead of given a third panel — see Concept-map gaps.
primitives.templateRationale: Exactly two panels, Linear and Equal-Percentage — the two characteristics an engineer actually chooses between for continuous throttling control. Quick-Opening was already shown whole on slide 55 and is excluded from this comparison in the text rather than forced into a panel the template has no room for.

primitives.t: The characteristic isn't a property of the whole valve — it's cut into one specific part. Cage-guided construction: the shape of the window machined into the cage wall controls how flow area opens as the plug travels past it; swap the cage and the characteristic changes without touching the plug or seat ring. Plug-guided (non-cage) construction: the same job is done by the contour ground into the plug surface next to the seat ring — as the plug lifts, that contour's changing shape changes the exposed flow area directly. Same governing principle, two different parts: flow-area-versus-travel geometry is what a characteristic physically is.

items.t: Cage-window shape (Quick-Opening / Linear / Equal-Percentage silhouettes) sets the characteristic in cage-guided construction; the cage swaps independent of plug and seat ring.
In plug-guided (non-cage) construction, the plug's own contour next to the seat ring does the same job, changing exposed flow area directly as the plug travels.

primitives.templateRationale: Composed as two separate images per Style Guide §5.14 (two independently-nameable production methods, not one flattened figure), stating the shared general principle; the explicit method-vs-method comparison is deferred to slide 59's formal two-panel contrast. Two single labelled figures are well within the mechanism template's capacity.

primitives.t: Worked case — quick-opening construction. Stem transmits actuator travel to the plug. Plug lifts off the seat ring, uncovering the port. Flow area is the unobstructed opening exposed at a given travel; port diameter sets the maximum flow area the construction can ever expose. Quick-opening's plug geometry uncovers most of that port diameter's flow area in the first small fraction of travel — the physical reason its curve rises steeply, then flattens.
primitives.templateRationale: A single labelled-parts figure — five named items (stem, plug, seat ring, flow area, port diameter) — comfortably within the nomenclature template's callout capacity.

primitives.t: Two ways to manufacture the same characteristic. Cage-guided: the characteristic lives in the cage window; plug and seat ring are common parts reused across characteristics, and the cage is field-interchangeable. Plug-characterized (non-cage): the characteristic is ground into the plug's own contour — changing it means specifying a new plug, not swapping one small part. Spec consequence: a cage-guided body can be re-characterized in the field after it's already in service; a plug-characterized body locks the characteristic in at the time the plug is ordered.

items.t: Cage-guided: characteristic is the cage window; plug and seat ring stay common; the cage swaps in the field to re-characterize the valve.
Plug-characterized (non-cage): characteristic is ground into the plug contour itself; changing it means specifying a new plug, not a field swap.

primitives.templateRationale: Exactly two panels, reusing the same two figures introduced generally at slide 57, now placed head-to-head — cage-guided vs. plug-characterized as the two physical production methods the objective calls for.

reground.hook: Picture three differently-shaped bathtub drain stoppers. Lift each one off the drain by the exact same small amount, and depending on how its underside is shaped, wildly different amounts of water escape — one drains almost fully in that first bit of lift, another drains in rough proportion to how far you lifted it, a third barely drains at first and then gushes once you lift it further. The stopper's shape decides which of those three drain patterns you get — not how hard you pulled, not the pipe underneath.
reground.bridge: A control valve's plug (or the cage window it rides inside) is exactly that shaped stopper. As it lifts off its seat, the shape of the opening it uncovers — a cage's window cut, or the plug's own contour — decides whether flow rises fast-then-flat, steadily, or slow-then-fast. That decision is manufactured into one specific part, and it's made before the valve ever ships — exactly why flow characteristic is a selection question, not something to fix later with the controller.
reground.depth:
Inherent flow characteristic — Cv vs. travel at constant ΔP, a bench-test curve, not as-installed behavior — takes one of three standard shapes: quick-opening (steep initial rise, flattens fast; on/off service, not continuous control), linear (Cv proportional to travel, constant gain; fits a loop where the valve itself carries nearly all the system's pressure drop), and equal-percentage (gain rises with flow; fits the more common case where piping and process equipment absorb most of the drop and only a small, variable fraction reaches the valve).

The physical mechanism: in cage-guided construction the characteristic is cut into the cage-window shape, a part that swaps independent of plug and seat ring, giving real field flexibility to re-characterize a valve already in service; in plug-guided (non-cage) construction the identical job is done by the contour ground into the plug surface next to the seat ring, which locks the characteristic in at the time the plug is ordered — a real rework/liability consideration if the process later needs a different curve.

The quick-opening construction is the clean worked case for the general mechanism: stem transmits travel to the plug, the plug lifts off the seat ring, flow area is what's exposed at a given travel, port diameter caps the maximum area the construction can ever expose, and quick-opening's own geometry exposes most of that port diameter's area within the first small increment of travel.

Scope boundary held throughout: this module stops at inherent characteristic and its physical production; how this same curve gets distorted once installed in a real system (the installed-vs-inherent divergence driven by the system's own pressure-drop ratio) is ch4-m2's competency, not repeated here.

activities.title: Cage & Plug — Predict the Characteristic
activities.description: In pairs, work four unlabeled cage-window/plug-contour silhouette cards (redrawn from the module's own Figure 3.37 cage-window set and Figure 3.39 plug-contour set). For each silhouette, predict from geometry alone which inherent characteristic — linear, equal-percentage, or quick-opening — it would produce as the plug travels off the seat, and justify the prediction in one sentence (e.g., 'a window that widens fast near the seat passes a disproportionate jump in flow at low travel — quick-opening'). Pairs then check their predictions against the module's own construction figures. Debrief covers any geometry the class read wrong and why, tying the miss back to the mechanism just taught.
materials: Four unlabeled cage-window/plug-contour silhouette cards, redrawn from Figures 3.37 and 3.39
activities.sourceNote: Geometry-to-characteristic mapping is the mechanism just taught, drawn directly from cvh-topic-flow-characterization-mechanism and the cage/plug figures shown on slides 57-59 (cvh-cmp-characterized-cages-globe, cvh-cmp-plug-contour-flow-characterization) — a live application of that mechanism to new geometry instances, no invented shape or unsourced claim.

modules.title: Installed Characteristic & Rangeability
modules.stakes: An engineer who selects 'equal-percentage' off a catalog without accounting for system pressure-drop ratio gets an installed characteristic that behaves nothing like equal-percentage in the real piping.
modules.objective: Predict how installed characteristic diverges from inherent characteristic as system pressure-drop ratio changes, and select a flow characteristic that delivers the rangeability a given positioner/control scheme needs.

primitives.t: Why this distinction is worth a whole module: a controller tuned against the inherent (bench) curve assumes one constant gain across the valve's whole travel; if the installed gain actually varies a lot from one end of travel to the other, the same tuning is too aggressive at one end and too sluggish at the other — a loop that can look stable on paper and still hunt or respond unevenly in the field. The two curves diverge because of how much of the system's total, fixed pressure drop the valve itself actually holds at a given flow — the smaller the valve's own share, the more its installed gain distorts from the bench-tested inherent curve. The next two slides turn that into a checkable ratio.
primitives.sourceNote: figures: [] in the CVE1 asset-variant registry for eng.selection.flow-characteristic-and-rangeability.predict-installed-vs-inherent-divergence — confirmed genuine against the Subject-Matter Index (cvh-topic-installed-vs-inherent-characteristic, CVH 6th ed. §2.1.4/§2.1.4.1/§2.1.4.2, pp. 44-46, prose-only). The topically closest figures — cvh-cmp-installed-characteristic-and-gain and cvh-cmp-valve-style-control-range-comparison — are already committed to cve1-ch2-m1's eng.foundations.process-variability-and-loop-performance.oversizing-distortion-effects (built, slides 21-22, framed narrowly around the oversizing special case). Decision: do not reuse them here — there is no declared buildsOn between cve1-ch4-m2 and cve1-ch2-m1, so Stage 3 has no signal to treat this as a callback rather than fresh content, and a person has not confirmed the competency×asset-variant reuse per curriculum-development.md's asset-variant discipline. Same non-borrowing call cve1-ch1-m2 slide 10 already made against this identical topic. Flagged under Asset-variant gaps for Stage 3 origination: an originated two-condition (bench/fixed-ΔP vs. installed/varying-ΔP) schematic, not a Handbook redraw.
primitives.templateRationale: Terse consolidation-then-pivot: the bench-vs-installed distinction was already introduced in full at ch1-m2 slide 10 (buildsOn reaches it transitively via cve1-ch4-m1), so this slide restates only enough to re-anchor the two terms before slide 62 supplies the actual pressure-drop-ratio mechanism. Single mechanism role; no figure available (see sourceNote).

primitives.t: How far installed diverges from inherent is set by the valve's own share of the total system pressure drop at design flow — the pressure-drop ratio. A high ratio (the valve takes most of the system ΔP) tracks close to the inherent curve; a low ratio (piping and process equipment absorb most of the drop, and vary it as load changes) distorts installed gain heavily, regardless of which inherent curve was ordered. This is exactly why equal-percentage exists as a deliberate pairing choice, not an arbitrary catalog option: a process vessel's own gain typically falls as throughput rises, and equal-percentage's rising-with-flow gain can net the two out to a roughly linear, well-behaved installed characteristic. The target is loop gain — every device's gain in the loop except the controller — held within about a 4:1 spread across the operating range (the EnTech consensus figure, a practitioner benchmark, not a hard physical law); outside that band, dynamic performance degrades unacceptably no matter how correct the inherent curve looked on the bench.
primitives.sourceNote: figures: [] in the CVE1 asset-variant registry for this competency (see slide 61's sourceNote for the full non-borrowing rationale against cvh-cmp-installed-characteristic-and-gain / cvh-cmp-valve-style-control-range-comparison, already committed to cve1-ch2-m1). Content verified against cvh-topic-installed-vs-inherent-characteristic (CVH 6th ed. §2.1.4/§2.1.4.1/§2.1.4.2, pp. 44-46), which explicitly states the EnTech 4:1 loop-gain figure and the equal-percentage/vessel-gain rationale as prose, not figure-anchored.
primitives.templateRationale: The module's core analytical mechanism — pressure-drop ratio as the causal driver, the equal-percentage/vessel-gain pairing, and the EnTech 4:1 loop-gain band as its quantitative content — at analyze level. No figure exists in the registry for this competency; Stage 3 will need an originated diagram (valve ΔP-share vs. installed-gain distortion, or a paired vessel-gain/valve-gain sketch) rather than a Handbook redraw — flagged under Asset-variant gaps.

primitives.t: A characteristic selected straight off the catalog's inherent curve, with no check on the valve's own share of system pressure drop, passes every static spec check and still ships a loop where **the installed valve's actual gain bears no resemblance to the curve that was ordered — and no amount of controller retuning corrects a characteristic that was never verified against how the loop actually loads it.**

Consequence stated is the direct corollary of cvh-topic-installed-vs-inherent-characteristic's own pressure-drop-ratio mechanism (CVH 6th ed. §2.1.4/§2.1.4.1/§2.1.4.2, pp. 44-46) — not a gap here specifically, since the caution card's supporting photo is optional (cve1-ch1-m2 slide 13 precedent) and the card carries the consequence sentence alone.

Recorded as slide--tmpl-caution, not slide--role-caution: no .slide--role-caution class exists in the CSS (gallery.css §7 documents Template 6, .slide--tmpl-caution, as the caution role's real master template) — same class cve1-ch1-m2 slide 13 already uses.

primitives.t: These are two different levers for the same problem, and they trade off differently: swapping body style is a design-time decision that changes nothing once the valve ships, while adding a characterized positioner is available even after installation as a field fix — but it inherits the positioner's own response lag, making it a poor late fix on a fast, high-gain loop where that lag itself can degrade control.
primitives.sourceNote: pss-cmp-flow-characteristic-curves (Fisher Power & Severe Service Sourcebook, 4th ed., Fig. 1-14, p.1-8) depicts the four inherent characteristic curves (quick-opening/linear/modified-parabolic/equal-percentage) only — it re-anchors the vocabulary from ch4-m1 (a different sourcebook's version of the same chart, avoiding the redundant-figure citation ch4-m1 slides 55/56 already ruled out) but does not itself depict rangeability-by-body-style or positioner behavior. Those two claims are prose-only, verified against pss-topic-flow-characteristic-rangeability-positioners (same sourcebook, pp. 1-8–1-9), the one Subject-Matter Index entry that explicitly names both the rotary-vs-sliding-stem rangeability finding and the positioner-substitution/frequency-response tradeoff. ogas-cmp-flow-characteristic-curves (the near-duplicate three-curve Oil & Gas version) is reserved for slide 65 rather than cited redundantly here.
primitives.templateRationale: Recalled characteristic-curve figure anchors the vocabulary; rangeability-by-style and positioner-limits are text layered onto that recall, well within the mechanism template's single-figure capacity — no separate contrast panel needed since body style and positioner are two additive selection levers, not a this-vs-that pairing.

primitives.t: Worked selection: a stated service names its required turndown, the fraction of system ΔP the valve will hold at design flow, and the control scheme (a nonlinear positioner in play or not). Reasoning folds all three preceding slides together — read the pressure-drop ratio first (slide 62) to predict how far any candidate's installed curve will drift from its inherent one; reject a candidate whose rated rangeability can't clear the required turndown even before distortion is considered (slide 64); then check whether a characterized positioner is actually available to help close a gap, or whether its own frequency-response/phase-lag limit rules that compensation out for this loop. The characteristic that survives all three checks — not the one with the best-looking inherent curve on the bench — is the one to specify.
primitives.sourceNote: ogas-cmp-flow-characteristic-curves (Fisher Oil & Gas Sourcebook, Fig. 1-10, p.1-7) depicts the three inherent characteristic curves (quick-opening/linear/equal-percentage) as the visual reference the worked selection walks against — the near-duplicate of slide 64's Power & Severe Service figure, deliberately not repeated (see slide 64's sourceNote). The turndown/pressure-drop-ratio/positioner reasoning applied to the stated scenario is prose-derived from ogas-topic-flow-characteristic-and-rangeability (pp. 1-6–1-7) and pss-topic-flow-characteristic-rangeability-positioners (positioner limits), applying — not re-deriving — the mechanisms already taught on slides 61-64; no invented numbers.

Evaluate-level capstone folding slides 61-64 together, matching the module objective's own 'select ... that delivers the rangeability a given positioner/control scheme needs.'

reground.hook: Aim a garden hose nozzle at a flower bed, then aim the same nozzle, turned exactly the same amount, at mud on a driveway — the spray changes completely, not because the nozzle changed, but because how much of the hose's total pressure gets 'used up' right at the nozzle versus lost earlier in a long, narrow run changes with what's downstream. The same twist of the same nozzle behaves like a different nozzle depending on where the pressure actually gets spent.
reground.bridge: That's the installed-vs-inherent problem exactly: a valve's catalog curve is measured with the pressure drop held constant, all of it happening right at the valve — but installed in a real system, the piping, vessels, and other equipment take a variable share of that drop, and how much is left for the valve itself (the pressure-drop ratio) decides how far real behavior strays from the curve on the data sheet. Picking a characteristic, and a rangeability, that survive that shift — not just the ones that look best on the bench curve — is the actual selection task, and getting it wrong is invisible until the loop is already built and hunting.
reground.depth:
Inherent characteristic is Cv vs. travel at a fixed, held ΔP; installed characteristic is the same relationship once the loop's own varying ΔP acts on the valve, and installed gain (the slope of that installed curve) is what actually governs loop stability. How far the two diverge is set by the valve's pressure-drop ratio — its own share of total system ΔP at design flow: a high ratio tracks close to inherent, a low ratio (piping and process equipment absorbing most of the drop, and varying it as load shifts) distorts installed gain heavily regardless of which inherent curve was specified.

This is why equal-percentage is paired deliberately with processes whose own gain falls as throughput rises (a vessel, typically) — its rising-with-flow gain nets out to a roughly linear, controllable installed characteristic — with the target being loop gain (every device's gain except the controller) held within about a 4:1 spread (the EnTech consensus figure). A characteristic picked straight off the catalog curve with no pressure-drop-ratio check passes every static spec check and can still ship a loop whose installed gain bears no resemblance to what was ordered, uncorrectable by retuning.

Rangeability — max-to-min controllable flow — adds a second selection axis: rotary designs, especially partial-ball, generally out-rangeability sliding-stem globe trim, and a characterized positioner can partially substitute one inherent characteristic for another, bounded by the positioner's own frequency response and phase lag, and not universally beneficial (some high-gain processes are hindered by adding one).

The capstone selection task chains all of it: predict the installed drift from the pressure-drop ratio, screen candidates on rated rangeability against the required turndown before distortion is even considered, then check whether a positioner genuinely helps or is limited out of contention for this loop — the characteristic that survives all three checks, not the one with the prettiest inherent curve, is the one to specify.

activities.title: Predict the Drift — Pressure-Drop Ratio Cards
activities.description: In pairs, work three scenario cards, each naming a candidate valve's inherent characteristic (linear, equal-percentage, or quick-opening) and the share of total system pressure drop the valve itself will take at design flow (e.g., 80% of system ΔP vs. 20% of system ΔP). For each card, pairs predict — using the installed-vs-inherent mechanism just taught — whether the installed characteristic will track close to the inherent curve or diverge from it, and in which direction, then justify the prediction in one sentence. Debrief compares the three predictions side by side and ties the correct pattern back to why the equal-percentage/linear pairing guidance in the source material exists at all: to compensate for the rest of the loop's own gain changes, not as an arbitrary catalog rule.

chapters.title: Shutoff/Leakage Classification, Pressure-Temperature Rating & Standards
chapters._source: Enabling Competency `eng.selection.shutoff-leakage-and-standards` — see Curriculum — CVE1.md and Competency Hierarchy — CVE1, CVE2, CVE3 v3.md, Chapter 5. Modules below are STUBS ONLY (status: outline, empty keyConcepts) pending a real Stage 1 arc-cut per module.

modules.title: Leakage Classification & Fugitive-Emissions Standards
modules.stakes: A valve specified against the wrong leakage class is a commissioning or audit failure — expensive to catch late, avoidable by treating standards as a first-class selection criterion.
modules.objective: Classify a service's required shutoff via FCI 70-2/ANSI leakage classes and select trim/seat to meet it, and interpret ISO 15848-1 fugitive-emissions qualification requirements and measured leak-rate data.

primitives.t: A valve spec'd to Class VI when the service only ever needed Class IV isn't the safe choice — it's the expensive one, in purchase price and in ongoing maintenance. A valve spec'd to Class IV when the service actually needed Class VI is the one that fails a commissioning audit or leaks the plant's own methane inventory to atmosphere. Which class does THIS service genuinely require, and which standard would you point to if asked to prove it before the valve ships?
primitives.sourceNote: Prime opens on the module's own stakes line plus cvh-topic-seat-leakage-classification/ogas-topic-shutoff-leakage-classification's shared finding that 'users commonly overestimate the shutoff class they actually need' — no single figure represents the over/under-spec stakes question itself. The atmosphere/methane framing reaches ahead to this module's second competency (ISO 15848-1 fugitive emissions) since prime opens the whole module, not just the first competency, per this course's own convention on other multi-competency modules.
primitives.templateRationale: A stakes-framing question before either standard's detail arrives, per Axis 3's prime role. No figure represents the over-spec/under-spec tension as a concept in its own right, so this uses the plain-tagline shape.

primitives.t: ANSI/FCI 70-2 and IEC 60534-4 define six seat-leakage classes, and each is a genuinely different test, not just an escalating number on one scale. Class I requires no test at all — supplier/user agreement only. Classes II, III, and IV are air-or-water tests at a fixed differential pressure, allowing 0.5%, 0.1%, and 0.01% of rated capacity respectively — roughly a ×10 tightening step by step. Class V is a water test run at the valve's actual maximum service pressure drop, rated in ml/min per inch of port diameter per psi differential — a different kind of test, not just a smaller number on the Class II-IV scale. Class VI, the tightest, is an air/nitrogen bubbles-per-minute test against a submerged-tube apparatus, tabulated separately by port diameter.

No valve-seat photo or cutaway exists to attach numbered part markers to; the six-row class table is the content itself.

primitives.t: Before specifying a seat/trim construction, first confirm the shutoff class the service duty genuinely requires against the six-class table just taught — the classification is a factory-test comparison basis among similarly-configured valves, not a field-leakage guarantee, and it is common to over-specify past what the duty actually needs, at real and recurring cost (a tighter class costs more to buy and to maintain). Once the real target class is set, meeting it is a construction decision, not a spec-sheet checkbox: it depends on matched seat material, seat preparation, and adequate seat load together — the same class number claimed with an inadequate seat load or the wrong seat material for the service will not hold in the field even though it passed the factory test. The stakes rise sharply with pressure drop: at high ΔP, seat leakage that would be a minor nuisance at low pressure can progress to trim erosion and eventual trim destruction — the case where paying for both the tighter class and the construction it actually demands is justified.

The worked selection above stays to what those four sources actually state (the class-selection judgment, the factory-test-vs-field-performance caveat, seat material/preparation/load as the real construction lever, and the high-ΔP trim-destruction consequence) rather than asserting a specific seat-material-to-class ceiling (e.g. 'metal seat tops out at Class IV/V, soft seat reaches Class VI') — that mapping is common Handbook knowledge and is even implied by cvh-cmp-seat-load-graph's own metal-seated-valves-only Class II-V seat-load chart, but that figure and its topic (cvh-topic-seat-load) are registered in this course to a different competency (eng.actuation.actuator-selection-and-force-torque-sizing.calculate-sliding-stem-thrust), and curriculum-development.md's asset-variant discipline treats a competency×asset-variant reuse as a human-curated call, not one Stage 2 should make unilaterally. Not a case-walkthrough or multi-panel contrast — one reasoning chain, one table.

primitives.t: ISO 15848-1 qualification runs three separate measures together, not one pass/fail number. A mechanical-cycle count set by valve type — 20,000/60,000/100,000 cycles for control-valve classes CC1/CC2/CC3, but a genuinely different and far lower 205/1,500/2,500 cycles for isolation-valve classes CO1/CO2/CO3, because an isolation valve doesn't stroke repeatedly in service the way a control valve does. A thermal-cycle count run alongside that mechanical cycling. And a tightness class (AM/BM/CM) cross-referenced to a fixed measured-leak-concentration ceiling (<50/<100/<500 ppm, EPA Method 21 sniffing). A qualification result is only meaningful as the combination of all three — a tightness class quoted with no cycle count attached doesn't say how hard the seal was actually worked to earn it.

primitives.t: Reading a real qualification report means checking a specific measured number against a specific class threshold on the correct scale. A stem-seal design's measured leak rate (mg·s⁻¹·m⁻¹ of stem perimeter, or atm·cm³·s⁻¹·mm⁻¹ of stem diameter) is checked against the AH/BH/CH maximum-rate thresholds to assign a leak-RATE tightness class. Its measured leak concentration (ppm, EPA Method 21 sniffing) is checked separately against the AM/BM/CM concentration thresholds to assign a leak-CONCENTRATION tightness class — two independently measured results, denoted by the H and M suffixes, not the same number read on two scales. Class A, the tightest letter on either scale, is realistically achievable only with a bellows design — a plain packing gland reporting a Class A result is a number worth re-checking against the actual test method before it is accepted at face value.

reground.hook: A screw-top lid on a jar does two separate jobs, and testing it for one doesn't test it for the other. First: does it actually stop the jar's contents from sloshing out when you tip it over? Some lids only need to mostly not spill; a lid on something dangerous needs to genuinely not open at all, and there's a real, tested difference between those two promises. Second, and separately: even a lid that stops sloshing might still slowly seep vapor around the threads for years — a completely different failure, tested a completely different way, with its own separate pass/fail line.
reground.bridge: A control valve carries exactly that same two-part promise, at industrial scale, each with its own named standard. FCI 70-2's six classes (I through VI) are the 'does it actually shut off' test — how much process fluid can still get through the closed valve, tested once at the factory. ISO 15848-1 is the completely separate 'does it leak to atmosphere over time' test — how much of what's inside the valve seeps out around the moving stem, tested across thousands of open/close cycles and thermal swings, because a seal that's tight on day one can fail slowly, the way a jar lid can start seeping months after it was sealed. Specifying only one of the two, or assuming a good score on one implies a good score on the other, misses that they are answering different physical questions with different tests.
reground.depth:
ANSI/FCI 70-2 (harmonized with IEC 60534-4) defines six seat-leakage classes, each a genuinely different test rather than a point on one continuous scale: Class I requires no factory test at all, by supplier/user agreement; Classes II, III, and IV are air-or-water tests at a fixed differential pressure, allowing 0.5%, 0.1%, and 0.01% of rated capacity respectively; Class V is a water test at the valve's actual maximum service pressure drop, rated in ml/min per inch of port diameter per psi differential; Class VI, the tightest, is an air/nitrogen bubbles-per-minute test against a submerged-tube apparatus, tabulated separately by port diameter.

Selecting a class is a judgment call, not a default to the tightest option: the class is a factory-test comparison basis among similarly-configured valves, not a guarantee of actual field leakage (real service leakage depends on pressure drop, temperature, sealing-surface condition, and actuator force, none of which the class number alone captures); users commonly over-specify past what the duty genuinely needs; and a tighter class costs measurably more to buy and to maintain.

Once a target class is genuinely justified, meeting it in the field depends on matching seat material, seat preparation, and seat load to that class — not just naming the class on a spec sheet — and the consequence of getting this wrong scales sharply with pressure drop: at high ΔP, seat leakage that would be a minor nuisance at low pressure can progress to trim erosion and eventual trim destruction, which is exactly the scenario where paying for both the tighter class and the construction it demands is justified.

ISO 15848-1 governs an entirely separate leakage path — stem-seal (packing) leakage to atmosphere, not seat shutoff — and qualifies a design against three measures at once, not a single number: a mechanical-cycle count set by valve type (20,000/60,000/100,000 cycles for control-valve classes CC1/CC2/CC3; a much lower 205/1,500/2,500 cycles for isolation-valve classes CO1/CO2/CO3, reflecting how much less often an isolation valve actually strokes), a thermal-cycle count run alongside that mechanical cycling, and a tightness class assigned from measured data on one of two independent bases: a leak-RATE basis (classes AH/BH/CH, measured in mg·s⁻¹·m⁻¹ of stem perimeter or atm·cm³·s⁻¹·mm⁻¹ of stem diameter) or a leak-CONCENTRATION basis (classes AM/BM/CM, measured in ppm via EPA Method 21 sniffing, cross-referenced to the same <50/<100/<500 ppm thresholds the qualification-requirements table states).

These are two different measured results on two different physical bases, denoted by their H and M suffixes — not the same number expressed two ways — and Class A on either scale is realistically achievable only with a bellows-sealed design, itself worth checking before a Class A claim on ordinary packing is accepted at face value. A qualification result quoted as a bare tightness class, with no cycle count attached, has not actually stated how hard the seal was worked to earn that class.

For each card, pairs read off the FCI 70-2/ANSI leakage class the stated duty actually requires from the classification table just taught, then pick the trim/seat construction level (metal seat, resilient/soft seat, lapped soft seat) that meets that class and justify the pick against the table's own test-medium and allowable-leakage columns — not a guess at which sounds 'tighter.' Debrief compares the three picks and ties each back to the specific class definition that drove it.

modules.title: P-T Rating & Code Jurisdiction
modules.stakes: A body/bonnet rated for the wrong pressure-temperature class or the wrong code jurisdiction is a mechanically sound valve that still fails inspection.
modules.objective: Apply pressure-temperature rating classes and material-selection criteria to verify a body/bonnet's rated class, and cross-reference applicable standards to identify the correct code jurisdiction.

primitives.t: A body/bonnet nameplate reads Class 300 — is that adequate for this service, at this temperature, on this installation? Two separate questions hide inside that one number. First: a pressure class isn't a fixed rating — the same Class 300 body holds less pressure as service temperature climbs, and a class chosen for the wrong temperature is a body that looks correctly specified and isn't. Second, even a body/bonnet whose class genuinely fits the service can still fail an inspection if it sits somewhere a different code governs — a valve connected straight to a boiler drum answers to different jurisdiction, administered differently, than a mechanically identical valve installed a few feet downstream on ordinary plant piping. Verifying a class and identifying the correct jurisdiction are two separate checks, and skipping either is what turns a mechanically sound valve into a rejected shipment.
primitives.sourceNote: Prime opens on the module's own stakes line, framed against both of this module's competencies since prime opens the whole module, not just the first competency (same convention this course's own cve1-ch5-m1 slide 67 prime uses). The P-T half draws on pss-topic-pressure-temperature-material-selection-criteria/pss-topic-pressure-rating-classes's own point that not every class is available in every material and that a class's real pressure ceiling falls with rising temperature; the jurisdiction half reaches ahead to pss-topic-boiler-piping-code-jurisdiction's boiler-proper/external-piping boundary. No single figure represents the combined verify-the-class/identify-the-jurisdiction tension as a concept in its own right.

primitives.t: ANSI B16.34 divides pressure-temperature ratings into four real tiers, not one scale with different numbers. Standard Class covers the normal ANSI 150-4500 ratings most products use, published for a variety of materials. Intermediate Standard Class falls between standard ratings — reached with extra body/bonnet wall thickness and stronger body-to-bonnet bolting, no NDE required, and available only on butt-weld-end (BWE) valves, which lets a cheaper product serve a higher-duty application. Special Class is typically higher than standard ratings, obtained instead by ultrasonic or radiographic testing (NDE) of the body and bonnet castings, and is available on any BWE globe or angle valve. Intermediate Special Class requires BOTH the NDE of Special Class AND the extra wall thickness/bolt strength of Intermediate Standard, and is only available on BWE valves that already carry intermediate ratings. All three non-standard classes carry real pricing implications. Because NDE (radiographic, ultrasonic, magnetic-particle, or liquid-penetrant examination — B16.34's own methods are preferred over the comparable MSS standards for broader acceptance) gates the special and intermediate-special ratings, the personnel performing it must be qualified per SNT-TC-1A: the rating-class decision and the personnel-qualification requirement are directly coupled, not independent purchasing choices.

primitives.t: Three General Selection Criteria interlink to set a body/bonnet's actual spec, and none of the three stands alone. Pressure rating is ordinarily set by ANSI pressure class — 150/300/600 are the most common for steel and stainless — and each class's own maximum-pressure ceiling decreases as service temperature rises, per the material's own strength curve; not every product is available in every class, so this genuinely narrows real choices rather than just labeling them. Temperature considerations layer on top: body-material strength and ductility limits, relative thermal expansion, and soft-part limits — elastomers to roughly 200-350°F, PTFE to roughly 450°F. Moving from PTFE to metal seals to survive higher temperature generally increases shutoff leakage, and high-temperature metal bearing sleeves in rotary valves impose more shaft friction than PTFE bearings, which reduces the pressure-drop load the shaft can withstand at shutoff — a temperature decision has real downstream consequences for sealing and shutoff performance, not just material cost. Material selection is the most complex of the three: corrosion, erosion, flashing, cavitation, and process pressure/temperature are weighed together. Piping material usually indicates body material, but valve-internal velocity typically runs higher than pipe velocity, so other factors often make the valve and piping materials genuinely differ. Trim material follows from body material, temperature range, and fluid properties; bar stock or lined bodies get considered specifically when the service's needed body material isn't available as carbon, alloy, or stainless steel.

The source itself treats these three criteria (pressure/temperature/material) as one interlinked Table 1-1 entry rather than three separable facts, since temperature drives material limits and material drives pressure-class availability — preserved as one slide rather than split, matching the source's own structure.
primitives.templateRationale: How the three criteria physically interlink (temperature limits driving material choice, material choice constraining which pressure class is even available) is a structure to understand, the Axis 3 default treatment for 'understand' content, even though the content is prose/tabular rather than a cutaway — no schematic exists for this reasoning chain.

primitives.t: Verifying a stated body/bonnet class is a specific sequence, not a glance at the nameplate. First, read the nameplate class (say, Class 300) and check it against the real service pressure and temperature — because a class's maximum allowable pressure falls as temperature rises, the same class number that comfortably covers the service at low temperature can fail to cover it at high temperature, so the check has to be run at the actual service condition, not the class's headline rating. Second, identify which of ANSI B16.34's four tiers the nameplate class actually claims: Standard Class needs no further check; but a claimed Intermediate Standard, Special, or Intermediate Special rating is only valid on a butt-weld-end valve, and it has to be backed by the matching documentation — extra wall-thickness/bolting records for the intermediate tiers, NDE records (radiographic, ultrasonic, magnetic-particle, or liquid-penetrant) for the special tiers, performed by SNT-TC-1A-qualified personnel. A non-standard class claimed with no such documentation on file is a rating that has not actually been earned. Third, confirm material suitability at the same service condition: soft parts (elastomers, PTFE) within their real temperature limits, and trim material appropriate to the service's corrosion/erosion/flashing/cavitation profile, not just carried over from the body material by default.

primitives.t: Power-plant code compliance turns on which side of a real physical boundary a valve sits on. The 'boiler proper' — superheaters, economizers, reheaters, steam/water drums, and other pressure parts connected directly to the boiler with no intervening valve — falls under the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code's (BPVC) administrative AND technical jurisdiction; Fisher does not manufacture equipment installed there at all. 'Boiler external piping' begins at a specific, code-defined termination point — the first circumferential weld end, the face of the first flange, or the first threaded joint — and can still include real control equipment (the source's own example is a steam-drum level controller); it is governed administratively by ASME BPVC but technically by ASME Section Committee B31.1, meaning the design and construction rules live in ANSI/ASME B31.1 while code certification, data forms, stamping, and inspection follow ASME BPVC Section I when required. The practical consequence: vendors must be able to supply inspection records, data reports, and stamping for boiler-external equipment, unless a specific BPVC Section I waiver applies — parts already compliant with an ANSI product standard or a manufacturer's standard, meeting separate material/welding/radiography/heat-treatment documentation requirements, which lets Fisher comply with BPVC Section I without code stamping. Power-plant piping that is neither boiler-proper nor boiler-external is covered by ANSI/ASME B31.1 alone, with ANSI B16.34 as the applicable valve design standard; the code prohibits ungasketed, screwed bonnets on steam-service valves rated over 250 psig.
