primitives.t: The chapter positions a cluster of standards relative to ANSI B16.34 rather than treating each as independent — some now superseded, some still current, one explicitly out of scope for control valves. ANSI B16.5 (flange/flanged-fitting design) was itself a valve design standard before 1973 (butt-weld end) and 1977 (flanged end); design responsibility then transferred to B16.34, and B16.5 now mainly serves as a dimensional/rating reference — 'mates with ANSI XXX flanges' — though older specs may still cite it as the design basis. MSS SP-66, a valve design standard published before B16.34 existed, should generally now be superseded by B16.34 conformance; its 'special inspections' concept for raising pressure-temperature ratings is replaced by B16.34's own special-class ratings. MSS SP-67 (butterfly-valve design/test performance and its own three leak classes — Type I tight shutoff, Type II low-leakage, Type III nominal leakage) has had those leak classes superseded in most control-valve usage by ANSI/FCI 70-2 classes; the source adds a caution not captured there — its seat-leak test procedure isn't adequate to recognize leak-rate differences across different trim styles and sizes, so for control valves specifically the source directs the reader to ISA S75.19 and ANSI/FCI 70-2 instead, though SP-67 still supplies face-to-face dimensions for certain butterfly valves. ANSI B16.10 (face-to-face dimensions for gate/plug/check/ball/control valves within named size and class bounds) is current and unsuperseded. ANSI B16.37 (hydrostatic testing at 1.5× cold working pressure per B16.34) is current; Fisher's actual practice adds a post-assembly aerostatic test to confirm gasket-joint integrity beyond the bare code requirement. MSS SP-53/54/55 (magnetic-particle, radiographic, and visual examination of castings, respectively) are effectively superseded — B16.34 or ASTM E94-equivalent methods are recommended instead for broader acceptance. MSS SP-61 (pressure testing of steel valves generally) is not superseded but is out of scope here — it is explicitly NOT intended for control valves; its seat-closure tests are written for shutoff/isolation/on-off/block valves.

primitives.t: Identifying the correct code jurisdiction for a real installation means running the boundary rule and the standards crosswalk together, in sequence, not treating either alone as the answer. First, locate the valve's connection point against the boiler-proper/boiler-external-piping boundary using the termination-point rule — the first circumferential weld end, the face of the first flange, or the first threaded joint. That placement fixes jurisdiction: inside the boundary, ASME BPVC governs both administratively and technically and Fisher doesn't supply equipment there at all; on boiler-external piping, ASME BPVC governs administratively while ANSI/ASME B31.1 governs technically, and inspection/data-report/stamping documentation is required unless a specific BPVC Section I waiver applies; everywhere else on power-plant piping, B31.1 governs alone. Second, once the governing code is fixed, cross-reference which of the design/test/dimensional standards actually apply under it: ANSI B16.34 as the design standard itself; ANSI B16.10 for face-to-face dimensions; ANSI B16.37 for hydrostatic testing; and — critically — checking whether an older spec's citation of MSS SP-66, MSS SP-67's leak classes, or MSS SP-53/54/55 is still valid or has been superseded by B16.34/ANSI-FCI-70-2/ASTM E94 conformance. Getting the code jurisdiction right while still citing a superseded standard for the supporting requirement is only half the cross-reference done.

Kept as a plain case-walkthrough rather than a decision table — unlike slide 78's flat current/superseded listing, this slide's content is a two-step reasoning chain applied to one scenario, not a lookup table, so the case-walkthrough shape (matching this module's own m2-act2 activity framing) fits better than a table.

reground.hook: A rope rated to hold 500 pounds doesn't hold 500 pounds at every temperature — heat it up and the exact same rope frays and gives out at a fraction of that load. And a rope that is genuinely strong enough for the job can still be the wrong rope for where it's being used: a rope hung over a practice climbing wall answers to different inspection rules than a mechanically identical rope holding an elevator car, even though nothing about the rope itself changed.
reground.bridge: A control valve's body/bonnet carries exactly that same two-part catch. Its nameplate pressure class isn't one fixed number — the pressure it can actually hold falls as service temperature climbs, so the class stamped on the tag has to be checked against the real operating condition, not just read off at face value. And separately, even a body/bonnet whose class is entirely correct for the service can still fail an inspection if it happens to sit in the wrong place: a valve connected straight to a boiler drum answers to a different code, administered differently, than a mechanically identical valve installed a few feet downstream on ordinary plant piping.
reground.depth:
ANSI B16.34 governs a body/bonnet's pressure-temperature rating through three interlinked General Selection Criteria that never separate cleanly: pressure rating is set by ANSI class (150/300/600 most common for steel/stainless), and each class's real pressure ceiling falls as temperature rises per the material's own strength curve — not every class is even available in every material, so this genuinely narrows real choices. Temperature also bounds soft-part selection (elastomers to roughly 200-350°F, PTFE to roughly 450°F) and reaches into sealing performance: swapping PTFE for metal seals at high temperature generally increases shutoff leakage, and high-temperature metal bearing sleeves in rotary valves add shaft friction that reduces the pressure-drop load the shaft can withstand at shutoff. Material selection is the most complex of the three, weighing corrosion, erosion, flashing, cavitation, and process pressure/temperature together; valve materials often differ from piping materials because in-valve velocity runs higher, and bar-stock or lined bodies get considered specifically when the needed body material isn't available as carbon, alloy, or stainless steel.

Within that pressure-class framework, ANSI B16.34 further divides ratings into four real tiers, not one continuous scale: Standard Class (the normal ANSI 150-4500 ratings); Intermediate Standard Class (extra body/bonnet wall thickness and stronger bolting, no NDE required, butt-weld-end (BWE) valves only); Special Class (higher ratings via ultrasonic or radiographic NDE of the body/bonnet castings, available on any BWE globe or angle valve); and Intermediate Special Class (requires BOTH Special Class's NDE and Intermediate Standard's extra wall thickness/bolting, on BWE valves that already carry intermediate ratings). All three non-standard tiers carry real cost implications, and because NDE gates them, the personnel performing it must be SNT-TC-1A qualified — rating class and personnel qualification are coupled requirements, not independent purchasing decisions.

Verifying a stated class in practice means checking the nameplate class against the real service pressure AND temperature (not the class's headline rating), confirming which tier is actually being claimed, and — for a non-standard tier — confirming the BWE construction and the matching wall-thickness/bolting or NDE documentation is actually on file, alongside confirming soft-part and trim-material suitability at that same service condition.

Code jurisdiction runs on a separate, physically-defined boundary. The 'boiler proper' (superheaters, economizers, reheaters, steam/water drums and other pressure parts connected directly to the boiler with no intervening valve) falls under ASME BPVC's own administrative AND technical jurisdiction, and Fisher does not manufacture equipment installed there. 'Boiler external piping' begins at a specific termination point — the first circumferential weld end, the face of the first flange, or the first threaded joint — and can still carry real control equipment (the source's own example is a steam-drum level controller); it is governed administratively by ASME BPVC but technically by ANSI/ASME B31.1, so design/construction rules live in B31.1 while certification, data forms, stamping, and inspection follow BPVC Section I when required — unless a specific Section I waiver applies (parts already compliant with an ANSI product standard or a manufacturer's standard, backed by separate material/welding/radiography/heat-treatment documentation), which lets Fisher comply with Section I without code stamping. Power-plant piping that is neither boiler-proper nor boiler-external falls to B31.1 alone, with B16.34 as the applicable valve design standard, and the code prohibits ungasketed, screwed bonnets on steam-service valves over 250 psig.

Naming the governing code is only half the cross-reference: a cluster of supporting standards has to be checked for whether it is still current. ANSI B16.5 was itself a valve design standard before 1973/1977, superseded by B16.34, and now mainly a flange/dimensional reference. MSS SP-66, a pre-B16.34 design standard, is generally superseded by B16.34 conformance, its 'special inspections' concept for raising ratings replaced by B16.34's own special-class ratings. MSS SP-67's own butterfly-valve leak classes (Type I/II/III) have been superseded in most control-valve usage by ANSI/FCI 70-2, though SP-67 still supplies face-to-face dimensions for certain butterfly valves, and the source flags that its seat-leak test procedure can't reliably distinguish leak-rate differences across trim styles and sizes — for control valves the source points instead to ISA S75.19 and ANSI/FCI 70-2. ANSI B16.10 (face-to-face dimensions) and ANSI B16.37 (hydrostatic testing at 1.5× cold working pressure, with Fisher adding its own post-assembly aerostatic test) remain current and unsuperseded. MSS SP-53/54/55 (magnetic-particle/radiographic/visual casting examination) are effectively superseded by B16.34 or ASTM E94-equivalent methods. MSS SP-61 (pressure testing of steel valves generally) isn't superseded but is simply out of scope for control valves — its seat-closure tests are written for shutoff/isolation/on-off/block valves. A verification that gets the governing code right while still citing a superseded supporting standard has only done half the job.

chapters.title: Actuator Selection & Force/Torque Sizing
chapters._source: Enabling Competency `eng.actuation.actuator-selection-and-force-torque-sizing` — see Curriculum — CVE1.md and Competency Hierarchy — CVE1, CVE2, CVE3 v3.md, Chapter 6. Modules below are STUBS ONLY (status: outline, empty keyConcepts) pending a real Stage 1 arc-cut per module.

modules.title: Actuator Mechanism Types & Selection
modules.stakes: An actuator selected without regard to fail-safe action fails to the wrong position on loss of air — a safety-critical mistake, not a performance one.
modules.objective: Distinguish actuator mechanism types — spring-diaphragm, piston, rack-and-pinion, electric, manual — from photo/cutaway, and select an actuator type and fail-safe action for a given service and orientation.

primitives.t: Direct- and reverse-acting spring-and-diaphragm actuators are built from the same core parts — diaphragm casing, diaphragm and plate, actuator spring, spring seat and adjuster, yoke, stem connector, travel indicator and scale — with air pressure and spring force driving the stem in opposite directions between the two designs; the reverse-acting unit additionally carries a seal bushing and O-rings, handwheel-mounting bosses, an integral air passage, and an integral DVC6200 mounting pad not found on the direct-acting baseline.

items.t: Direct-acting — the baseline 12-part construction: diaphragm casing, diaphragm, diaphragm plate, actuator spring, spring seat/adjuster, yoke, stem connector, travel indicator disk and scale.

Reverse-acting — the same core parts with action reversed, plus four features the direct-acting design doesn't carry: seal bushing and O-rings, integrated handwheel-mounting bosses, an integral air passage, and an integral DVC6200 mounting pad.

primitives.templateRationale: Two fully-labelled cutaways (CVH Figs. 1.9/1.12), each carrying its own printed numbered key — Style Guide §6.2 applies (the source's own numbering stays as printed; Stage 3's on-slide key reads off each figure's own callout numbers rather than a house renumbering). Composed per §5.14 as two separate images if placed on one slide; the item captions summarize each figure at the whole-image level — the individual 12-/16-part callout labels are read directly off each figure's own printed key, not restated here.

primitives.t: A spring-and-diaphragm actuator drives the same basic mechanism whether the valve is sliding-stem or rotary — air pressure against the diaphragm working against the spring. On a sliding-stem valve that motion is delivered straight through the stem; on a rotary valve the identical linear stem motion is converted to disk or ball rotation through a lever and shaft. The actuator's power mechanism doesn't change type between the two — only how its output motion reaches the closure member does.

items.t: A typical spring-and-diaphragm actuator assembly — the linear, sliding-stem output this design normally delivers.
The rotary counterpart: the same loading-pressure/diaphragm/spring construction, with a lever and shaft converting the actuator stem's linear motion into disk or ball rotation.

primitives.templateRationale: Cross-chapter pairing verified against each figure's own teaches text before use: CVH Fig. 8.4 (ch8) is confirmed generic — 'not specific to direct- or reverse-acting configuration' — the right choice to stand for the sliding-stem case without reusing slide 81's already-shown direct-/reverse-acting figures; CVH Fig. 1.17 (ch1) is confirmed by its own catalog note to be 'the rotary counterpart to the sliding-stem actuator cutaways in Figures 1.9/1.12, showing how linear actuator stem motion is converted to disk/ball rotation through the lever and shaft' — exactly the mechanism this slide teaches. Mechanism role (schematic/cutaway, Axis 3's default for understand) fits; two images are necessary because the conversion mechanism can't be shown in one image alone.

primitives.t: A piston actuator uses a piston with an O-ring or quad-ring seal inside a cylinder, supplied with plant air up to 150 psig — higher pressure than a spring-and-diaphragm design uses — for higher thrust and faster stroking. Air to only one side of the piston makes it single-acting (spring-return, inherently fail-open or fail-closed); air to both sides makes it double-acting, giving maximum force in both directions but requiring an accessory such as a trip valve or lock-up system to fail safely on loss of supply pressure.

items.t: The baseline piston-actuator construction: loading pressure connection, piston, piston seal, cylinder, cylinder closure seal, seal bushing, stem connector.
The double-acting variant — air supplied to both sides of the piston for maximum force in either direction, at the cost of needing a fail-safe accessory the single-acting design doesn't.

primitives.templateRationale: Base 7-part cutaway (CVH Fig. 1.10, its own printed key, §6.2) plus the double-acting variant photo (CVH Fig. 3.46) — grounded directly by cvh-topic-actuator-mechanism-basics' single-/double-acting distinction (CVH §8.5.1-8.5.2) plus each figure's own teaches text. Mechanism role fits: how the piston actuator works, and the one construction choice (one-side vs. two-side air supply) that produces the double-acting variant.

primitives.t: Because the yoke arm's mechanical advantage changes continuously through the stroke, a Scotch-yoke actuator's torque output isn't flat across its rotation the way a diaphragm actuator's force curve is — it varies with rotation angle. That's part of why rotary actuator sizing (covered later this chapter) checks torque at more than one point in the stroke instead of a single nominal number.
primitives.templateRationale: Single figure (CVH Fig. 3.47), no key needed beyond a plain caption — the piston family's rotary-conversion variant, following directly from slide 83's base piston/double-acting content.

primitives.t: Manual actuators trade automatic control for low cost and simplicity — commonly actuating the bypass valve in a three-valve bypass loop, for manual process control during maintenance or shutdown of the automatic loop. Construction differs only by valve family: a sliding-stem version for globe-style valves, a rotary version for rotary valves; some models of either add a dial-indicating device for accurate plug or disk repositioning.

items.t: Sliding-stem manual actuator — for globe-style valves, often the bypass-loop actuator during maintenance or shutdown of the automatic loop.
Rotary manual actuator — same role, for rotary valves.

primitives.templateRationale: Exactly two named variants (sliding-stem, rotary) of the same manual-actuator concept — the canonical two-panel contrast shape (CVH Figs. 3.48/3.49, same §3.8.3 description).

primitives.t: Backlash is what actually blocks precision throttling, not just a spec-sheet limitation: when the control signal reverses direction, the pinion has to travel through the play in the gear mesh before the rack — and the valve stem with it — starts moving the other way, so small corrections near a setpoint don't produce a proportional valve response. That dead zone doesn't matter for a valve that's only ever fully open or fully closed, which is why rack-and-pinion stays an on/off choice.
primitives.templateRationale: Single figure (CVH Fig. 3.50), no key needed — states the one selection-relevant limitation (gear backlash forces on/off-only duty) directly from the source.

primitives.t: Electric actuators use a motor with gear reduction to move the valve — traditionally on/off-only, though some modern designs support continuous control; brushless motors reduce or eliminate motor burnout from frequent on/off cycling. Construction differs only by valve family (sliding-stem or rotary); initial cost stays above pneumatic actuation, so electric actuators are usually reserved for sites without instrument air or with too few valves to justify a compressor system.

items.t: Electric actuator for a sliding-stem valve — motor plus gear reduction.
Electric actuator for a rotary valve — same motor/gear-reduction construction.

primitives.templateRationale: Two variant photos (CVH Figs. 3.51/3.52) of the same mechanism, kept under the mechanism role Stage 1 assigned to this slide. Note: this slide shares the identical sliding-stem/rotary-pairing shape as slide 85's contrast role — flagged under Concept-map gaps as a possible Stage 1 role inconsistency, not changed here per the outer-field-preservation rule.

primitives.t: Five parameters quickly narrow an actuator choice, before any specific type is picked: power-source availability (air, electricity, or hydraulic/pipeline pressure — weighed on the cost and reliability of supplying it at the valve, plus backup power for critical loops), fail-safe requirement, torque/thrust requirement, control function (two-position on/off versus continuous throttling — throttling additionally demands compatibility with the instrument signal and low hysteresis/minimal deadband that can't be bolted on after the fact), and economics (initial cost, maintenance, and reliability together, not cost alone).
primitives.sourceNote: figures: [] in the CVE1 asset-variant registry for eng.actuation.actuator-selection-and-force-torque-sizing.select-actuator-type-and-failsafe — the five parameters are prose-only content (pss-topic-actuator-selection-parameters, Power & Severe Service Sourcebook).
primitives.templateRationale: Opens this module's second competency on the framing question — the five parameters that govern every actuator selection to follow — before any specific construction category is compared, per Axis 3's prime role (comes first, before the mechanism). No figure exists for this framing list; the module's own stakes line already primes the fail-safe half, this slide supplies the other four.

primitives.t: Actuators fall into four general categories — spring-and-diaphragm, pneumatic piston, electric motor, electro-hydraulic — available for either sliding-stem or rotary bodies; the four categories differ only by linkage, not by power source. A rotary actuator needs a linkage, gear, or crank arm to convert the actuator's linear diaphragm/piston motion into the 90-degree rotation a rotary valve needs, introducing a lost-motion risk at every linkage point; a sliding-stem actuator is rigidly fixed to the valve stem with no linkage at all, so it has no lost motion and inherently better control characteristics. Where a linkage does exist, the coupling method matters: a slotted connector on a milled shaft flat is generally unsatisfactory, a pinned connection suits nominal torque, and a splined connector rigidly clamped to a splined shaft eliminates lost motion entirely and handles high torque.
primitives.sourceNote: figures: [] in the registry for this competency — pss-topic-actuator-design-categories-and-linkage (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook) is prose-only; no figure anchors the four-category/linkage distinction.
primitives.templateRationale: How-it-works content (rotary linkage vs. sliding-stem no-linkage, and why coupling method matters) is the Axis 3 default mechanism treatment even without a figure — same precedent as cve1-ch1-m2 slides 10/16. No figure is registered; Stage 3 will need an originated diagram (four category icons plus the rotary-linkage/sliding-stem-no-linkage contrast) rather than a Source Library redraw — flagged under Asset-variant gaps.

primitives.t: The real cost/thrust/speed/fail-safe tradeoffs across all five actuator types, side by side: spring-and-diaphragm is lowest cost, throttles without a positioner, and is inherently fail-safe, but has limited output and larger size/weight for the thrust delivered; pneumatic piston gives high thrust in a compact, lightweight package with fast stroking, but costs more, needs an accessory or spring to fail safely, and needs a positioner for throttling; electric motor is compact and very stiff with high output, but has no inherent fail-safe, a limited duty cycle, and slow stroking; electro-hydraulic gives the highest output, stiffness, and throttling performance with fast stroking, but at the highest cost and hardest maintenance. The closing guidance holds regardless of the table: consider the simplest design — spring-and-diaphragm — first, and trade away that simplicity only for a thrust, speed, or duty-cycle requirement it genuinely can't meet.
primitives.sourceNote: figures: [] in the registry for this competency — pss-topic-actuator-type-comparison-summary (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook, its own real Table 2-6) is prose-only; the comparison is the source's own named table, not an image.

primitives.t: Given a stated service — power source available, mounting orientation, duty (on/off vs. continuous throttling), and how critical the fail-safe position is — work the five selection parameters and the type-comparison table just shown into one actuator-type-plus-fail-safe-action call, the same judgment a real selection spec has to make.

This is also the direct lead-in to the module's own act2 case-walkthrough activity.

reground.hook: Every powered gate, garage door, or airport jet bridge is moved by some 'muscle' behind it — a motor, a piston, a spring pushing back against pressure. Different muscles suit different jobs: a garage-door spring is cheap and self-closes if the power goes out, but nobody would put that same spring on a dump-truck bed — that job needs a hydraulic ram.
reground.bridge: A control valve's actuator is exactly that muscle, and this module is the same choice made for real: five families — spring-and-diaphragm, piston, rack-and-pinion, electric, manual — each with a different mix of cost, speed, thrust, and what happens if the power source itself fails, where picking the wrong one for a given service and mounting orientation is a spec mistake with the same shape as bolting a garage-door spring onto a dump truck.
reground.depth:
Five actuator mechanism families move a control valve's closure member, and each is built as either a linear (sliding-stem) or rotary design, drawing on the same underlying power-source options. Spring-and-diaphragm actuators are the most common — dependable, simple, economical, inherently fail-safe — and come direct-acting or reverse-acting (net thrust is diaphragm force minus opposing spring force in both cases; the reverse-acting design adds a seal bushing/O-rings, handwheel-mounting bosses, an integral air passage, and a DVC6200 mounting pad the direct-acting baseline doesn't carry), with a rotary version that converts the identical linear stem motion to disk/ball rotation through a lever and shaft.

Piston actuators trade some of that simplicity for thrust and speed: supplied with plant air up to 150 psig, they are single-acting/spring-return (inherently fail-open or fail-closed) or double-acting (maximum force in both directions, but needing an accessory such as a trip valve or lock-up system to fail safely on loss of supply); the Scotch-yoke is the piston family's rotary-conversion variant, translating linear piston motion into shaft rotation through a yoke.

Manual actuators trade automatic control away entirely for low cost, most often actuating the bypass valve in a three-valve bypass loop during maintenance or shutdown of the automatic loop. Rack-and-pinion actuators are compact and economical for rotary valves, but backlash in the gear mesh confines them to on/off duty, never precision throttling. Electric actuators (motor plus gear reduction) suit sites without instrument air or with too few valves to justify a compressor, traditionally on/off-only though some now support continuous control, with brushless motors reducing burnout from frequent cycling — at a purchase cost that stays above pneumatic actuation.

Selection itself runs on five parameters — power-source availability, fail-safe requirement, torque/thrust requirement, control function (two-position vs. throttling, where throttling additionally demands low hysteresis and minimal deadband that can't be added after the fact), and economics (cost, maintenance, and reliability together) — layered onto four underlying construction categories (spring-and-diaphragm, piston, electric, electro-hydraulic) that differ only by linkage: a rotary actuator needs a linkage, gear, or crank arm converting linear motion to 90-degree rotation, with a lost-motion risk at every linkage point (mitigated by coupling choice — a splined, clamped connector eliminates lost motion and handles high torque, while a slotted connector on a milled flat generally does not), while a sliding-stem actuator has no linkage and no lost motion at all. The real cost/thrust/speed/fail-safe tradeoffs across all five types (the source's own Table 2-6) favor starting with the simplest design — spring-and-diaphragm — and moving to piston, electric, or electro-hydraulic only when a specific thrust, speed, or duty-cycle requirement the simpler design genuinely can't meet forces the upgrade.

Orientation is a selection factor in its own right: sliding-stem assemblies mounted anything other than actuator-vertical-and-on-top let gravity act asymmetrically on internal parts, concentrating wear at the plug/cage, post/bushing, and seat interfaces and shortening packing life — driving an ENVIRO-SEAL packing recommendation whenever the mounting can't be corrected.

activities.title: Actuator Mechanism ID Sort
activities.description: Hand each small group an unlabeled photo/cutaway set — one image per construction just taught: spring-and-diaphragm (direct- or reverse-acting cutaway), piston (single- or double-acting), Scotch-yoke piston, manual (sliding-stem or rotary), rack-and-pinion, and electric (sliding-stem or rotary). Groups sort each image to its mechanism family and state the one construction feature from this module's own slides that identifies it — a diaphragm-and-spring stack means spring-and-diaphragm, a cylinder-and-piston means piston, a yoke converting linear motion to a turning shaft means Scotch-yoke, a handwheel with no power connection means manual, an external gear meshing a toothed shaft collar means rack-and-pinion, a motor-and-gearbox housing means electric. Debrief resolves any image placed by size or shape alone rather than by the actual construction feature taught.
materials: Unlabeled actuator photo/cutaway set: one image per construction shown this module (spring-and-diaphragm, piston, Scotch-yoke, manual, rack-and-pinion, electric)

activities.title: Actuator & Fail-Safe Selection Case
activities.description: Working from three short service cards (each stating power-source availability, mounting orientation, duty — on/off vs. continuous throttling — and criticality of the fail-safe position), select an actuator type and fail-safe action for each and justify the call against the module's own selection parameters and type-comparison summary — e.g. a throttling loop with no instrument air available and a non-vertical mounting rules out a plain spring-and-diaphragm unit and drives an electric or accessory-equipped piston actuator instead, with the mounting orientation also flagging an ENVIRO-SEAL packing recommendation. Debrief compares each group's justification against the real tradeoffs (cost, inherent fail-safe capability, throttling precision, orientation-driven wear) rather than a single 'correct' answer.

modules.title: Force & Torque Sizing
modules.stakes: An actuator sized from a rule of thumb instead of real unbalance-area/seat-load calculation stalls at the seat under real differential pressure — a shutoff failure discovered mid-upset.
modules.objective: Calculate the required thrust for a sliding-stem valve from unbalance area and seat load, and calculate the required torque for a rotary valve.

primitives.t: Actuator sizing for a sliding-stem valve is a real calculated match, not a rule-of-thumb oversize: Total force required = A + B + C + D — unbalance force, seat load, packing friction, and any application-specific extra — summed and checked directly against a specific actuator's own diaphragm area and bench-set range. Sizing 'big enough' by feel skips exactly the check that matters, because the valve has to close against the real differential pressure on the day it's called on, not the nameplate rating on the actuator's spec sheet.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure anchors the opening frame itself; grounded in cvh-topic-valve-balance's own 'Total force required = A+B+C+D' statement and cvh-topic-actuator-force-selection's 'actuator selection is a real match to a target, not bigger is always safer' — both Control Valve Handbook §5.11/§5.11.2, restating and sharpening this module's own stakes line into the concrete total-force framing slides 94-99 build out.
primitives.templateRationale: Opens the module on the stakes/framing question before any mechanism is introduced — Axis 3's prime definition (a question or the stakes, before the mechanism), matching the cve1-ch6-m1 slide-88 precedent for this module's sibling competency.

primitives.t: Unbalance force (A) is the fluid-pressure term: net pressure differential × net unbalance area. For a single-seated, flow-up design, net unbalance area is simply the port area; a balanced-trim design routes pressure to both sides of the plug to largely cancel the net force, but still retains a small residual unbalance area — read off Figure 5.2's port-diameter table for the actual construction, never assumed to be zero. Frequent practice takes the maximum upstream gauge pressure as the differential, unless the process design always guarantees back pressure at maximum inlet pressure.
primitives.templateRationale: Existing figure (crop) per Style Guide §5.8 default — Figure 5.2's port-diameter/balanced-vs-unbalanced table used directly, no redraw reason applies. Mechanism role fits the 'how A is obtained' step even though the figure is a data table rather than a cutaway — Axis 3 has no separate role for a computed-lookup step, and Stage 1 already fixed this concept's role at mechanism.

primitives.t: The real tradeoff behind picking a leak class: going higher than the service actually needs adds seat and actuator cost without benefit, while going too low risks excess leakage in a service where that's expensive or hazardous to tolerate — which is why this is read off the actual shutoff pressure drop for the real service, not chosen by habit or a generic default.
primitives.templateRationale: Analytical graph (CVH Fig. 5.3), used directly per Style Guide §5.8 default — no redraw reason applies, axes and layout already compatible. Keyed per §5.3's swatch-entry list, the same `.tpl-list` mechanism the mechanism/nomenclature templates already share with a graph's key (§5.3's explicit unification). Flagged under Concept-map gaps: five class lines sits above §6.4's 2-4-entry comfort ceiling for a graph key — worth a Stage 3 check on whether this needs splitting or a wider key column.

primitives.t: The recommended seat-load lookup table (Figure 5.4) is the practical number a real sizing calculation actually uses: by leak class, a flat lbf-per-lineal-inch value — Class II: 20; Class III standard seat: 40; Class IV standard seat: 80 (above a 4-3/8 in. port); Class VI metal seat: 300. Class V is the one exception — its row instructs 'determine from Figure 5.2' instead of giving a flat number, because Class V's real seat load depends on the valve's own unbalance area, not a fixed constant.
primitives.templateRationale: Existing figure (crop) per Style Guide §5.8 default — the practical companion lookup to slide 95's graph. Figure 5.4's own cross-reference to Figure 5.2 for Class V is the source's own internal instruction, used as printed per Style Guide §6.2/§6.3's discipline of respecting a source figure's own structure rather than flattening or renumbering it.

primitives.t: Work the check as the source does: total force required = 275 lbf (from the A + B + C + D calculation just built). Candidate actuator: air-to-open diaphragm, 100 sq. in. of effective area, bench set 6 to 15 psig, expected operating range 3 to 15 psig. Precompression: the operating range starts 3 psig below the bench-set floor (6 psig − 3 psig), the pressure that must be overcome before the diaphragm produces any net closing force — precompression force = 3 psig × 100 sq. in. = 300 lbf. Compare: 300 lbf exceeds the 275 lbf required, so the actuator is an adequate selection, with 25 lbf of real margin.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure anchors this worked check (prose and worked example only, not figure-anchored) — grounded in cvh-topic-actuator-force-selection (Control Valve Handbook §5.11.2, p. 126) and independently confirmed against pss-topic-actuator-force-calculation-globe (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook), which restates the identical 275 lbf / 100 sq in. / 6-15 psig bench-set numbers as its own real worked example — the same case appears in two source documents. Verified directly against the primary Control Valve Handbook PDF text (pp. 125-126).
primitives.templateRationale: A 3-step numeric comparison procedure, apply-level, no photographed physical sequence — matches this course's own precedent at cve1-ch1-m2 slide 12 (rangeability worked comparison), which chose procedure-image over procedure-worked/-callout/-sequence for the identical reason. No figure is registered to attach step markers to (the unbalance-area and seat-load figures were slides 94-96's own subjects); Stage 3 will need an originated force-total/precompression comparison graphic, not a Handbook redraw — flagged under Asset-variant gaps.

primitives.t: Piston actuators without springs size more simply than the diaphragm case just worked: thrust = piston area × minimum supply pressure = available thrust — no bench-set/precompression check, because there is no spring range to overcome. Keep units compatible (piston area in sq. in., pressure in psig, thrust in lbf). Piston actuators WITH springs are sized the same A + B + C + D way as the diaphragm actuator. The manufacturer publishes the actuator's own thrust, effective area, and spring data, including a maximum-stem-load check — because an actuator that supplies too much force is its own separate failure mode.
primitives.sourceNote: cvh-topic-actuator-force-selection and pss-topic-piston-thrust-calculation give the formula and its reasoning but no solved numeric case, unlike slide 97's diaphragm example. Checked directly: no piston-thrust worked example exists anywhere in the indexed Subject-Matter Index (Control Valve Handbook ch5, Oil & Gas Sourcebook ch2, Power & Severe Service Sourcebook ch2, including the primary PDF text) — the formula is real, a solved case is not. Left as the formula rather than inventing a piston-area/pressure pair; flagged under Concept-map gaps.

No figure is registered for the piston-thrust case specifically; Stage 3 will need an originated piston/cylinder cross-section labelling area and supply pressure, not a Handbook redraw — flagged under Asset-variant gaps.

primitives.t: An actuator sized bigger than the calculated requirement is not automatically the safer choice: too much thrust can **buckle the valve stem, bend it enough to leak, or damage the valve internals** — a real failure mode the manufacturer's published maximum-stem-load check exists specifically to catch before it happens in the field.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure in the registry for this competency; consequence stated is the direct restatement of cvh-topic-actuator-force-selection's own over-force warning (Control Valve Handbook §5.11.2, p. 126), independently confirmed by pss-topic-piston-thrust-calculation's identical statement (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook) — not a gap here specifically, since the caution card's supporting photo is optional (cve1-ch1-m2 slide 13 / cve1-ch4-m2 slide 63 precedent) and the card carries the consequence sentence alone.
primitives.templateRationale: Single caution consequence sentence with the failure clause bolded, per Style Guide §8.3/§4.4 — no figure needed, matching the caution role's established Axis-3 treatment and this course's own precedent.

primitives.t: Breakout and dynamic torque don't necessarily peak at the same point in the stroke, so an actuator has to clear both, not just whichever number looks bigger: breakout is highest at the very start of motion, against full shutoff pressure and static friction/seal drag with the valve not yet moving; dynamic applies once it's underway. An actuator sized only against the dynamic number can still stall right at the seat.
primitives.sourceNote: cvh-cmp-rotary-actuator-cutaway is the CVE1 asset-variant registry's only figure for this competency, but that exact figure (CVH Fig. 1.17) is already placed at cve1-ch6-m1 slide 82 for a different competency (distinguish-actuator-mechanism-types, the sliding-stem/rotary linear-to-rotary conversion mechanism). Per curriculum-development.md's asset-variant discipline ('a competency × asset-variant reuse is a human-curated call, not one Stage 2 should make unilaterally') — the same discipline already applied at this course's own cve1-ch5-m1 slide 69 — this concept is grounded directly in cvh-topic-rotary-actuator-torque / ogas-topic-rotary-actuator-torque-sizing / pss-topic-rotary-actuator-torque-methodology's own teaches text instead of citing the figure. Flagged under Asset-variant gaps for a human decision: reusing the cutaway here is arguably a genuinely strong case (this slide's own framing depends on the lever/shaft conversion the cutaway shows), but it is not this agent's call to make.
primitives.templateRationale: How the sizing method fundamentally works (torque vs. force, the two-equation reduction) — Axis 3's mechanism default. No image assigned pending the human reuse call above.

primitives.t: Because the fixed B term (500 lbf·in here) applies even at zero ΔP, this valve needs meaningful actuator torque just to break static friction and seal drag before any pressure differential is even in the picture — sizing off the pressure-dependent term alone would undersize the actuator for a low-differential but still tight-shutoff service.
primitives.sourceNote: cvh-topic-rotary-actuator-torque / pss-topic-rotary-actuator-torque-methodology / ogas-topic-rotary-actuator-torque-sizing all confirm the A=1.80/B=500/C=1.10 (60°)/max TD=4,140 lbf·in factors for a 6 in. NPS V-Notch ball valve — verified directly against the Control Valve Handbook's own printed Table §5.13.1 (PDF pp. 126-127). No source in the Subject-Matter Index solves TB/TD against an actual ΔPshutoff/ΔPeff pair (checked the Control Valve Handbook, Oil & Gas Sourcebook, and Power & Severe Service Sourcebook directly, including the primary PDF text) — every real worked case in the library stops at the factor table, not a solved final torque. Left ΔPshutoff/ΔPeff as the real service input the source itself never fixes to a number, rather than inventing a pressure differential to force a single final answer. Flagged under Concept-map gaps. Style Guide §7.3 states torque as N·m primary with lbf·ft in parentheses; this source publishes lbf·in directly and no worked value exists to convert without introducing a derived number not in the source — flagged under Wording I'm unsure of for a terminology decision.
primitives.templateRationale: Worked numeric substitution of real published factors into the two governing equations — same procedure-image shape as slides 97/98 and the cve1-ch1-m2 slide-12 precedent. The natural supporting figure is the torque-factor table itself (Table 5.13.1), which is reference data excluded from the figure index under the standing tables-vs-figures rule (per cvh-topic-rotary-actuator-torque's own source locator). Stage 3 will need to either reproduce the row directly on-slide as a small table or originate one — flagged under Asset-variant gaps.

primitives.t: Maximum rotation is normally 90° — the ball or disk rotates fully from closed to wide-open. Some pneumatic actuators are deliberately limited to 60° or 75° instead: for a spring-and-diaphragm actuator, the shorter rotation allows a higher initial spring compression, which increases breakout torque — a real tradeoff, not a compromise. The actuator lever's effective length changes with rotation angle, and published torque values — particularly for pneumatic piston actuators — already account for that change, so the A/B/C factors and TB/TD equations stay valid across either rotation choice with no separate correction needed.
primitives.sourceNote: cvh-topic-rotary-actuator-torque / pss-topic-rotary-actuator-torque-methodology / ogas-topic-rotary-actuator-torque-sizing name this exact 90°-vs-60°/75° tradeoff identically across all three sources, prose-only — no figure in the registry depicts rotation angle.
primitives.templateRationale: Exactly two named cases (standard 90° rotation vs. limited 60°/75° rotation) with a real, stated tradeoff between them — Axis 3's contrast role, two-panel default. No figure exists; Stage 3 will need an originated angle diagram (two rotation arcs, 90° vs. 60-75°) — flagged under Asset-variant gaps.

reground.hook: Think of pushing a heavy door shut against a strong wind. Knowing the door feels 'heavy enough' isn't good enough — you need to know exactly how hard the wind pushes back, how hard the latch needs to click shut, and how much the hinges themselves drag, before you can trust that your own push (or a motor pushing for you) is strong enough every single time, not just on a calm day.
reground.bridge: A control valve actuator is that motor, and 'the wind, the latch, and the hinge drag' are three of the four real forces (or, for a valve that turns instead of slides, the twisting instead of pushing) an actuator has to beat every time it closes: the fluid pressure pushing back through the valve, the seat load needed for a tight-enough shutoff, and packing friction. Sum them, compare the total against what a specific actuator can actually deliver at its worst operating point, and only then is the selection trustworthy — not a guess dressed up as a spec.
reground.depth:
For a sliding-stem valve, Total force required = A + B + C + D. A (unbalance force) = net pressure differential × net unbalance area — for a single-seated flow-up trim, net unbalance area is the port area (Fig. 5.2); a balanced trim retains a small residual unbalance area read from the same table, never zero. B (seat load) is set by the required leak classification (ANSI/FCI 70-2 / IEC 60534-4, Class II-VI): Fig. 5.3 plots minimum required seat load against shutoff pressure drop as five class lines; Fig. 5.4 gives the practical flat lookup value per class (Class II: 20 lbf/lineal in.; Class III standard: 40; Class IV standard: 80 above a 4-3/8 in. port; Class VI metal seat: 300 — Class V alone has no flat number, its row instructing 'determine from Figure 5.2' because Class V's real seat load depends on the valve's own unbalance area). C (packing friction) depends on stem size, packing type, and compressive load, and is explicitly NOT fully repeatable — live-loaded graphite packing especially. D covers any additional application-specific force (bellows stiffness, unusual seal friction).

The source's own real worked check: 275 lbf required; candidate actuator is air-to-open diaphragm, 100 sq. in. of effective area, bench set 6-15 psig, operating range 3-15 psig. Precompression margin = (6 psig bench-set floor − 3 psig operating-range floor) × 100 sq. in. = 3 psig × 100 sq. in. = 300 lbf. Since 300 lbf exceeds the 275 lbf required, the selection is adequate — with 25 lbf of real margin, not a guess.

A piston actuator without a spring sizes more simply: thrust = piston area × minimum supply pressure, with no bench-set check because there's no spring range to overcome; a piston actuator WITH a spring is sized the same A+B+C+D way as the diaphragm case. In every case, TOO MUCH force is its own real failure mode — it can buckle the stem, bend it enough to leak, or damage valve internals — so the check runs both directions, not just 'is it big enough.'

For a rotary valve, the same total-force logic becomes total torque, reduced to two equations: Breakout Torque TB = A(ΔPshutoff) + B (torque needed to break the valve loose from a dead stop against shutoff pressure) and Dynamic Torque TD = C(ΔPeff) (torque needed to keep it moving once underway). A, B, and C are real, published, valve-design-specific factors — a 6 in. NPS V-notch ball valve with a 1 in. shaft: A = 1.80, B = 500, C = 1.10 at 60° rotation, maximum TD = 4,140 lbf·in. The fixed B term alone (500 lbf·in) has to be overcome before any pressure differential is even applied; neither source ever solves TB/TD against an actual ΔP pair, so ΔPshutoff and ΔPeff stay the real service inputs the factors get multiplied through, not fixed numbers.

Maximum rotation is normally 90°, but some pneumatic actuators are limited to 60° or 75° — a real tradeoff: less travel lets the spring be pre-compressed further, raising breakout torque, and the actuator lever's changing effective length across that shorter rotation is already baked into the published torque numbers, so no separate correction is needed.

modules.title: Bench Set & Extreme-Service Variants
modules.stakes: A bench set left unadjusted means the actuator never delivers its rated travel in service, regardless of how correctly the thrust/torque calculation was done.
modules.objective: Perform bench-set adjustment and explain its criticality to travel accuracy, and select an actuator design variant — piston vs. diaphragm, electric, electro-hydraulic — for extreme-force or non-pneumatic services.

primitives.t: The force/torque calculation in the last module sizes the actuator correctly on paper — it says nothing about whether that actuator actually delivers its full rated travel once mounted. Bench set is the calibration step that closes that gap: an actuator sized right but bench-set wrong still short-strokes or over-strokes the valve, and neither the total-force nor the total-torque check catches that failure mode. Sliding-stem valves are the more travel-critical mechanism type of the ones this module compares, and depend on bench set most directly.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure anchors the framing question itself; grounded in cvh-topic-bench-set-adjustment and cvh-topic-valve-travel-criticality — the same 'sized correctly is not the same as set correctly' gap those two topics establish, restated here as this module's own opening stakes.
primitives.templateRationale: Opens the module on the stakes/framing question before any mechanism is introduced — Axis 3's prime definition, matching the cve1-ch6-m2 slide-93 precedent for this same module family.

primitives.t: Bench set is the initial compression placed on the actuator spring by the spring adjuster — the calibration that sets the diaphragm-pressure range needed to fully stroke the valve to its rated travel, made and read with the valve on the bench (atmospheric pressure at the plug, not the real installed process load). For an air-to-open actuator, the bench set's lower value fixes both the available force and the pressure at which opening travel actually begins; for air-to-close, that same lower value fixes where closing travel begins. Seating force at any point in the stroke equals applied pressure minus bench set minus the spring compression already used up by travel — Figure 8.10 plots exactly that relationship across the full 0-100% travel range, showing the bench-set band, its interaction with deadband, and the reference line for an actuator connected to the valve with deadband present.
primitives.templateRationale: CVH Fig. 8.10 used directly per Style Guide §5.8 default. Note for Stage 3: unlike 14101 ch3-m6's bench-set slides (where §5.8's bounded-redraw exception applied because each of THOSE slides isolates one interleaved line), this slide teaches the whole bench-set/seating-force relationship as one concept, so the redraw reason (#2, un-croppable to a sub-concept) does not obviously apply here — flagged, not decided, since the direct-use-vs-redraw call is Stage 3's to make against the rendered result, not Stage 2's.

primitives.t: The sequence starts from fully-seated specifically because every later setting in the calibration is measured relative to this one reference point — an error here doesn't stay local, it shifts the whole travel calibration that follows, unlike an error introduced partway through the range.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure anchors the adjustment steps themselves — the seating-force graph (slide 105's own subject) is the reference consulted WHILE performing this procedure, not a procedure photo, and is not re-cited here per the asset-variant reuse discipline (curriculum-development.md: a competency × asset-variant reuse is a human-curated call). Grounded directly in cvh-topic-bench-set-adjustment (CVH §8.5.5, p. 186) — the spring-adjuster step, the seating-force equation, and the spring-tolerance caution are stated there almost verbatim. No additional numeric worked example exists in this LO's registry-cited topics (unlike m2's force-sizing worked checks).
primitives.templateRationale: A genuine ordered physical sequence (seat the valve, adjust the spring, verify against the equation) with nothing to photograph or diagram at this engineering/introductory tier — procedure-list's own stated purpose (gallery.css: 'a real sequence with genuinely nothing to photograph or diagram... do not force a placeholder figure into procedure-image') fits this exactly, and is a deliberately different choice from m2's procedure-image (which suited a numeric worked comparison, not a physical step sequence).

primitives.t: Travel set wrong does not fail gracefully in either direction. Under-travel means the valve never reaches its designed flow rate no matter how hard the control loop calls for more. Over-travel is worse: it can **reduce the seat load the actuator actually delivers at the closed position — a real shutoff-capability loss — and damage the trim**, in the extreme letting the plug bottom against the bonnet and pull the stem straight out of the plug. Sliding-stem valves demand more attention to travel setting than rotary valves — this is the mechanism type where bench set earns every bit of the accuracy the last slide's procedure called for.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure in the registry for this competency; the consequence stated is the direct restatement of cvh-topic-valve-travel-criticality (CVH §8.5.6, p. 187) — the over-travel plug-bottoming/stem-pullout failure and the sliding-stem-vs-rotary attention difference are both stated there almost verbatim, not inferred.
primitives.templateRationale: Single caution consequence with the failure clause bolded, per Style Guide §8.3/§4.4 — no figure needed, matching this module's own cve1-ch6-m2 slide-99 caution precedent.

primitives.t: Bench set assumes a standard spring-and-diaphragm actuator working within its normal force range on compressed air. Real services regularly break one of those two assumptions — a force or torque demand a standard diaphragm can't reach, or no instrument air at the mounting location at all. Four real design axes answer that: piston vs. diaphragm construction, electric motors, and electro-hydraulic units — differing mainly by power source and force ceiling, not by a single 'go bigger' default. Picking among them is a real spec decision, not an escalation from the standard case.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure anchors the framing question; grounded in ogas-topic-actuator-design-taxonomy's own four-category framing and ogas-topic-actuator-selection-process-summary's opening statement that the fundamental requirement is knowing the application (control signal, power source, thrust/torque, fail-safe position) before comparing designs.
primitives.templateRationale: Opens this competency's own arc on the stakes/framing question before any mechanism is introduced — matches this module's own slide-104 and the course's established prime precedent.

primitives.t: Which failure state to choose is a process-safety decision, not a mechanical preference: a fuel-gas valve is typically specified fail-closed, to stop supply if instrument air is lost, while a reactor cooling-water valve is typically specified fail-open, to keep cooling flowing through that same failure — the hardware in this list is how you get any of these behaviors, not which one a given service actually needs.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure registered for this competency's fail-safe-mechanism concept; grounded in ogas-topic-fail-safe-action-mechanism and pss-topic-failsafe-mechanism, which state the stored-energy mechanism, the fail-open/fail-closed/hold-last-position options, and the Type 164A fail-lock detail identically across both sourcebooks.
primitives.templateRationale: How fail-safe fundamentally works across all four actuator types — Axis 3's mechanism default. No image assigned; the registry's four figures for this competency are reserved for the multi-spring/diaphragm-rotary pair (slide 110) and the handwheel pair (slide 113), per this module's own figure-distribution instruction.

primitives.t: Two genuinely distinct actuator families answer the extreme-force problem differently. Piston actuators solve it with higher raw thrust at higher supply pressure, but that leaves fail-safe as a separate design choice: a large, high-output spring sized to overcome valve fluid forces entirely on its own (loaded like a spring-and-diaphragm, by a single-acting positioner) is one real variant; a much smaller spring that only assists — relying on the valve's own unbalance forces to help drive fail-safe action, and behaving like a plain double-acting piston in normal operation — is the other. Diaphragm actuators answer the same force problem without leaving the spring-and-diaphragm family at all.
primitives.sourceNote: Piston's two spring-return variants (this slide's left panel) have no figure registered for this competency — the registry's four figures are the diaphragm/handwheel set. Grounded directly in ogas-topic-piston-actuator-design-variants and pss-topic-piston-actuator-mechanism-variants, which state the same two-variant distinction identically across both sourcebooks.

items.t: The diaphragm family's own extreme-force answer: multiple springs raise total force output past what a standard single-spring diaphragm actuator delivers, while the actuator stays field-convertible between direct- and reverse-acting — a real alternative to abandoning the diaphragm design for piston or electric construction.

The same diaphragm approach adapted to a rotary shaft: the actuator lever's orientation on the shaft determines whether increasing pressure opens or closes the valve, and net output thrust equals diaphragm force minus the opposing spring force — the diaphragm's extreme-force answer is not limited to sliding-stem construction.

primitives.templateRationale: Two real design answers to the same extreme-force requirement — piston (two spring-return subtypes, prose-only, no figure registered) vs. diaphragm (multi-spring construction plus its rotary-valve extension). The diaphragm panel composes its two registered figures as one two-image panel per Style Guide §5.14 (several named items in one figure area, each its own clickable image) rather than a third contrast panel — contrast is structurally two `.tpl-panel` siblings, not three (Style Guide §6.4/gallery.css).

primitives.t: Piston actuators are widely believed to be the faster of the two designs, and a full 100%-step stroking-time test bears that out — higher thrust drives a complete stroke quickly. But normal regulatory control almost never asks for a full stroke: it asks for small signal changes, on the order of 0.25-2% of travel, correcting the process continuously. At that scale, documented industry research shows the result reverses — spring-and-diaphragm actuators consistently outperform piston actuators. The mechanism is friction, not thrust: piston actuators carry more of it by construction (O-ring seals, more guide surfaces, alignment sensitivity, and lubrication that degrades over time), and friction specifically degrades small-signal responsiveness even though it barely shows up on a full-stroke thrust test. Selecting on the full-stroke number alone is exactly the mistake this finding corrects.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure registered for this competency's speed-myth concept; grounded in pss-topic-piston-diaphragm-speed-myth (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook, 'Valve Response Time,' p. 14-6) — the only Subject-Matter Index entry in the vault stating this specific full-stroke-vs-small-signal reversal and its friction mechanism, and confirmed absent from Control Valve Handbook's own response-time/deadband topics per that entry's own cross-check note.
primitives.templateRationale: Two measurement conditions with opposite winners — full-stroke (100%) speed vs. small-signal (0.25-2%) responsiveness — a genuine two-panel contrast, not a single mechanism explanation, because the whole teaching point IS the reversal between the two conditions. No figure exists in the Source Library for either panel; Stage 3 will need an originated stroking-time-vs-signal-size comparison graphic or stay text/swatch-only — flagged under Asset-variant gaps.

primitives.t: Electric and electro-hydraulic actuators both suit remote mounting where no other power source is available, but they answer different problems. An electric actuator (a motor plus gear train) is the simpler, lower-cost path — economical only in small size ranges, though, since larger electric units run slower and heavier than a pneumatic equivalent, and typical fail action is lock-in-last-position rather than a true fail-open or fail-closed. Duty cycle is the selection factor that matters most: continuous closed-loop control needs a suitable duty cycle a standard electric operator may not have, and only high-performance units — continuous-rated DC motors, ball-screw output — reach precise control at 100% duty cycle. Electro-hydraulic actuators pump oil internally to a piston, giving high stiffness, analog-signal compatibility, and excellent frequency response and positioning accuracy — an excellent throttling choice — but fail-safe is not inherent here either: it requires a return spring or a hydraulic accumulator, in either a self-contained configuration (its own motor, pump, and reservoir, which can be built with spring-return fail action) or an externally powered one (a separate motor/pump/reservoir/hose unit, which needs an accumulator to achieve any fail mode at all) — at the cost of high initial price, complexity, and difficult maintenance.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure registered for this competency's electric/electro-hydraulic concept; grounded in ogas-topic-electric-actuator-selection-factors / pss-topic-electric-actuator-characteristics and ogas-topic-electro-hydraulic-actuator-configurations / pss-topic-electro-hydraulic-configurations, which state the same duty-cycle/fail-action/self-contained-vs-externally-powered facts identically across both sourcebooks.
primitives.templateRationale: Two named actuator types with a real, stated set of opposite tradeoffs (cost/simplicity vs. throttling performance/complexity) — Axis 3's contrast, two-panel default. No figure exists in the registry or, per ogas-topic-electro-hydraulic-actuator-configurations' own note, anywhere in the Oil & Gas Sourcebook's chapter for the electro-hydraulic half at all — Stage 3 will need an originated pair of simplified schematics — flagged under Asset-variant gaps.

primitives.t: A manual-override handwheel matters most exactly where this module's own extreme-force and non-pneumatic questions live: a service with no guaranteed instrument air, or an actuator sized near the edge of its force range, still needs a way to move the valve by hand. Mounting position is the real spec decision once a handwheel is called for — side-mounted and top-mounted are the two real options, and which one fits depends on the clearance and access actually available at the valve's install location, not a default choice.
primitives.sourceNote: cvh-cmp-actuator-side-handwheel / cvh-cmp-actuator-top-handwheel (CVH Figs. 4.26/4.27, p. 97) are captioned in the Subject-Matter Index itself as a companion pair contrasting mounting position. The top-mounted handwheel's added travel-stop/emergency-operation function is not stated in the CVH figure's own caption — it is confirmed via the Power & Severe Service Sourcebook's own top-mounted-handwheel figure (pss-cmp-spring-diaphragm-handwheel, not itself cited in this LO's registry), which states that function explicitly for the same physical feature; included as a real, cross-sourcebook-confirmed fact about top-mounted handwheels generally, not invented.

items.t: Side-mounted handwheel: a manual-override mechanism for operating the actuator without pneumatic supply, mounted where lateral clearance at the yoke or actuator housing allows it.

Top-mounted handwheel: the same manual-override function from the top of the actuator stack, the mounting choice where overhead clearance is available rather than lateral clearance — and, on a spring-and-diaphragm actuator, commonly doing double duty as a travel stop as well as a means of manual or emergency operation.

primitives.templateRationale: Two companion figures already captioned by the source as a mounting-position contrast (CVH Figs. 4.26/4.27) — a direct two-panel fit, matching Style Guide §5.8's default of using source figures directly.

primitives.t: Work a real selection: a remote pipeline block valve, no instrument air available at the site, moderate force requirement, infrequent position changes. Electric actuation fits — it needs no compressed-air infrastructure at all, and the infrequent-cycling duty here doesn't demand the high-duty-cycle unit a continuous throttling loop would need; lock-in-last-position fail action is acceptable because this is an on/off block valve, not a service depending on a true fail-open or fail-closed. Change the scenario to a high-cycle throttling loop needing fine small-signal correction, still with no instrument air: electro-hydraulic now fits better than electric — it reaches the stiffness, positioning accuracy, and frequency response continuous throttling needs, at the cost of the complexity and maintenance burden that's worth paying here specifically because electric's precision at small signal sizes doesn't compete with a piston or diaphragm design working the same throttling duty on instrument air. Change it once more to a standard throttling loop WITH instrument air available, but a force requirement above a standard single-spring diaphragm actuator's range: the diaphragm family doesn't have to be abandoned for piston — a field-reversible multi-spring construction reaches higher force while keeping fail-safe inherent and construction familiar — unless the force margin needed is large enough that piston's higher raw thrust is the only real fit, in which case which of piston's two spring-return variants to specify still depends on whether full spring-fail closure is a hard requirement or valve fluid forces can be relied on to help. In every case the justification is a named tradeoff against the actual service conditions, not a single actuator type applied by default.
primitives.sourceNote: No figure anchors this evaluate-level synthesis; grounded in ogas-topic-actuator-selection-process-summary's Table 2-6 comparative tradeoffs across all four actuator families (cost, fail-safe, output, duty cycle, complexity) and its own chapter guidance to consider spring-and-diaphragm first — the same comparative logic this module's own slides 108-113 built up, applied here to named scenarios rather than restated as a rule.

reground.hook: A new pair of hiking boots feels right in the store, but you still have to lace them tight enough that your foot doesn't slide inside — skip that step and the boots are the right size on paper and useless on the trail. And when the trail itself changes — deep mud, an icy slope, no dry ground to stand on at all — the right boot design changes too; the best boot for pavement isn't the best boot for ice, no matter how well either one is laced.
reground.bridge: The lacing is bench set: an actuator sized exactly right in the last module still won't deliver its rated travel unless the spring is calibrated to the correct starting compression, checked at the single point (fully seated) that has to be the most accurate of the whole adjustment. And the changing trail is the extreme-force or non-pneumatic service: once a job needs more force than a standard diaphragm design, or there's no compressed air to work with, the actuator itself has to change form — piston, electric, or electro-hydraulic — each a real answer to a different problem, not an escalation of the same one.
reground.depth:
Bench set is the actuator spring's initial compression, set at the spring adjuster with the valve fully seated — the single point in the whole adjustment that demands the greatest accuracy, because real spring manufacturing tolerance means some variation in spring angle should be expected even on a correctly built unit. For an air-to-open actuator the lower bench-set value sets both the available force and the pressure at which opening travel begins; for air-to-close, the same value sets where closing travel begins. Seating force at any point equals applied pressure minus bench set minus the spring compression already used by travel — CVH Fig. 8.10 plots that relationship across the full travel range, including the bench-set band and its interaction with deadband. Get it wrong and the actuator sized correctly in the last module still fails: under-travel keeps the valve from reaching its designed flow rate; over-travel can reduce the seat load actually delivered — a real shutoff-capability loss — and damage trim, in the worst case letting the plug bottom against the bonnet and pull the stem out of the plug. Sliding-stem valves need more attention to this than rotary valves.

Once a service exceeds a standard spring-and-diaphragm actuator's practical range — too much force, or no instrument air at the mounting location — four real actuator families answer differently, and correctly picking among them is a spec decision grounded in the service, not a default escalation. All four can be fail-open, fail-closed, or (for some) fail-lock via a piped pneumatic switching valve (a Fisher 164A example), because fail-safe is fundamentally a stored-energy mechanism: mechanical spring energy for spring-and-diaphragm and most piston designs, a pneumatic volume tank or hydraulic accumulator for the rest.

Piston actuators reach higher force at higher supply pressure, but their fail-safe has to be engineered in as a separate choice: a large, high-output spring that alone overcomes valve fluid forces (loaded like a spring-and-diaphragm via a single-acting positioner), or a much smaller spring that only assists — relying on the valve's own unbalance forces to help drive fail-safe action, behaving like a plain double-acting piston day to day.

Diaphragm actuators answer the same extreme-force problem without leaving the family at all: a field-reversible multi-spring construction raises total force output well past a standard single-spring design while staying convertible between direct- and reverse-acting in the field, and the same diaphragm approach extends to rotary valves through the actuator lever, with net output thrust equal to diaphragm force minus opposing spring force.

The genuinely counter-intuitive finding: piston actuators are widely believed faster because they win a full 100%-step stroking-time test on raw thrust — but for the small (0.25-2%) signal changes that real regulatory throttling control actually makes almost continuously, documented industry research shows spring-and-diaphragm actuators consistently outperform piston actuators. The cause is friction, not thrust: piston construction carries more of it by design (O-ring seals, more guide surfaces, alignment sensitivity, lubrication that degrades over time), and friction specifically degrades small-signal responsiveness in a way a full-stroke thrust test never reveals. Selecting a piston actuator for a throttling service on the strength of its full-stroke speed number alone repeats exactly the mistake this finding corrects.

Electric actuators (motor plus gear train) suit remote mounting with no other power source, are economical only in small size ranges, get slower and heavier than pneumatic equivalents at larger sizes, and typically hold last position on power loss rather than failing open or closed — duty cycle is the selection factor that matters most, since continuous closed-loop control needs a suitable duty cycle a standard electric operator may not have; only high-performance units (continuous-rated DC motors, ball-screw output) reach precise control at 100% duty cycle.

Electro-hydraulic actuators pump oil internally to a piston, giving high stiffness, analog-signal compatibility, and excellent frequency response and positioning accuracy — an excellent throttling choice — but fail-safe again is not inherent: it needs a return spring or a hydraulic accumulator, in either a self-contained configuration (its own motor, pump, and reservoir, which can be built with spring-return fail action) or an externally powered one (separate motor/pump/reservoir/hoses, which needs an accumulator to get any fail mode at all) — at the cost of high initial price, complexity, and difficult maintenance.

A manual-override handwheel matters specifically in this module's own territory — a non-pneumatic or force-marginal service still needs a way to move the valve by hand — and mounting position (side vs. top) is a real spec decision driven by the clearance actually available at the install location, with a top-mounted handwheel on a spring-and-diaphragm actuator commonly doing double duty as a travel stop as well as manual/emergency operation.

Selecting correctly among all of this is the same discipline as the module's own bench-set half: name the actual service conditions, weigh the real, opposite tradeoffs (cost, inherent fail-safe, duty cycle, small-signal responsiveness, complexity), and justify the pick against them — never default to the biggest or the most familiar option.
