chapters.title: Packing Selection & Fugitive-Emissions Control
chapters._source: Enabling Competency `eng.packing.selection-and-fugitive-emissions` — see Curriculum — CVE1.md and Competency Hierarchy — CVE1, CVE2, CVE3 v3.md, Chapter 7. Modules below are STUBS ONLY (status: outline, empty keyConcepts) pending a real Stage 1 arc-cut per module.

modules.title: Packing Material & Arrangement Selection
modules.stakes: Packing selected on stem-friction cost alone, without regard to the emissions class the site actually needs, passes acceptance today and becomes a compliance finding within a year.
modules.objective: Select a packing material and arrangement — PTFE V-ring, duplex, graphite ULF, EnviroSeal variants — for a given temperature, friction, and emissions-class requirement, and explain how packing friction is measured.

primitives.t: A packing system chosen on stem friction and price alone can pass acceptance testing today and still surface as a fugitive-emissions compliance finding within a year, if the site's actual emissions class was never checked against it. Every packing decision ahead in this module sits on two independent requirements — the service's pressure/temperature envelope, and the emissions class the installation must meet — and satisfying one does not imply satisfying the other.
primitives.sourceNote: Prime opens on the module's own stakes line rather than a figure — no single figure represents the two-axis selection risk itself; grounded in cve1-ch7-m1's stakes field and cvh-topic-packing-selection-criteria's own framing that pressure/temperature and emissions class are separate checks against the same packing system.
primitives.templateRationale: Opens on the stakes question before any packing system is shown, per Axis 3's prime role and this course's own prime precedent (e.g. the guiding-method and rotary-universality primes elsewhere in this course) — no figure represents 'why the two axes matter' as a concept in its own right.

primitives.t: PTFE packing builds from a V-ring stack: upper wiper, packing follower, female and male adaptors bracketing the V-ring, a lantern ring, a loading spring, and a box ring doubling as the lower wiper. Graphite packing is the simpler stack: filament ring, laminated ring, a lantern ring, and — where corrosion risk calls for it — a sacrificial zinc washer. Every specific packing system named later in this module is a variation on one of these two part sets.
primitives.templateRationale: A labelled-parts figure sequenced first, per Axis 3's nomenclature-before-mechanism ordering — Figure 1.11's two-panel PTFE/graphite composite is the generic reference every specific system in this module builds on. The figure carries its own printed field callouts (Style Guide §6.3); the list names each field by its printed label rather than re-marking with numbered circles.

primitives.t: The same PTFE V-ring or graphite stack builds up three ways for a globe body. Single — one packing set, the baseline. Double — two packing sets stacked around a lantern ring, adding a tap point between them. Leak-Off — a double arrangement with that tap piped away to a safe collection point instead of left open to atmosphere. Arrangement is a configuration decision layered on top of the material decision, not a substitute for it.
primitives.templateRationale: Mechanism treatment for the configuration concept, sequenced after nomenclature per Axis 3's soft ordering. This is the second of two source figures both captioned Figure 3.24 (confirmed against the Subject-Matter Index's own duplicate-caption note, distinct from the bellows-bonnet Figure 3.24 on printed p. 67); it carries its own printed field callouts on both panels (Style Guide §6.3), so the list names each field verbatim rather than re-marking.

primitives.t: Same PTFE V-ring element, two spring designs, and the difference is the reason to specify one over the other. Single PTFE V-ring uses a coil spring and holds the lowest friction of any system in this module, but its envelope is narrow — 300 psi (20.7 bar) and 93°C (200°F) maximum, sliding-stem only, and it does not meet the low-emission criteria for rotary valves at all. ENVIRO-SEAL PTFE's live-load spring pack carries the same PTFE ring to 750 psi (51.7 bar) and 232°C (450°F), in sliding-stem or rotary bodies, and holds that seal over a longer service life even outside environmental service. Live-loading costs some friction; it buys pressure/temperature range and rotary applicability in return.

items.t: Coil spring; ≤300 psi (20.7 bar) / -18 to 93°C (200°F); sliding-stem only; lowest friction of any system in this module; does not meet the low-emission criteria for rotary valves.
Live-load spring pack; up to 750 psi (51.7 bar) / 232°C (450°F); sliding-stem and rotary; also specified for non-environmental high-temperature/pressure service for its longer service life.

primitives.templateRationale: A genuine this-vs-that pairing on the same PTFE element and exactly two figures — the structural precondition for slide--role-contrast's two-panel layout.

primitives.t: Both systems answer the same problem — PTFE alone won't survive this temperature — for different reasons. ENVIRO-SEAL Duplex combines PTFE and graphite components to hold low friction and low emission up to 232°C (450°F) in sliding-stem valves, and it carries a fire-tested rating to API Standard 589 — the choice where fire-safety qualification is itself part of the requirement. It has no rotary version. ENVIRO-SEAL Graphite ULF is a graphite-based design built for service above 232°C, where Duplex's PTFE content would fail outright; its patented construction interleaves very thin PTFE layers inside the graphite rings specifically to recover friction and cycle life that graphite alone gives up. Duplex's temperature ceiling is Graphite ULF's floor — that handoff point is the real selection criterion, not a preference between the two.

items.t: PTFE and graphite combination; low friction, low emission; fire-tested to API Standard 589; up to 232°C (450°F); sliding-stem only, no rotary version.

Graphite-based; patented ULF construction with very thin PTFE layers inside the packing rings; built for environmental applications above 232°C (450°F), where Duplex's PTFE content no longer survives.

primitives.templateRationale: Exactly two figures, a genuine temperature-handoff pairing rather than a spectrum — Duplex's stated ceiling (232°C) is Graphite ULF's stated floor (above 232°C), which is what makes this a contrast rather than two independent mechanism slides. Both figures carry their own printed field callouts (Style Guide §6.3).

primitives.t: Rotary valves need their own packing system because the stem itself moves differently: it rotates in place rather than sliding axially through the packing bore, loading and wearing the packing rings in a different pattern than a sliding-stem globe valve does — reusing a sliding-stem system's geometry wouldn't seal or wear the same way.
primitives.templateRationale: Schematic/cutaway treatment, the default mechanism shape for an understand-level 'how it's built and what it's rated for' concept — Figure 3.34 is the sole figure for this system.

primitives.t: Every system this module has shown sits on the same two independent axes: the pressure/temperature envelope it clears, and the emissions class it satisfies — with sliding-stem-versus-rotary as a third, harder constraint that rules some systems out entirely. Single PTFE V-ring: ≤300 psi / 93°C, sliding-stem only, lowest friction, fails the rotary emissions criterion. ENVIRO-SEAL PTFE: ≤750 psi / 232°C, sliding-stem or rotary. ENVIRO-SEAL Duplex: ≤232°C, fire-tested to API 589, sliding-stem only. ENVIRO-SEAL Graphite ULF: above 232°C, where Duplex's PTFE content fails. ENVIRO-SEAL Graphite for rotary: the only environmental-class option above 232°C in a rotary body, to 316°C at 1500 psi. Specifying on friction or cost before checking which of these cells the actual service point falls into is exactly how a packing spec passes acceptance and fails a compliance audit a year later.

items.t: ≤300 psi (20.7 bar) / 93°C (200°F); sliding-stem only; lowest friction; fails the rotary low-emission criterion.
≤750 psi (51.7 bar) / 232°C (450°F); sliding-stem or rotary.
≤232°C (450°F); fire-tested to API Standard 589; sliding-stem only.
Above 232°C (450°F); the system for service beyond Duplex's PTFE ceiling.
Rotary only; ≤1500 psi (103 bar) to 316°C (600°F) environmental, to 371°C (700°F) non-environmental.

primitives.sourceNote: The two-axis framing itself (pressure/temperature AND emissions class as independent checks, not one combined judgment) is cvh-topic-packing-selection-criteria's own framing; the five envelope figures are the same figures already introduced on slides 117-121, restated here as one synthesis rather than newly sourced.
primitives.templateRationale: A decision table is the content itself — five packing systems reviewed against pressure/temperature, emissions class, and body-style constraints is naturally a System / Envelope / Emissions class / Body style table, the tp-009 decision-table application variant (Style Guide §5.10/§9.2, .slide--role-application:has(.tmpl-table)). Column order departs from §9.4's given-to-answer default: the row key here is the packing system (already named on prior slides), with envelope/class/body-style as the given columns being checked against it, since the teaching task is comparing five already-taught systems rather than selecting one label from stated criteria. No corroborating figure is available for the variant's paired-figure pane — all seven registry figures for this competency are already placed on slides 117-121 — flagged under Concept-map gaps; Stage 3 should run the table full-width rather than force an unrelated image into the figure slot.

primitives.t: Packing friction is measured empirically, by stem size and pressure class, and tabulated per packing type — it is not a fixed design constant the way seat load is. Figure 5.5's own values show the spread: a 5/16-inch stem at Class 125 runs 20 lbf with single PTFE, while a 3/4-inch stem at Class 600 runs 320 lbf with graphite — roughly an order of magnitude apart, driven by the packing material choice itself as much as by stem size or pressure class. Friction here is explicitly NOT 100% repeatable the way the other actuator-sizing force terms are: live-loaded designs, graphite especially, carry real shot-to-shot variation, which is why an actuator force-margin calculation treats packing friction as a real, variable input rather than a number looked up once and trusted.
primitives.sourceNote: cvh-topic-packing-friction (§5.11.1.3) is the prose source for the non-repeatability claim and the A+B+C+D actuator-sizing force-total framing (packing friction is force C); Figure 5.5 is the tabulated data behind it.
primitives.templateRationale: Mechanism treatment for the how-it's-measured concept. Figure 5.5 is a table-formatted figure, catalogued as a figure per the Subject-Matter Index's own table-as-figure rule; it is used as the .tpl-fig content inside the mechanism shape rather than switched to .slide--tmpl-table, since the teaching point is the sizing methodology this data feeds into, not the table as a standalone reference object.

primitives.t: Same packing systems, two different guideline charts, because the emissions requirement redraws the envelope, not the hardware. Figure 5.17 plots each system's pressure/temperature envelope under the 100 PPM (fugitive-emissions-regulated) standard; Figure 5.18 plots the identical systems under non-environmental service, with envelopes that open up substantially — HIGH-SEAL Graphite ULF, for example, is rated to 1500 psi / -7 to 315°C under the 100 PPM chart but 4200 psi / -198 to 538°C non-environmental, for the identical physical packing. Reading the wrong chart for the service's actual emissions requirement does not just under- or over-spec the packing — it can pass a service point the correct chart would have rejected outright.

items.t: Figure 5.17 — pressure/temperature envelope per packing system under the 100 PPM fugitive-emissions standard; narrower envelopes throughout.
Figure 5.18 — same packing-system set under non-environmental service; wider envelopes (e.g. temperature axis extends to roughly 1200°F versus Figure 5.17's roughly 600°F).

primitives.sourceNote: The HIGH-SEAL Graphite ULF comparison (1500 psi/-7 to 315°C vs. 4200 psi/-198 to 538°C) is cvh-topic-packing-selection-criteria's own worked example of how far the two charts diverge for one identical packing system.
primitives.templateRationale: Two panels, same chart shape and packing-system set, differing only by which emissions standard applies — exactly two figures, a genuine this-standard-vs-that-standard pairing. These are analytical graphs (Style Guide §5), not part cutaways — each retains its own §5.3 key rather than the §6 part-callout treatment if placed on a slide.

reground.hook: Picture a rotating shaft or sliding rod passing straight through the wall of a pressurized container — the plunger on a bicycle pump, at toy scale, is the same idea. Whatever seals around that rod has to keep sealing while the rod keeps moving, survive however hot the container gets, and — if the rules say so — leak less than an amount you could barely detect with a sniffer.
reground.bridge: That sealing material is packing, and the rod is the valve stem. This module is about choosing which packing material and arrangement to specify — plain PTFE, graphite, or a live-loaded combination of the two — for a stated pressure, temperature, and how strict the site's emissions rule is, and about how the extra force that packing adds to moving the stem gets measured and accounted for in an actuator's sizing.
reground.depth:
Stem packing comes from two base part families: a PTFE V-ring stack (upper wiper, packing follower, adaptors, V-ring, lantern ring, spring, box ring/lower wiper) or a graphite stack (filament ring, laminated ring, lantern ring, optional sacrificial zinc washer). Either stack is then built up in one of three arrangements for a globe body — Single, Double, or Leak-Off (a double arrangement with the lantern-ring tap piped away rather than vented).

Five real systems, each occupying a distinct cell of the pressure/temperature-by-emissions-class-by-body-style space, are what a real spec actually chooses among: Single PTFE V-ring (coil spring, ≤300 psi/20.7 bar, -18 to 93°C/200°F, sliding-stem only, lowest friction of the five, fails the rotary low-emission criterion outright); ENVIRO-SEAL PTFE (live-load spring pack, ≤750 psi/51.7 bar, 232°C/450°F, sliding-stem or rotary, also specified non-environmental for its longer service life); ENVIRO-SEAL Duplex (PTFE and graphite, ≤232°C/450°F, fire-tested to API Standard 589, sliding-stem only, no rotary version); ENVIRO-SEAL Graphite ULF (graphite-based with thin PTFE layers inside the rings to recover friction/cycle life, built for service above 232°C/450°F, where Duplex's PTFE content fails); and ENVIRO-SEAL Graphite for rotary valves (rotary-only, ≤1500 psi/103 bar to 316°C/600°F meeting the 100 ppmv EPA criterion, to 371°C/700°F non-environmental, or specified independently for fire safety).

Packing friction (force C in the actuator-sizing A+B+C+D total) is measured empirically by stem size and pressure class, tabulated per material (Figure 5.5: 20 lbf for single PTFE at a 5/16-inch stem/Class 125 versus 320 lbf for graphite at a 3/4-inch stem/Class 600 — roughly an order of magnitude apart) and is explicitly not 100% repeatable, unlike the other three force terms — live-loaded and graphite designs carry real shot-to-shot variation an actuator margin has to absorb.

Selection itself runs on two independent axes, not one: the pressure/temperature envelope, and whether the service is 100 PPM (fugitive-emissions-regulated, Figure 5.17) or non-environmental (Figure 5.18) — the identical physical packing can see a roughly 3x pressure difference and a far wider temperature range between the two charts (HIGH-SEAL Graphite ULF: 1500 psi/-7 to 315°C at 100 PPM versus 4200 psi/-198 to 538°C non-environmental). A spec built on friction or cost alone, without checking the emissions-class envelope against the correct chart, is exactly the failure mode that passes acceptance testing today and surfaces as a compliance finding within the year.

Debrief resolves any group that picked on friction/cost alone without checking the emissions-class envelope — the module's own stakes failure.

modules.title: Emissions Standards & Compliance
modules.stakes: A packing system that can't be verified against a real measurement-frequency requirement is a compliance gap, not a documentation gap.
modules.objective: Apply fugitive-emissions standards and VOC/LDAR measurement-frequency requirements to select a packing system that meets a stated emissions target.

primitives.t: US fugitive-emissions regulation (LDAR — Leak Detection and Repair) requires periodically monitoring every valve in regulated service against a 500 ppmv leak threshold — 100 ppmv in some cities — because non-point-source VOC leaks with no single point to inspect add up to an estimated 400 million lb/year nationally. Module 1 selected a packing system against a pressure/temperature and emissions-class envelope; that selection is not itself the compliance record. A packing system that can't be verified against a real, ongoing measurement-frequency requirement is a compliance gap, not a documentation gap — this module is that verification step.
primitives.sourceNote: Prime opens on the module's own stakes line and the regulatory scale/threshold facts rather than a figure — no single figure represents the ongoing-verification stakes as a concept in its own right; grounded in cvh-topic-fugitive-emissions-standards (400 million lb/year fugitive-emissions estimate; 500 ppmv threshold, 100 ppmv in some cities) and pp-topic-fugitive-emissions-regulatory-framework's same regulatory-driver framing.

primitives.t: LDAR monitoring frequency is not fixed — it steps down as the fleet's own leak performance improves. A facility starts at Monthly LDAR; falling below 2% of valves found leaking above the 500 ppmv threshold steps the interval to Quarterly, below 1% to Semi-Annual, and below 0.5% to Annual. A facility that fails to hold a threshold on re-monitoring feeds into a Quality Improvement Plan rather than simply reverting a level — the interval is earned by demonstrated fleet-wide performance, not granted by installing a 'better' packing system alone.

ENVIRO-SEAL PTFE, Duplex, and Graphite ULF are all documented as 'environmental'-service systems, but none carries a stated ppmv number in this citation — they support the general LDAR threshold, not a proven match to a stated 100 ppmv target, until verified against the actual applicable standard. A sliding-stem service given a stated 100 ppmv target, inside Single PTFE V-Ring's own envelope, is the one Module 1 system with a documented match; a rotary service given the same target has exactly one documented match, ENVIRO-SEAL Graphite for rotary. Meeting a stated emissions target is a real cross-reference against what a system is actually documented to meet — not an assumption that any 'environmental'-labelled system satisfies any stated number.

reground.hook: Think of a large building's smoke-detector network: installing good detectors once and calling it done isn't the rule — code requires walking the building on a schedule and confirming they still work, and how often you have to walk it depends on how many alarms have actually been going off lately.
reground.bridge: A valve's packing system is the building's detector, and LDAR (Leak Detection and Repair) is the walk-the-building-on-a-schedule half of the same regulation Module 1's material-and-envelope choice only set up. The packing chosen there still has to be verified on an ongoing measurement-frequency schedule, set by how many valves in the fleet are actually found leaking above a real numeric emissions threshold — not just specified once and filed away.
reground.depth:
US fugitive-emissions regulation (LDAR) requires periodic monitoring of every regulated valve against a 500 ppmv leak threshold (100 ppmv in some cities), because non-point-source VOC leaks with no single inspectable point add up to an estimated 400 million lb/year nationally.

The monitoring interval itself is not fixed: a facility starts at Monthly LDAR and steps down as its own leak performance improves — below 2% of valves found leaking above threshold moves it to Quarterly, below 1% to Semi-Annual, below 0.5% to Annual — with a Quality Improvement Plan branch for a facility that fails to hold a threshold on re-monitoring, rather than a simple revert. That interval is earned by demonstrated fleet-wide performance, not granted by installing a 'better' packing system alone — though a lower-leakage system is exactly what makes clearing a given threshold achievable.

Cross-referencing Module 1's own five packing systems against what each is actually documented to meet sharpens this further: only Single PTFE V-Ring (sliding-stem, ≤300 psi/93°C) and ENVIRO-SEAL Graphite for rotary valves (≤1500 psi/316°C) are explicitly documented against the tighter 100 ppmv EPA criterion in the sourcebook; ENVIRO-SEAL PTFE, Duplex, and Graphite ULF are documented as 'environmental'-service systems generally but without a stated ppmv number, so a spec asked to hit a tightened target — a stricter city ordinance, or a fleet trying to earn a longer monitoring interval — must verify the actual applicable standard rather than assume any environmental label clears any stated number.

modules.title: Bonnet Types & End Connections
modules.stakes: The wrong bonnet type for a temperature extreme defeats the packing selection entirely, regardless of how correctly the packing material itself was chosen.
modules.objective: Select a bonnet type — standard, extension, bellows-seal, cryogenic-extension — for a temperature/isolation requirement, and select an end connection while identifying galvanic-corrosion and oxygen-service precautions.

primitives.t: A bonnet is not just a mounting point for the actuator — it's a pressure-retaining component that also decides how far the packing box sits from process temperature, and how much stem leakage the service can tolerate. Get bonnet type wrong for a temperature extreme or an isolation requirement and it defeats a correctly-selected packing system outright: packing rated to 232°C accomplishes nothing if the bonnet lets the packing box itself run hotter than that.
primitives.sourceNote: Prime opens on the module's own stakes line rather than a figure — no single figure represents the bonnet-defeats-packing stakes as a concept in its own right; grounded in cve1-ch7-m3's stakes field and cvh-topic-bonnet-function-and-types' dual framing of the bonnet as a pressure-retaining component that also sets packing-box temperature.
primitives.templateRationale: Opens on the stakes question before any bonnet type is shown, per Axis 3's prime role and this course's own prime precedent (cve1-ch7-m1's slide 116, cve1-ch7-m2's slide 126) — no figure represents 'why bonnet choice can defeat packing selection' as a concept in its own right.

primitives.t: Every bonnet type in this module is a variation on one baseline assembly: the bonnet itself (the pressure-retaining casting the stem passes through), the packing that seals the stem, the packing box (the bored recess cut into the bonnet that the packing sits in — not the casting as a whole), and the valve stem. A standard bonnet is exactly this assembly, unmodified; every other type in this module changes one part of it to meet a specific temperature or isolation requirement.
primitives.templateRationale: A labelled-parts figure sequenced first, per Axis 3's nomenclature-before-mechanism ordering — CVH Figure 1.6 is the generic bonnet-assembly baseline every other type in this module modifies. The figure carries its own printed numbered callouts (1. Bonnet, 2. Packing, 3. Packing Box, 4. Valve Stem, Style Guide §6.2) in the same order the list already needs, so the list follows the figure's own numbering rather than re-marking.

primitives.t: The four bonnet types this module covers all modify the same baseline assembly for one of two reasons — temperature or leakage isolation. Standard: the baseline itself, unmodified, near-ambient service. Extension — cast: moves the packing box away from a high-temperature process; cast construction dissipates heat well via emissivity. Extension — fabricated: moves the packing box away from a cryogenic process; thin-wall stainless tubing minimizes heat influx into the packing box instead of dissipating it out. Bellows-seal: does not relocate the packing box at all — it isolates the stem from the process entirely, for near-zero leakage, with a standard or environmental packing box retained above the bellows purely as a catastrophic-failure backup.
primitives.sourceNote: The four-type breakdown itself is cvh-topic-bonnet-function-and-types' own framing (standard/cast-extension/fabricated-extension/bellows-seal). cvh-cmp-bonnet-variations (Figure 3.20) is kept only as a general 'range of bonnet constructions' illustration per its own teaches field — the Subject-Matter Index flags it low-confidence (the source page text never enumerates which specific styles the photo shows, and the image itself was not visually inspected), so this slide does not assert the photo depicts these four specific types.

A plain four-row reference table (Style Guide §9.2, .slide--tmpl-table) is the correct shape; cvh-cmp-bonnet-variations runs alongside it as a general illustration rather than a per-type key, given its own low-confidence flag.

primitives.t: An extension bonnet moves the packing box far enough from the process that packing temperature stays inside its rated range — the same mechanism serves both ends of the temperature scale, with opposite construction logic. Fabricated extensions (smooth-surface stainless tubing, shown here) are built for cold/cryogenic service, where thin-wall construction minimizes heat influx into the packing box. Cast extensions serve the hot end instead — their construction dissipates heat outward via emissivity rather than blocking it. A concrete number from the packing side: an extension bonnet stops being optional, not just preferred, once packing-box temperature would otherwise exceed roughly 427°C (800°F).
primitives.sourceNote: cvh-topic-bonnet-function-and-types is the basis for the cast (hot-end)/fabricated (cold-end) construction contrast. The 427°C (800°F) extension-bonnet threshold is ref-topic-laminated-filament-graphite-packing's own specific number (Refining Sourcebook ch3, cited under the end-connection competency's topic list) — a real, verified fact bearing directly on this bonnet-type decision, cited here for the concrete threshold an evaluate-level audience needs rather than left as a qualitative 'hot service' description.

primitives.t: Bellows-seal bonnets isolate the stem from the process with a metal bellows instead of relocating the packing box — the near-zero-leakage answer (<1×10⁻⁶ cc/sec helium) for toxic, volatile, radioactive, or high-value fluids. A standard or environmental packing box is retained above the bellows regardless, as a catastrophic-failure backup, not the primary seal. The bellows element itself is built one of two ways, and the choice is a real tradeoff: welded-leaf construction gives a shorter overall package height, but its manufacturing method can limit service life; mechanically-formed construction is taller, but its more repeatable manufacturing process gives it higher reliability. Neither is a universal 'better' choice — the tradeoff is height budget against expected service life.

items.t: Generic bellows-seal cutaway (CVH Fig. 1.5) — bonnet, packing, packing box, bellows, and stem in one 5-part labelled assembly; the backup packing box sits above the bellows, not in place of it.

ENVIRO-SEAL's own bellows-seal bonnet assembly (CVH Fig. 3.22, printed p.67) — the production construction the welded-leaf/mechanically-formed comparison fits inside; used for near-zero leakage toward toxic, volatile, radioactive, or very expensive process fluids.
Welded-leaf bellows element (CVH Fig. 3.23) — shorter overall package height; manufacturing method can limit service life.

Mechanically-formed bellows element (CVH Fig. 3.24, printed p.67 — a confirmed source duplicate caption distinct from the packing-arrangement Figure 3.24 on printed p.68) — taller than welded-leaf; more repeatable manufacturing gives higher reliability.

primitives.t: Every bonnet type in this module answers one of two questions: does the packing box need to move away from a temperature extreme, or does stem leakage itself need to go to near zero? Standard: neither question applies — near-ambient service, no modification. Extension (cast): the high-temperature question — packing-box temperature would otherwise exceed its rated range, and by roughly 427°C (800°F) an extension bonnet stops being optional. Extension (fabricated): the same question at the opposite end — a cryogenic or cold process, where thin-wall construction minimizes heat influx instead of dissipating it. Bellows-seal: the isolation question — the service can't tolerate any stem leakage (toxic, volatile, radioactive, or high-value fluid), and near-zero leakage matters more than either temperature extreme; welded-leaf versus mechanically-formed only differ in package height against expected service life. Defaulting to bellows-seal as a blanket 'safest' choice, or reaching for an extension bonnet to solve what is actually an emissions/isolation requirement rather than a temperature one, both fail this check.

items.t: Standard — no modification; near-ambient service.
Extension — cast for the hot end (~427°C/800°F and above), fabricated stainless for the cold/cryogenic end; either moves the packing box out of the process-temperature extreme.
Bellows-seal — near-zero stem leakage (<1×10⁻⁶ cc/sec helium) for toxic/volatile/radioactive/high-value fluids; standard/environmental packing box retained above the bellows as backup only.

primitives.t: Bolted flanges and welded ends trade the same three things off in opposite directions: economy, serviceability, and temperature/pressure range. Bolted flanges — flat-face, raised-face, or ring-type joint — are easily removed, and between the three styles cover the full working range most control valves are built for, to roughly 815°C or 15,000 psig depending on style; that removability is what lets a bolted-flange valve come out of the line for service without touching the surrounding pipe. Welded ends — socket-weld or butt-weld — are leak-tight at any pressure or temperature and cheaper in first cost, but removing one means cutting it out of the line, and construction is limited to weldable body materials.

items.t: Flat-face (low-pressure cast-iron/brass), raised-face (Class 250 steel/alloy standard, to 6000 psig/815°C), ring-type joint (to 15,000 psig, not for high temperature) — all bolted, all removable without cutting the line.

Socket-weld (≤NPS 2, fillet weld) or butt-weld (≥NPS 2-1/2, full-penetration weld) — leak-tight at any pressure/temperature, cheaper first cost, but the valve comes out of the line only by cutting it out.

Each figure carries its own printed sub-style labels (Flat-Face/Raised-Face/Ring-Type Joint; Socket Weld-Ends/Butt Weld-Ends — Style Guide §6.3), so the items name them verbatim rather than re-marking with numbered circles.

primitives.t: Because the same bolt pattern is doing three sealing/alignment jobs at once, an uneven or under-torqued bolt-up doesn't just risk a body-bonnet leak — it can let the cage shift out of alignment with the seat ring, binding or unevenly seating the plug, which is why this bonnet type calls for a proper torque sequence on reassembly rather than just tightening until it stops leaking.

primitives.t: Graphite packing carries a real galvanic-corrosion risk to the stem under humid conditions with chlorides and oxygen present — a risk the number of variables involved makes near-impossible to predict in advance. Fisher mitigates it with a nonmetallic passivating inhibitor built into the base graphite material and a sacrificial zinc washer on every graphite packing system except nuclear service, but neither measure eliminates the risk outright. The safest storage policy would be shipping the valve with no packing installed at all — except that trades one risk for a worse one: **someone could put the valve into service without realizing it has no packing installed**, which is exactly why every Fisher valve ships with packing already in, accepting the corrosion risk to avoid the bigger one.
primitives.sourceNote: pss-topic-galvanic-corrosion-and-storage (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook ch11, printed p.11-3) — a prose-only topic with no supporting figure in the source.
primitives.templateRationale: Axis 3 caution role — the orange warning treatment (Style Guide §4.4/§8.3), one consequence stated plainly with the failure itself bolded ('someone could put the valve into service without realizing it has no packing installed').

primitives.t: Oxygen service — liquid or gaseous — needs one explicit precaution at the ordering stage: oxygen supports combustion of most lubricants and foreign material left in a packing system, so **oxygen service must be specified by name when the packing or other equipment is ordered**, so it ships already degreased. There is no figure for this in the source — it is a brief fact, but a safety-critical one, and it is easy to miss precisely because it is a paperwork step at the ordering stage rather than a hardware choice.

primitives.t: End-connection choice runs on the same economy/serviceability/temperature-range tradeoff bonnet type ran on temperature/isolation — plus two precautions that apply regardless of which connection is chosen. Bolted flange: removable without cutting the line, and between its three styles covers the full working range, the connection to specify when the valve will come out again. Welded: leak-tight at any condition and cheaper up front, but a piping spec calling for welded connections narrows the valve choice to sliding-stem bodies, and low-temperature composition trim must come out before welding to avoid heat damage. Either way: a dissimilar-metal flanged joint headed for extended outdoor storage carries the galvanic-corrosion risk just covered, and any packing ordered for oxygen service must be specified as such so it ships degreased — neither precaution is optional, and neither substitutes for the other.

Leak-tight at any pressure/temperature, cheapest first cost; removable only by cutting it out; a welded-only spec narrows the valve choice to sliding-stem bodies.

reground.hook: Think of a thermos: the lid isn't just a lid — it's built specifically so heat can't travel up the neck and defeat the insulation below it, and whether that lid can leak at all around its own seal is a completely separate design question from the insulation itself.
reground.bridge: The bonnet on a control valve is exactly that lid. It's chosen to keep an already-selected packing system from running hotter or colder than the packing itself was rated for, and — if the fluid is dangerous enough — to add a second, near-perfect seal against the stem instead of relying on packing alone. End connection is the separate decision of how the whole valve bolts or welds into the pipe it lives in, plus two precautions that apply no matter which connection gets picked.
reground.depth:
A bonnet is a pressure-retaining component the plug stem moves through; it also mounts the actuator, houses the packing box, and — on cage/retainer-trim bodies — supplies the bolting-up force that seals the body-bonnet joint and aligns the cage (and through it the plug/stem). Four real types answer one of two selection questions. Standard is the unmodified baseline for near-ambient service. Extension bonnets move the packing box away from a process-temperature extreme: cast construction dissipates heat via emissivity for the hot end, fabricated stainless tubing minimizes heat influx for the cold/cryogenic end, and an extension bonnet stops being optional once packing-box temperature would otherwise exceed roughly 427°C (800°F).

Bellows-seal bonnets answer the isolation question instead — a metal bellows seals the stem from the process entirely, for near-zero leakage (<1×10⁻⁶ cc/sec helium) toward toxic, volatile, radioactive, or high-value fluids, with a standard or environmental packing box retained above the bellows purely as a catastrophic-failure backup, never the primary seal; the bellows element itself is welded-leaf (shorter package, potentially shorter service life) or mechanically-formed (taller, more reliable manufacturing).

The most common bolted-flange bonnet is an integral flange forged to body-equivalent material, whose bolting compresses three gaskets at once — a flat sheet gasket at the body-bonnet joint, a spiral-wound gasket on the cage, a second flat sheet gasket below the seat ring — while retaining the packing follower on the bonnet's own yoke boss.

End connection is a parallel, independent tradeoff among economy, serviceability, and temperature/pressure range: bolted flanges (flat-face, raised-face, ring-type joint) are removable without cutting the line and between them cover the full range most control valves are built for, to roughly 815°C or 15,000 psig depending on style; welded ends (socket-weld, butt-weld) are leak-tight at any condition and cheaper up front, but come out of the line only by being cut out, and a welded-only piping spec narrows the valve choice to sliding-stem bodies.

Two precautions apply on top of whichever connection is chosen, independent of it: graphite packing carries a galvanic-corrosion risk to the stem under humid, chloride-bearing, oxygen-present conditions that is near-impossible to predict — Fisher mitigates but does not eliminate it with a passivating inhibitor and a sacrificial zinc washer (except in nuclear service), and every valve ships with packing already installed as a deliberate safety-over-corrosion tradeoff rather than shipped bare for storage; and oxygen service must be specified by name at the ordering stage, since oxygen supports combustion of lubricants or foreign material, so the packing ships already degreased.

modules.title: Liquid Sizing & Critical Pressure Ratio
modules.stakes: A sizing error doesn't fail gracefully — undersized can't pass rated flow at any opening, oversized operates nearly closed for its whole service life.
modules.objective: Calculate required Cv for a liquid service using the standard equation with piping-geometry correction, and determine liquid critical pressure ratio to check for choked liquid flow.

reground.hook: Picking a valve's Cv is like choosing a garden-hose nozzle for a specific job: too narrow and you can't get enough water through no matter how hard you open the tap; too wide and the last inch of twist barely changes the flow at all. There's also a hard physical ceiling built into the nozzle itself — squeeze the opening down far enough and the water starts flashing into vapor right at the narrowest point, so past that point opening it further buys you nothing.
reground.bridge: Cv sizing is choosing that nozzle size by calculation instead of by feel — solving for the one capacity number (Cv) that matches the real flow rate, pressures, and specific gravity of the service, then correcting for whatever piping the valve is actually bolted into. Checking the liquid critical pressure ratio is confirming, ahead of installation, whether that valve's operating point sits past the vaporization ceiling — because past it, opening the valve further doesn't add flow, and which failure mode you get (cavitation damage downstream vs. flashing) depends on where in the valve the pressure recovers.
reground.depth:
The ISA/IEC liquid-sizing procedure is a six-step loop, not a single formula: (1) specify q, P1, P2/ΔP, T1, Gf, Pv, Pc; (2) pull the unit constant N1 (volumetric) or N6 (mass) from the equation-constants table; (3) determine Fp, the piping geometry factor, only if reducers/elbows/tees are attached directly to the valve's own connections (Fp=1.0 and drops out otherwise); (4) determine ΔPmax or qmax to check for choked flow; (5) solve Cv = q/(N1·Fp·√(ΔP/Gf)) using the lesser of the actual ΔP and ΔPmax; (6) select the valve size from the flow-coefficient table, and repeat the loop if the calculated Cv exceeds the assumed valve's rated capacity. Kv = 0.865·Cv and Av = 2.40×10⁻⁵·Cv convert to the coefficients used outside North America. Fp = [1 + (ΣK/N2)·(Cv/d²)²]^(-1/2), ΣK = K1 + K2 + KB1 − KB2; KB1/KB2 cancel when the piping is the same size on both sides, and for a valve between identical concentric reducers ΣK collapses to K1+K2 = 1.5·(1−d²/D²)².

The source's own worked case, transcribed exactly (Fisher Control Valve Sourcebook, Oil & Gas and Power & Severe Service editions — identical numbers in both): an NPS 8 propane line, ASME CL300 globe valve with equal-percentage cage, q=800 gpm, P1=314.7 psia, P2=289.7 psia (ΔP=25 psi), Gf=0.50, Pv=124.3 psia, Pc=616.3 psia. Assume NPS 3 (Cv=121 rated): ΣK=1.5·(1−9/64)²=1.11, Fp=0.90, required Cv=(1.0·0.90)⁻¹·800·√(25/0.50)... solved directly from the source = 125.7 — exceeds the NPS 3 valve's own 121 rating, so the assumption fails. Reassume NPS 4 (Cv=203 rated): ΣK=0.84, Fp=0.93, required Cv=121.7 — under 203, but far enough from the 203 used to derive Fp that one more pass is warranted: feed 121.7 back into the Fp equation, get Fp=0.97, required Cv converges to 116.2 — close enough to 121.7 to stop. Final selection: NPS 4 valve, roughly 75% open.

Choked flow is vaporization, not a friction ceiling: once static pressure inside the valve drops below the liquid's own vapor pressure, it flashes at the vena contracta and additional ΔP stops increasing flow. ΔPmax(L) = FL²·(P1−FF·Pv) with no fittings, or the Fp/FLP-corrected ΔPmax(LP) with fittings; FF (the liquid critical pressure ratio factor) reads off a chart — water gets its own curve (vapor pressure at the valve inlet, dual psia/bar axis), every other liquid uses the general curve (dimensionless Pv/Pc) — or off FF = 0.96 − 0.28·√(Pv/Pc). Whichever of ΔPmax and the actual ΔP is smaller goes into the Cv equation; if ΔPmax is the smaller value, the flow is choked, and the outlet-pressure test then tells you which failure mode: below the liquid's vapor pressure is flashing, above it is cavitation.

Running the same propane case through this check: Pv/Pc=124.3/616.3≈0.202, FF≈0.96−0.28·√0.202≈0.83, and against the actual ΔP of 25 psi, ΔPmax comes out larger — the source states plainly that 'based on the small required pressure drop, the flow will not be choked' — so for this specific case the cavitation-versus-flashing diagnostic never triggers at all, which is itself a real part of the skill: recognizing when the check doesn't apply.

primitives.t: An undersized valve can't pass rated flow at any opening; an oversized one spends its whole service life riding near closed, with no control resolution left to work with. The six-step ISA/IEC sizing procedure exists to catch both before the spec is issued — not to make the arithmetic look rigorous after the fact.

Once it is, the outlet pressure tells you which failure mode: below the liquid's vapor pressure it's flashing; above it, cavitation — the collapse happens downstream instead.

modules.title: Compressible Sizing & Choked Flow
modules.stakes: Missing a choked-flow condition in a compressible sizing calculation means the valve can never pass the flow the spec sheet claims, no matter how far it opens.
modules.objective: Calculate required Cv for a compressible (gas/steam) service, and apply expansion factor and Xtp piping-geometry correction to determine whether a compressible service is choked.

reground.hook: Blowing hard through a straw eventually stops helping — past a point, the air already moving through it is going as fast as it can, and blowing harder doesn't push any more through. A gas or steam control valve hits the exact same ceiling: past a certain pressure drop, the gas is already moving at the speed of sound right at the valve's narrowest point, and dropping the downstream pressure further doesn't add flow — it just wastes energy.
reground.bridge: Sizing a compressible-service valve is finding the right straw diameter (Cv) for a stated gas or steam flow — the same kind of calculation as liquid sizing, but with an extra correction (the expansion factor Y) built in because the gas's own density keeps changing as it drops through the valve. Checking whether the service is choked is finding out, before the valve ships, whether it's already being blown as hard as it can be — and the piping bolted around the valve (through Xtp) can genuinely move where that ceiling sits.
reground.depth:
The compressible-fluid ISA/IEC procedure branches from liquid sizing at step 1: it needs the gas's molecular weight (M) and specific-heat ratio (k) in addition to the liquid variables, and the unit-constant choice forks in two directions at once — volumetric vs. mass flow, and which gas property (Gg or M) is actually specified — giving four constants (N6/N7/N8/N9) where liquid sizing only needs two (N1/N6). Governing equation for mass-flow units with specific weight g1 known: Cv = w/(N6·Fp·Y·√(x·P1·g1)); volumetric forms substitute N7 (Gg known) or N9 (M known). Fp is the identical piping-geometry correction m1 already taught, unchanged in form. Y, the expansion factor, is new: Y = 1 − x/(3·Fk·xT) (or xTP with fittings attached), Fk = k/1.4, x = ΔP/P1. Choking is a sonic-velocity ceiling at the vena contracta, not liquid sizing's vaporization ceiling: once x reaches or exceeds Fk·xT (or Fk·xTP), Y locks at exactly 0.667 and further ΔP buys nothing. When fittings are attached at the valve's own connections, xT is replaced by xTP = (xT/Fp²)·[1 + (xT·Ki/N5)·(Cv/d²)²]⁻¹, Ki = K1 + KB1 (the same K-factor piping geometry Fp already uses).

Two real worked cases exist in the source (Fisher Control Valve Sourcebook — Power & Severe Service, 4th ed., Chapter 4). Sample Problem 1 (8-inch Design V250 ball valve, natural gas, q=6.0×10⁶ scfh, P1=214.7 psia, ΔP=150 psi, x=0.70) is genuinely choked: at the assumed 100%-travel xT=0.137, FkxT=0.129 is far below x=0.70, so Y=0.667 and the resulting Cv=1515 corresponds to roughly 83° opening — but at 83° the valve's own real xT is 0.252 (not the rated 0.137), so FkxT recalculates to 0.237, dropping the required Cv to 1118 (between 75° and 80° opening); one more pass at 78°'s xT=0.328 gives FkxT=0.308 and Cv=980, close enough to the 75° figure to stop there — three iterations to converge, a materially different and more involved iteration than liquid sizing's iterate-by-valve-size approach (m1's propane case), because here the valve's OWN xT changes with opening angle, so the choking threshold itself moves as the calculation converges.

This module's continuing worked case is Sample Problem 2 instead — a 4-inch ANSI Class 300 Design ED valve with linear cage, installed with reducers in a 6-inch line, superheated steam at w=125,000 lb/h, P1=500 psig (514.7 psia), P2=250 psig (264.7 psia), x=0.49, T1=500°F, g1=1.0434 lb/ft³, k=1.28. N6=63.3. Fp=0.95 (from the same SK=1.5·(1−(4/6)²)²=0.463 geometry m1 already covers). xT=0.688 (rated); Ki=0.5·(1−(4/6)²)²+[1−(4/6)⁴]=0.96; xTP=(0.688/0.95²)·[1+(0.688·0.96/1000)·(236/16)²]⁻¹≈0.67. Fk=1.28/1.40=0.91, so Fk·xTP=0.61 — above the actual x=0.49, so the service is NOT choked, Y=1−0.49/(3·0.91·0.67)=0.73. Cv=125,000/(63.3·0.95·0.73·√(0.49·514.7·1.0434))=176, against the 4-inch valve's own rated Cv=236 (the next size down, 3-inch, rates only 148) — confirmed correct on the first assumption, no resizing pass needed.

This is the source's only worked demonstration of xTP specifically (the gas case has no fittings, Fp=1, and never touches xTP at all) — which is why it, not the more dramatic iterative gas case, is this module's continuing worked example; the gas case is used only as the choked-flow mechanism's illustrating contrast. Kv=0.865·Cv and Av=2.40×10⁻⁵·Cv convert to the coefficient systems used outside North America, unchanged from liquid sizing.

primitives.t: A compressible-service Cv calculation that skips the choked-flow check can pass on paper and still never deliver rated flow in the field — once the pressure-drop ratio crosses the valve's own critical value, opening it further buys nothing. The same ISA/IEC sizing logic from liquid sizing carries over, but two new gas-specific variables (molecular weight, specific-heat ratio) and a ratio-based choking test replace the liquid procedure's absolute ΔPmax.

primitives.t: Y = 1 − x/(3·Fk·xTP) — the expansion factor drops linearly from 1.0 (no expansion) toward its 0.667 floor as x approaches the choked ratio. When the valve carries reducers or other fittings at its own connections, xT is replaced by xTP = (xT/Fp²)·[1 + (xT·Ki/N5)·(Cv/d²)²]⁻¹, where Ki=K1+KB1 is the inlet head-loss coefficient (built from the same K-factor piping geometry m1's Fp equation already uses) and N5 is the usual unit constant. xTP folds the fittings' own resistance into the choking threshold itself — a smaller valve in a larger line can choke at a different point than the flow-coefficient table's rated xT alone would suggest.
primitives.sourceNote: pss-topic-choked-flow-expansion-factor / pss-topic-xtp-piping-geometry-correction — confirmed prose-only (figures: []). chapters.title: Installation Practice: Piping Arrangement, Orientation & Commissioning
chapters._source: Enabling Competency `eng.installation.piping-practice-and-orientation` — see Curriculum — CVE1.md and Competency Hierarchy — CVE1, CVE2, CVE3 v3.md, Chapter 9. Modules below are STUBS ONLY (status: outline, empty keyConcepts) pending a real Stage 1 arc-cut per module.

modules.title: Piping Arrangement & Line Sizing
modules.stakes: A correctly selected and sized valve installed against the wrong piping arrangement underperforms in a way that gets blamed on the valve itself.
modules.objective: Apply standard piping-arrangement guidelines for a control valve installation, and evaluate whether line size matches valve size to identify velocity-limitation violations.

primitives.t: A control valve sized and selected correctly on paper can still fall short in the field — not because the valve is wrong, but because the piping immediately around it, and the line it's dropped into, change what the valve can actually deliver. Piping arrangement measurably cuts real capacity independent of the valve's own rating, and a line size mismatched to the valve carries its own strength and velocity risks — and when either goes wrong, the valve is what gets blamed.
primitives.sourceNote: Prime opens on the module's own stakes line rather than a figure, drawing the framing from pss-topic-control-valve-piping-arrangement's own opening point (adjacent piping arrangement measurably affects a control valve's real capacity, not just its nameplate rating) and pss-topic-line-size-vs-valve-size / pss-topic-velocity-limitations for the line-size/velocity half of the module; all three are confirmed prose-only (figures: [] in the registry), so no single figure represents the stakes framing itself.
primitives.templateRationale: A stakes-framing statement before either guideline set is taught, per Axis 3's prime role — matches this course's other module-opening prime slides (e.g. slide 152). No figure exists for either competency (confirmed prose-only), so this uses the plain-tagline shape.

primitives.t: A close-coupled reducer sized down to the valve, with block valves matched to valve size, cuts a typical 2-inch valve's real capacity by roughly 5%; that loss grows toward 10% as valve size increases at the same 2:1 ratio, and adding elbows between the reducers and the valve can push it to 15%. Moving the block valves out to line size, clear of the reducers, removes most of this effect. Avoid an inlet arrangement that creates a nozzle effect (it alters the flow characteristic itself), avoid close-coupled inlet block valves reduced from line size, and avoid sharp turns close to the inlet — straight-line sections into and out of the valve should reproduce the piping the valve's own capacity and characteristic data were established against, generally 10-20 pipe diameters upstream and 5-10 diameters downstream. **Get this wrong and a correctly sized valve can lose up to 15% of its rated capacity — a shortfall the installation caused, not the valve.**
primitives.sourceNote: pss-topic-control-valve-piping-arrangement (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook ch13, "Control Valve Piping," printed pp. 13-1–13-2) — confirmed prose-only, no figure in the source. The 5%/10%/15% capacity-reduction figures, the 10-20/5-10 pipe-diameter straight-run guideline, and the avoid-list (nozzle effect, close-coupled reduced block valves, sharp turns near the inlet) are transcribed exactly from the source's own described test data.
primitives.templateRationale: Axis 3 caution role — the orange warning treatment (Style Guide §4.4/§8.3), one consequence stated plainly with the failure itself bolded, matching this course's other caution slides (e.g. slides 138/139).

primitives.t: Applied correctly: an 8-inch line carrying a 6-inch valve, with the block valves left out at the full 8-inch line size rather than reduced down to the valve, 15 pipe diameters of straight run upstream and 8 diameters downstream, and no elbows within several diameters of the inlet — this reproduces the straight-line piping the valve's own capacity and characteristic data were established against, so the valve delivers what its sizing calculation promised. Move those same block valves in tight against a close-coupled reducer at the valve's own size, and the identical valve now sits in exactly the nozzle-effect, reduced-capacity arrangement the guidelines warn against — the hardware hasn't changed, only what surrounds it.
primitives.sourceNote: Grounded in pss-topic-control-valve-piping-arrangement's own straight-run guideline (10-20 diameters upstream, 5-10 downstream) and its close-coupled-reducer/block-valve-placement finding; the specific 8-inch/6-inch installation is an illustrative worked scenario applying those real guidelines, not a source-reported case.
primitives.templateRationale: The mechanism in a real situation, Axis 3's application treatment — a before/after installation scenario applying slide 161's guidelines directly, setting up the immediately-following Piping Arrangement Compliance Check activity (afterConcept: 2). No figure exists for this competency (confirmed prose-only); a plain scenario, not a decision table, since nothing here is being compared across multiple already-taught named items.

primitives.t: Two rules of thumb answer 'is this valve too small for its line' — and the source proves outright they don't agree. Rule 1: valve size not less than half the pipe size. Rule 2: valve size not less than two nominal sizes below the line size. Worked on the source's own 20-inch line: Rule 1 allows down to a 10-inch valve; Rule 2 allows down to a 16-inch valve. Either rule, followed on its own, gives adequate safety assurance — the question both are answering is pipe/valve strength, not flow capacity — but a valve sized to Rule 2's 16-inch floor is nowhere near Rule 1's 10-inch floor on the same line, so the two rules are not interchangeable and must not be assumed to agree.
primitives.sourceNote: pss-topic-line-size-vs-valve-size (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook ch13, "Line Size Versus Valve Size," printed p. 13-2) — confirmed prose-only, no figure in the source. The 20-inch/10-inch/16-inch comparison is the source's own worked example, transcribed exactly to demonstrate the two rules genuinely conflict rather than merely differ in derivation.
primitives.templateRationale: A genuine two-way this-vs-that — Rule 1 (half the pipe size) vs. Rule 2 (two nominal sizes below line size) — not a three-value case: the 20-inch/10-inch/16-inch figures are one worked instantiation of both rules against the same line, not a third rule, so the two-panel slide--role-contrast layout fits directly (panel A: Rule 1 worked to 10-inch; panel B: Rule 2 worked to 16-inch, both against the same 20-inch line so the disagreement reads side by side). No items array — sources is empty for this prose-only topic (items pairs to sources by id per curriculum-development.md), so the single t carries the full worked contrast instead.

primitives.t: Velocity limits gas and liquid service for different reasons entirely. Gas/vapor service has no velocity limitation at all except where noise is a concern — Fisher's own published ceilings are 0.3 Mach for Whisper Trim III and 0.5 Mach for Whisper Trim I. Liquid service's older velocity guidelines were built for top-and-bottom-guided valves, to head off guide wear, vertical instability ('buffeting'), body erosion, and noise; a cage-guided valve largely removes the need for them — the cage shields the plug from direct fluid impingement and guides it exactly where the pressure drop occurs, so it can run at full rated pressure drop without the guide-wear risk a top-and-bottom-guided valve carries, and a single-seated balanced trim minimizes the static and dynamic forces that cause buffeting in the first place. Counter-intuitive finding stated directly by the source: in clean fluid there is NO correlation between velocity and body erosion — virtually every reported erosion case traces to cavitation, flashing, wet-steam erosion, or abrasive fines, not velocity itself. Net rule: size on capacity requirements first; velocity-driven sizing is the exception, particularly for cage-guided valves.
primitives.sourceNote: pss-topic-velocity-limitations (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook ch13, "Velocity Limitations in Control Valves," printed pp. 13-2–13-3) — confirmed prose-only, no figure in the source. The 0.3/0.5 Mach Whisper Trim ceilings and the clean-fluid no-correlation-with-erosion finding are transcribed exactly from the source; the topic's own relatedTopics cross-reference cvh-topic-noise-generation-and-prediction (Mach-driven noise limits) and cvh-topic-cavitation/cvh-topic-flashing (the real trouble sources behind reported erosion), named here as background, not re-taught.
primitives.templateRationale: How the two service types differ mechanically is the default understand/mechanism treatment per Axis 3 — introduced before the culminating evaluation slide (165). Confirmed prose-only; no figure to overlay, so Stage 3 composes this as a textual/diagrammatic gas-vs-liquid mechanism panel rather than a photo or schematic overlay.

primitives.t: Checking a real installation runs both evaluations together, not either alone. Line-size check: apply both rules of thumb (valve ≥ half the pipe size; valve ≥ two nominal sizes below line size) to the stated line size and flag anything the selected valve size fails on either — remembering the two rules don't always agree, so 'fails one, passes the other' is a real outcome, not a contradiction to resolve away. Velocity check: for a gas/vapor service, compare the calculated Mach number against 0.3 (Whisper Trim III) or 0.5 (Whisper Trim I); for a liquid service, ask whether the valve is cage-guided — if it is, the historical guide-wear/buffeting/erosion concerns largely don't apply, and if it isn't, they do, and clean-fluid velocity alone still isn't grounds for an erosion limit. Worked example: an 18-inch line fitted with a 9-inch cage-guided valve in clean liquid service passes Rule 1 (half of 18 is 9) but fails Rule 2 (two sizes below 18-inch is 14-inch); because the valve is cage-guided, the liquid velocity concerns are not the deciding factor here — the line-size rule disagreement is the real open question, not an assumed erosion risk.
primitives.sourceNote: Grounded in pss-topic-line-size-vs-valve-size's own two rules of thumb and pss-topic-velocity-limitations' gas-Mach / liquid-guide-wear-and-cage-guided distinction, both confirmed prose-only (figures: [] in the registry). The 18-inch/9-inch worked installation is an illustrative scenario applying those real rules and limits together, not a source-reported case — it sets up the immediately-following Line-Size & Velocity Violation Audit activity (afterConcept: 5).
primitives.templateRationale: The culminating analyze-level application for this LO — a concrete installation run through both checks at once, Axis 3's application treatment. Not a decision table: this evaluates one installation against two independent criteria in sequence rather than comparing several already-taught named items side by side, so the plain scenario shape fits better than .slide--role-application:has(.tmpl-table).

reground.hook: Picture a garden hose rated for a strong, steady stream — but you've screwed a smaller fitting onto the end and added a couple of sharp bends right before the nozzle. The hose itself hasn't changed, but what comes out the end has, and it's tempting to blame the hose.
reground.bridge: A control valve is the hose in that picture. Piping arrangement — a reducer sized down to the valve, a block valve crowded in against it, an elbow too close to the inlet — can quietly rob a correctly sized valve of real capacity the same way that fitting and those bends rob the hose of its stream, even though the valve's own rating never changed. Line size and velocity are the companion question: is the pipe the valve sits in actually a fit for it, both in strength (can the pipe safely carry a valve this size) and in what's moving through it (is the flow inside the pipe within the limits that fluid and hardware can tolerate)?
reground.depth:
Piping arrangement measurably changes a control valve's real capacity independent of its nameplate rating. A close-coupled reducer sized down to the valve, with block valves matched to valve size, cuts a typical 2-inch valve's capacity by roughly 5%; the loss grows toward 10% as valve size increases at the same 2:1 ratio, and elbows added between the reducers and the valve can push it to 15%. Moving the block valves out to line size, clear of the reducers, removes most of the effect. The guidelines to avoid: a nozzle effect at the inlet (it alters the flow characteristic itself), close-coupled inlet block valves reduced from line size, and sharp turns close to the inlet — straight-line sections into and out of the valve should reproduce the piping the valve's own capacity/characteristic data were established against, generally 10-20 pipe diameters upstream and 5-10 diameters downstream. A required block-and-bypass arrangement is best placed with the control valve in a straight-through run, not a tortuous manifold built only for accessibility.

Line size versus valve size is fundamentally a strength question, not a flow-capacity question — is the valve strong enough relative to the pipe it sits in. Two rules of thumb apply and the source proves they genuinely disagree: Rule 1, valve size not less than half the pipe size; Rule 2, valve size not less than two nominal sizes below the line size. On the source's own 20-inch line, Rule 1 allows down to a 10-inch valve while Rule 2 allows down to a 16-inch valve — either rule alone gives adequate safety assurance, but they are not interchangeable.

Velocity limitations split along a different line entirely — gas versus liquid, for different physical reasons. Gas/vapor service has no velocity limitation except where noise is a concern: Fisher's published ceilings are 0.3 Mach for Whisper Trim III and 0.5 Mach for Whisper Trim I. Liquid service's older velocity guidelines were built for top-and-bottom-guided valves, against guide wear, vertical instability ('buffeting'), body erosion, and noise; a cage-guided valve largely eliminates the need for them, since the cage shields the plug from direct impingement and guides it exactly where the pressure drop occurs, allowing full rated pressure drop without premature guide failure, while a single-seated balanced trim minimizes the static and dynamic forces that cause buffeting. Counter-intuitively, in clean fluid there is no correlation between velocity and body erosion at all — real erosion cases trace to cavitation, flashing, wet-steam erosion, or abrasive fines, not velocity itself. Control valves should be sized on capacity requirements first; velocity-driven sizing is the exception, especially for cage-guided valves.

Evaluating a real installation runs the line-size and velocity checks together: apply both line-size rules and flag any case that fails either one (they can disagree, and that disagreement is itself the thing to catch, not resolve away), then separately check velocity against the Mach ceiling for a gas service or the guide-wear/buffeting/erosion exposure for a liquid service on a non-cage-guided valve.

modules.title: Welding Procedure & Commissioning Flush
modules.stakes: Skipping system flushing or installing sacrificial trim incorrectly is the single most common cause of premature trim failure complaints against a brand-new, correctly-sized valve.
modules.objective: Describe correct welding-procedure staging for a welded-end installation, and explain the purpose of system flushing and sacrificial trim.

primitives.t: A valve that was correctly selected, sized, and correctly piped can still fail within days of startup — not from a design flaw, but from what happens to it during welding and commissioning, before it ever sees real process fluid. Most power-service valves have buttweld or socket-weld ends, and welding those ends creates unusually high temperatures right at the valve that can damage trim; after welding, the slag and debris get cleared by a system flush, and that flush can damage trim of its own. Both events are staged around the valve, not performed by it — and both are avoidable failures once the staging is understood, which is exactly why premature trim-failure complaints against a brand-new, correctly-sized valve trace back here more than anywhere else.
primitives.sourceNote: pss-topic-welding-procedure-stages and pss-topic-system-flushing-and-sacrificial-trim (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook ch13, "Installation," printed p. 13-3, opening framing: "Two main areas of concern appear during valve installation: Welding procedures, System flushing... Welding procedures can create unusually high temperatures at the valve, and these temperatures may damage trim parts... The system flush may also damage trim parts.") — both confirmed prose-only (figures: [] in the registry), so this prime opens on that shared framing rather than a figure, matching the module's own stakes line.
primitives.templateRationale: Opens the module with the stakes/question framing before either mechanism is taught, per Axis 3's prime role — matches this course's other module-opening prime slides (e.g. slide 160). No figure exists for either competency (confirmed prose-only), so this uses the plain-tagline shape.

primitives.t: Because elastomeric and plastic trim parts can't tolerate any of these three heat stages, they have to come out — or the valve has to be disassembled — before welding starts. PWHT is the stage where that matters most even for parts that seem physically distant from the weld joint, since the roughly 1400°F is applied locally but conducts back through the whole body rather than staying confined to the joint.
primitives.sourceNote: pss-topic-welding-procedure-stages (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook ch13, "Installation — Welding Procedures," printed pp. 13-3–13-4) — confirmed prose-only, no figure in the source. The 300-500°F preheat/interpass range and the up-to-~1400°F PWHT figure are transcribed exactly from the source, not rounded further.
primitives.templateRationale: How the three welding stages work and what each risks is the default understand/mechanism treatment per Axis 3, sequenced before the PWHT-specific caution (169) — matches this course's other mechanism slots (e.g. slide 164). Confirmed prose-only; no figure to overlay, so Stage 3 composes this as a three-stage sequence panel rather than a schematic.

primitives.t: If post-weld heat treatment (PWHT) will be performed, remove all trim parts first — PWHT holds the welded area at temperatures up to roughly 1400°F for several hours, and even though the heat is applied locally, it conducts back into the valve body. The same caution applies during preheat and the welding pass itself whenever the joint temperature runs close to or above a part's own limit, since elastomeric and plastic parts (O-rings, seal rings, backup rings, packing rings, gaskets) have lower temperature limits than the surrounding metal. **When in doubt, remove the part — leaving elastomeric or plastic trim in place through PWHT, or through a preheat/interpass temperature it can't tolerate, damages trim that was never defective to begin with.**
primitives.sourceNote: pss-topic-welding-procedure-stages (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook ch13, "Installation — Welding Procedures," printed pp. 13-3–13-4) — transcribes the source's own general rule ("if PWHT is to be performed, all trim parts should be removed") and its preheat caution ("Caution should be used whenever the preheat temperature is close to or higher than the temperature limits for elastomeric or plastic parts in a valve. When in doubt, remove these components."). Confirmed prose-only, no figure in the source.
primitives.templateRationale: Axis 3 caution role — the orange warning treatment (Style Guide §4.4/§8.3), the failure itself bolded, matching this course's other caution slides (e.g. slide 161).

primitives.t: Flushing trim exists as sacrificial hardware specifically because both particulate scoring and chemical etching are cumulative, irreversible wear on precision sealing surfaces — running the real trim through a startup flush or a chemical clean would put non-refundable damage into expensive, precision-machined hardware before the valve ever regulates real process flow, which a cheap swap-in set avoids entirely.
primitives.sourceNote: pss-topic-system-flushing-and-sacrificial-trim (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook ch13, "Installation — System Flushing," printed pp. 13-3–13-4) — confirmed prose-only, no figure in the source. The sacrificial-parts list (cage/cage flange, seat ring, double-nutted stem, gaskets) is transcribed exactly from the source, not a generalized paraphrase.
primitives.templateRationale: Why flushing/chemical cleaning damages trim and how sacrificial flushing trim mitigates it is the default understand/mechanism treatment per Axis 3, sequenced before the reassembly caution (171) and mirroring the welding-mechanism slot (168) for the module's second competency. Confirmed prose-only; no figure to overlay.

primitives.t: Once a valve must be disassembled — to remove trim for welding/PWHT, or to install flushing trim — have a full extra set of gaskets and packing ready before reassembly. Gaskets should always be replaced when a valve has been disassembled, and packing should be replaced too: pulling the stem out of the packing box risks damaging packing that still looks reusable. **Reusing packing or gaskets can fail later as a leak, and the resulting damage can erode the gasket surface, the packing box bore, or the stem itself — turning a routine disassembly into a repeat failure.**
primitives.sourceNote: pss-topic-system-flushing-and-sacrificial-trim (Power & Severe Service Sourcebook ch13, "Installation — System Flushing," printed pp. 13-3–13-4) — transcribes the source's own reassembly recommendation ("Gaskets should always be replaced when the valve has been disassembled. It is recommended that the packing also be replaced due to potential damage from removing the valve stem from the packing box. Failure to replace these parts may lead to leaks and can result in erosion of the gasket surfaces, the packing box bore, or the valve stem."). Confirmed prose-only, no figure in the source.

reground.hook: Think of a brand-new car that gets its paint scratched and its radio wiring fried during the dealership prep work, before it's ever driven off the lot — the car itself was built right, but what happened to it after it left the factory and before the customer took the keys is what actually failed.
reground.bridge: A control valve can suffer exactly that kind of damage during its own installation: welding the pipe ends onto it, and then flushing the system clean before startup, both happen to the valve after it's already correctly selected, sized, and piped — and both can quietly ruin trim that was never defective, unless the crew doing the work knows when to pull the trim out and what to put in its place.
reground.depth:
Welding a buttweld or socket-weld valve end runs through three stages, each with its own trim risk. Preheating (piping-code-required, via pads or torch) reaches roughly 300-500°F depending on material and joint thickness — not damaging to most metal parts, but elastomeric/plastic parts (O-rings, seal rings, backup rings, packing rings, gaskets) can have lower limits; the packing box area is low-risk since the bonnet/body dissipate heat, but the body interior runs closer to the full preheat value. Welding's interpass temperature (the prior weld puddle's temperature when the pass returns to its starting point) must stay below a material-dependent maximum, typically the same 300-500°F band for chrome-moly/stainless steel, so the same caution applies.

Post-weld heat treating (PWHT) is the most severe stage: chrome-moly steel welding creates residual stresses that can crack the weld unless relieved by holding the area at up to roughly 1400°F for several hours; that heat conducts back into the valve body and can damage elastomeric/plastic parts, warp metal parts, and loosen shrink-fit or threaded connections — the general rule is to remove all trim parts before PWHT, and to remove any part elsewhere in the process whenever preheat or interpass temperature runs close to or above that part's own limit.

System flushing (water or steam, to clear weld slag and debris before startup) and chemical cleaning pose a separate risk: valves are flow restrictions, and drilled-hole/small-orifice trim (Whisper Trim, Cavitrol Trim, MicroFlat, standard drilled-hole trim) is especially exposed to plugging, plug-to-cage scoring, and seat nicking from solid particles, while chemical-cleaning solutions can etch seating/gasket surfaces if not neutralized or left standing. Fisher's mitigation for both is sacrificial 'flushing trim' — the cage or cage flange, the seat ring, a double-nutted stem sealing the bonnet stem hole, and gaskets — installed in place of the real trim so the fluid, particles, and cleaning solution pass through without touching the surfaces the valve will actually seal on in service; because so many different chemical-cleaning solutions exist, the real trim should simply never be exposed to one.

Whenever a valve is disassembled for either reason, gaskets and packing should always be replaced rather than reused — stem removal from the packing box can damage packing that still looks fine, and reused parts can fail later as a leak or erode the gasket surface, packing box bore, or stem itself.

modules.title: Emissions Scopes & Decarbonization Frameworks
modules.stakes: An engineer who can size a valve correctly but can't explain in Scope 1/2/3 terms why the Chapter 7 packing choice matters can't make the business case for the better option when it's actually needed.
modules.objective: Distinguish GHG emissions Scopes 1/2/3 and classify a valve-related emissions source into the correct scope, and explain how decarbonization pathways and a greening framework are typically structured at an industrial operator.

primitives.t: A packing system or an actuator choice you already know how to size correctly doesn't automatically count as 'sustainability content' on a customer's books — it only counts once you can say which of three emissions-accounting scopes it lands in. Most operators can report Scope 1 and Scope 2 with real confidence; Scope 3 is typically the largest single contributor to their total emissions and the one most haven't fully measured yet. Getting the scope right is what turns a correctly-selected valve into part of the business case for the better, costlier option — get it wrong, and the same hardware choice never shows up on the account it actually belongs on.

primitives.t: The scope a given emission falls into determines who's actually positioned to reduce it: a Scope 1 source, like gas-actuated valve instrumentation, is something the operating company directly controls and can act on immediately by swapping the hardware; Scope 2 depends on the grid's own generation mix; Scope 3 depends on suppliers and customers the company doesn't control at all — which is why Scope 1 is usually where a hardware decision has the most direct leverage.

primitives.t: Scope isn't a property of the hardware itself — it's relative to whose emissions inventory is counting it: the same replacement trim kit is the manufacturer's own Scope 1 (they made it) but the buyer's Scope 3 (an embedded upstream footprint), which is why the same physical valve can sit in a different scope bucket depending on which company's accounting you're standing in.

primitives.t: Decarbonization proceeds along two general pathways. Mitigation: deploying renewable resources and efficiency improvements to cut emissions at carbon-intensive industrial processes directly. CCUS — Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage: extracting point-source carbon emissions and sequestering them underground, with the potential to remove 90-99% of an industrial facility's carbon emissions; it's described as the only technology group that both reduces emissions in key sectors directly and removes CO2 already in the atmosphere. Energy efficiency sits behind both pathways as its own lever: only about one-third of the primary energy produced today actually performs its intended function — heating, cooling, moving something — the other two-thirds is lost to heat escape, braking, electrical line losses, and unoptimized processes, which is why efficiency improvement can move the needle before any capture technology is ever deployed.
primitives.sourceNote: cvh-topic-decarbonization-pathways (CVH §11.1-11.3, pp. 241-242) — the two-pathway split (mitigation vs. CCUS), the 90-99% CCUS removal figure, and the one-third/two-thirds energy-loss figure are all stated directly in the source prose, not inferred. No figure registered for this competency; Figures 11.2/11.3 are reserved for the module's closing application slide (178).
