Confirmed prose-only for this specific pathway distinction; Stage 3 composes this as a two-pathway mechanism panel.

primitives.t: A company's real sustainability program usually runs all three 'Greening' categories at once, not one alone. Greening OF: internal initiatives — a company's own actions to cut its own greenhouse-gas footprint (LED retrofits, automated lighting shutdown, compressed-air leak detection, tuned chilled-water scheduling) — plus engaging upstream suppliers to reduce emissions in what they supply. Greening BY: the products and services a company sells that help its customers decarbonize — control systems, software, electric actuation, environmental packing, valve condition monitoring — the category where control-valve hardware choices are themselves the sustainability offering. Greening WITH: industry-wide collaboration — forums, research-institution partnerships, multi-stakeholder alliances — on the premise that no single stakeholder (government, business, community, or academia) can manage the low-carbon transition alone.

reground.hook: Think about your own carbon footprint for a second. Driving your own car and burning your own gas is squarely your doing. The electricity your house pulls off the grid was generated by burning coal or gas somewhere else, at someone else's plant — indirect, but still traceable back to your meter. But the manufacturing of your phone, the fertilizer that grew your food, the freight that shipped your package — that emissions trail runs through hundreds of other companies' decisions before it ever reaches you, and almost nobody adds all of that up.
reground.bridge: That's exactly the Scope 1/2/3 accounting framework a company uses on itself, and it's the lens this module puts on a control valve. A packing gland leaking at the stem, or an instrument-air bleed, is the company's own direct emission — Scope 1, the equivalent of burning your own gas. An electric actuator drawing plant power is Scope 2 — indirect, purchased, like your home's electricity bill. And the replacement trim or actuator kit itself carries an upstream footprint before it ever reaches the customer's site — Scope 3, the hardest of the three to measure and, for most companies, the largest single piece of the total. Decarbonization pathways and the Greening OF/BY/WITH framework are how an operator organizes what to actually do about all three scopes — and the actuator and packing selections from Chapters 6 through 9 aren't incidental to that program, they're literally line items on it.
reground.depth:
The greenhouse gas protocol divides a company's footprint into three scopes by how directly the company controls the source. Scope 1 is direct: emissions from owned or controlled sources, including comfort heating and on-site industrial applications, and — in oil and gas specifically — natural gas vented or bled as valve-actuation and instrumentation motive force. Scope 2 is indirect-purchased-energy: emissions from generating the electricity a company buys, occurring at the point of generation (a coal or natural-gas plant) rather than at the company's own site. Scope 3 is indirect value-chain: all other indirect emissions, split into 15 named sub-categories (purchased goods and services, capital goods, fuel/energy-related activities not in Scope 1 or 2, upstream/downstream distribution, waste, business travel, employee commuting, upstream/downstream leased assets, processing/use/end-of-life of sold products, franchises, investments); industry-average figures put purchased goods/services at roughly 20-30% of total Scope 3, use of sold products at roughly 60-65%, and business travel plus employee commuting and logistics at roughly 2-3% each. Scope 3 is typically the largest single contributor to an organization's total emissions and the hardest to measure — many companies have reported Scope 1 and Scope 2 with confidence but have not fully measured Scope 3.

Applied to real valve-related sources: a packing gland's fugitive leak or a pneumatic positioner's continuous instrument-air bleed is Scope 1; an electric actuator's continuous draw on purchased grid power is Scope 2; a purchased replacement trim or actuator kit's own embedded manufacturing/materials/transportation footprint is Scope 3, on the customer's books, not the vendor's.

Decarbonization itself proceeds along two general pathways: mitigation (deploying renewable resources and efficiency improvements to cut emissions at carbon-intensive processes directly) and CCUS — Carbon Capture, Utilization and Storage (extracting point-source carbon emissions and sequestering them underground), which can remove 90-99% of an industrial facility's carbon emissions and is the only technology group that both reduces emissions in key sectors directly and removes CO2 already in the atmosphere. Energy efficiency is a lever behind both pathways: only about one-third of the primary energy produced today performs its intended function, with the remaining two-thirds lost to heat escape, braking, electrical line losses, and unoptimized processes.

A company's sustainability program typically runs three 'Greening' categories at once. Greening OF is internal — a company's own initiatives to cut its own footprint (LED retrofits, automated lighting shutdown, compressed-air leak detection, chilled-water scheduling) plus engaging upstream suppliers on their own emissions. Greening BY is what a company sells that helps its customers decarbonize — control systems, software, electric actuation, environmental packing, valve condition monitoring — the category where control-valve hardware is itself the sustainability offering. Greening WITH is industry-wide collaboration — forums, research partnerships, multi-stakeholder alliances — on the premise that no single stakeholder can manage the low-carbon transition alone.

The source's own five-category emerging-technology reference table (Hydrogen; Decarbonization/Carbon Capture; Alternative Fuel and Biochemical; Renewables; Electrification and Storage) names actuator electrification and fugitive-emissions reduction directly — placing this course's own Chapter 6 actuator-selection and Chapter 7 packing-selection content literally on that list. And a company's own ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance) reporting table places 'reducing greenhouse gas emissions' and 'emissions management' as named line items under its Environmental pillar — the pillar a packing or actuator hardware upgrade's real, measured emissions reduction actually reports into, which is what turns a correctly-selected, costlier packing or actuator option into a business case an engineer can actually make, not just a technically-correct answer nobody upstream can act on.

modules.title: Net-Zero Targets & the Valve's Contribution
modules.stakes: Closing the course without connecting packing/emissions selection to the operator's actual decarbonization target leaves the engineering disconnected from why it was funded.
modules.objective: Distinguish carbon-neutral from net-zero and explain typical net-zero target-setting, and explain how valve-related methane reduction contributes measurably to a decarbonization target.

primitives.t: You already made two hardware calls this course would call 'more sustainable' — an electric actuator over a gas-actuated one (Chapter 6), a lower-fugitive-emissions packing system (Chapter 7). Neither one, on its own, gets an operator to net-zero. A company can offset 100% of its reported emissions every single year and call itself carbon-neutral without ever having reduced what it actually emits. Before either hardware choice counts toward a real net-zero target, you need the distinction the source itself draws between the two claims — and what a target-setting process actually has to show to earn the word 'net-zero.'
primitives.sourceNote: cvh-topic-carbon-neutral-vs-net-zero and cvh-topic-net-zero-target-setting (CVH §§11.7, 11.12, pp. 244-245, 247-248) — the offsetting-permitted-vs-nothing-emitted distinction and the real target-setting bar (baseline year, SBTi, ≥90% absolute reduction) are both stated directly in source prose. No figure registered for either competency at this slot; this prime opens on the source's own conflated-terms framing, tied back to this course's own Chapter 6/7 hardware, matching this module's stakes line and the m1 prime's precedent (slide 173).

primitives.t: Carbon-neutral: any CO2 a company's activities release into the atmosphere is balanced by an equivalent amount being removed — offsetting is permitted, and expected. Net-zero: the activity releases net-zero carbon emissions in the first place — no carbon needs to be captured or offset, because none was emitted to begin with. Same stated goal, a balanced footprint; different mechanism, balancing after the fact versus not emitting at all. The source states the equivalence plainly: 'Total Net-Zero = Net Zero.'
primitives.sourceNote: cvh-topic-carbon-neutral-vs-net-zero (CVH §11.12 Commonly Used Terms in Sustainability, pp. 247-248) — verbatim source definitions, not a general-knowledge restatement; the source's own short glossary section. No figure registered for this competency.

No figure to overlay; each panel is a plain definition-and-mechanism pair.

primitives.t: Because Scope 1 sources are the most directly controllable (see the previous module), a net-zero design plan tends to prioritize eliminating them outright — replacing gas-actuated instrumentation with electric or low-bleed pneumatic alternatives, for instance — before leaning on offsetting, which this standard only permits for whatever residual can't otherwise be abated, never as a substitute for the reduction itself.

The 90% absolute-reduction threshold is stated directly in the source ('A robust net-zero design requires the absolute reduction of greenhouse gas emissions by at least 90%...'), not inferred from general climate-policy knowledge. No figure registered for this competency.

primitives.t: Both sources from the prior slide have named fixes, and they're the same hardware decisions this course already taught. Replacing a natural-gas-actuated valve with an electric actuator (Chapter 6) — often sold as a retrofit kit — delivers a dramatic reduction in methane venting. Low-bleed pneumatic instrumentation alternatives cut the continuous-bleed source without a full electrification retrofit. Very-low-power electric alternatives can run on a small solar system's own output, reaching a remote station with no grid connection at all. And improved packing designs — Chapter 7's own selection criteria — close the seal-leak path in chemical service. None of these four is a new competency; they're this course's actuator and packing selections, read as decarbonization levers.

That closes this course on itself. Sizing the valve, selecting the trim, calculating the actuator's force or torque, choosing the packing system — none of that was ever separate from this. They are the line items that make an operator's net-zero target something an engineer can actually deliver, not a number Corporate reports with nothing behind it.

reground.hook: Say you promise to stop littering by picking up twice as much trash as you drop. That's a fine promise, and it leaves the world no worse off on net — but you're still dropping trash every day, and the picking-up has to keep happening forever, by you or by someone you pay to do it. Now say you just... stop dropping it. Nothing to pick up, nothing to keep paying for, nothing that depends on the cleanup crew showing up next year too.
reground.bridge: That's the entire difference between carbon-neutral and net-zero — offsetting the mess after the fact versus never making it. A real net-zero target holds itself to that second, harder standard: a measured baseline, a science-based 90%-or-better actual reduction, offsets reserved only for the crumb that's left, checked every year so the promise doesn't quietly slide back into 'we bought enough offsets.' And the two real methane sources this module names — gas vented on every valve stroke at a remote station, packing leaking at the stem in chemical service — aren't abstract accounting categories. They're exactly the hardware this course spent nine chapters teaching you to select and size correctly.
reground.depth:
Carbon-neutral means any CO2 a company releases is balanced by an equivalent amount removed elsewhere — offsetting permitted, and normal. Net-zero means the activity releases net-zero emissions in the first place; nothing is emitted that then needs to be captured or offset. Same stated goal, a balanced footprint; different mechanism, and the source states the harder one plainly: 'Total Net-Zero = Net Zero.'

A real net-zero target is set by first analyzing a company's total emissions across Scopes 1, 2, and 3 to fix a baseline year, then setting a target year to reach net-zero from it, aligned to the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) Net-Zero Standard; a robust design requires at least a 90% absolute reduction in greenhouse-gas emissions from that baseline, with high-quality offsetting permitted only for whatever residual can't otherwise be abated, monitored yearly rather than declared once.

Against that bar, two real, hardware-traceable methane sources matter directly to this course's own content: remote oil-and-gas production and pipelines often run valve actuation and instrumentation on natural gas itself, venting methane with every stroke or bleeding it continuously; and in chemical service, control valves and pumps emit through packing and seal leaks — the same fugitive-emissions path Chapter 7's packing selection already exists to control. Both sources have named, hardware-level fixes that are not new competencies but this course's own: an electric actuator retrofit in place of gas actuation (Chapter 6), low-bleed pneumatic instrumentation, very-low-power alternatives that run on a small solar system with no grid connection required, and improved packing designs (Chapter 7) closing the seal-leak path.

And the reason an engineer gets to make this case at all, not just a sustainability office: in real cases, the savings from reduced methane loss, reduced regulatory testing burden, and the additional gas that stays saleable instead of venting are enough by themselves to pay for the upgrade. That is why decarbonization content sits inside an engineering selection-and-sizing course rather than a separate corporate-responsibility module — every Cv calculation, trim selection, actuator force/torque sizing, and packing specification this course taught is, read this way, a line item on an operator's actual net-zero target, not adjacent to it. Getting the engineering right is what makes the decarbonization claim real instead of an offset purchased to paper over hardware nobody actually changed.

activities.description: Given a real remote-pipeline scenario (a natural-gas-actuated valve venting methane on every stroke at an unmanned station, and a chemical-service valve with a known fugitive leak at the packing gland), students name which specific hardware change from this course's own Chapter 6 actuator-selection and Chapter 7 packing-selection content addresses each source, which emissions scope it falls under, and how the resulting savings (reduced methane loss, reduced regulatory testing burden, additional saleable gas) would be presented to the customer as the business case for the change — the course's own closing synthesis, tying the engineering already taught back to why it was funded.
